bullets: The new study “Beyond Leaderboard Ranks” reframes software-agent selection as an accuracy, cost, and uncertainty decision. Across 58,197 agent runs on seven benchmarks, 27 of 35 adjacent options on the accuracy-cost front had statistically unresolved accuracy differences, meaning their apparent ordering did not reliably distinguish performance. [E006] Why it matters: If you are buying or evaluating coding agents under a budget, this means a leaderboard winner may not justify its higher operating cost. Selection reports need confidence intervals and the cost of running enough evaluations to resolve meaningful differences, rather than rank and average accuracy alone. Evidence: E006. High confidence.

EVIDENT is a new benchmark that tests whether a web-browsing agent’s answer is supported by evidence it actually observed, rather than merely checking task completion. Its 220 English and Korean tasks include human-curated records of what evidence must be verified, and separate metrics score completion, evidence use, and their combination. [E012] Why it matters: If you are selecting a graphical user interface agent for research, compliance, or fact-finding, this design can reveal agents that reach plausible answers without inspecting the necessary page content. It changes the evaluation target from successful output alone to an auditable connection between navigation and answer. Evidence: E012. High confidence.

Benchmark Factory is a new system for constructing coding-agent benchmarks from an organization’s own completed code changes. An automated agent writes sourcing queries, tests candidate tasks with models of known relative strength, diagnoses failures, and revises the benchmark until it meets quality checks that do not require a human label for every task; humans remain at checkpoints. [E007] Why it matters: If public coding benchmarks do not resemble your repositories, this offers a concrete alternative to fully manual internal benchmark creation. The decision becomes whether its automated quality checks and sampled human review provide enough assurance for model selection in your own development environment. Evidence: E007. Medium confidence.

DetourBench, newly discovered in today’s feed, evaluates not only whether an interactive agent succeeds but how many actions it takes relative to an exactly computed minimum. It constrains each task to a finite environment where the shortest possible evidence-gathering route can be calculated. [E105] Why it matters: If agent actions carry latency, monetary cost, or exposure to sensitive data, endpoint success can hide wasteful exploration. This benchmark design lets evaluators distinguish direct evidence collection from broad, unnecessary browsing and identify agents that stop just short of the required evidence. Evidence: E105. Medium confidence.

EconSafeBench is a new safety benchmark with 828 cases across five executable economic scenarios. It matches three sources of pressure—explicit user instructions, other actors, and the agent’s own performance objective—and includes interactions lasting 30 periods rather than only static prompts. [E013] Why it matters: If you are evaluating agents that make financial or resource-allocation decisions, this means safety testing can include harmful behavior that emerges while pursuing a seemingly legitimate objective over time. That is a different product decision signal from refusal tests based only on explicitly unsafe user requests. Evidence: E013. High confidence.

Accelerate Bench is a new application-level optimization benchmark containing 32 central processing unit tasks adapted from scientific software and computing competitions. Each task specifies correctness requirements, timing boundaries, workload, and permitted edits; agents can iterate against public tests, while a separate verifier scores final submissions. [E010] Why it matters: If you are choosing a coding agent for performance engineering, this evaluates the full model-and-tool-wrapper combination on coordinated program changes, not isolated code snippets. The independent final verifier also reduces the risk that an agent improves measured speed by changing the required computation. Evidence: E010. High confidence.
bullets_zh: 新研究“Beyond Leaderboard Ranks”将软件智能体选型重新界定为一项需要权衡准确率、成本和不确定性的决策。在七个基准上的 58,197 次智能体运行中，准确率-成本前沿上 35 个相邻选项里有 27 个的准确率差异在统计上无法判定，这意味着它们表面上的排序无法可靠地区分性能。[E006] Why it matters: 如果你要在预算约束下采购或评估编码智能体，这意味着排行榜冠军可能并不足以证明其更高的运行成本是合理的。选型报告需要提供置信区间，以及为辨明有意义的差异而开展足够多次评估所需的成本，而不能只提供排名和平均准确率。Evidence: E006. High confidence.

EVIDENT 是一个新基准，用于测试网页浏览智能体给出的答案是否得到其实际观察到的证据支持，而不只是检查任务是否完成。其 220 项英语和韩语任务包含由人工整理的记录，明确必须验证哪些证据，并通过不同指标分别评估任务完成情况、证据使用情况及二者的综合表现。[E012] Why it matters: 如果你正在为研究、合规或事实核查选择图形用户界面智能体，这种设计可以识别出那些未检查必要页面内容却得出貌似合理答案的智能体。它将评估目标从仅关注输出是否成功，转变为关注导航过程与答案之间是否存在可审计的联系。Evidence: E012. High confidence.

Benchmark Factory 是一个新系统，可利用组织自身已完成的代码变更来构建编码智能体基准。自动化智能体会编写数据搜集查询，使用相对能力已知的模型测试候选任务，诊断失败原因，并持续修订基准，直至其通过无需为每项任务提供人工标签的质量检查；人工仍会参与关键检查点。[E007] Why it matters: 如果公共编码基准与你的代码仓库并不相似，这为完全依赖人工创建内部基准提供了一个具体替代方案。决策焦点将转变为：其自动化质量检查和抽样人工审核，能否为你在自身开发环境中选择模型提供充分保障。Evidence: E007. Medium confidence.

今天的信息流中新发现的 DetourBench 不仅评估交互式智能体能否成功，还会评估其实际操作次数相对于精确计算出的最少操作次数有多少。它将每项任务限制在有限环境中，从而可以计算出收集所需证据的最短可行路径。[E105] Why it matters: 如果智能体操作会带来延迟、金钱成本或敏感数据暴露风险，仅看最终是否成功可能会掩盖低效探索。这种基准设计让评估者能够区分直接的证据收集与大范围、不必要的浏览，并识别那些在即将获得所需证据时停止的智能体。Evidence: E105. Medium confidence.

EconSafeBench 是一个新的安全基准，包含分布在五个可执行经济场景中的 828 个案例。它结合了三类压力来源——明确的用户指令、其他参与者以及智能体自身的绩效目标——并纳入持续 30 个周期的交互，而不是只使用静态提示词。[E013] Why it matters: 如果你正在评估负责金融或资源分配决策的智能体，这意味着安全测试可以涵盖这样一种有害行为：智能体在长期追求看似正当的目标时逐渐表现出的有害行为。与仅基于明确不安全用户请求的拒绝测试相比，这提供了不同的产品决策信号。Evidence: E013. High confidence.

Accelerate Bench 是一个新的应用级优化基准，包含从科学软件和计算竞赛改编而来的 32 项中央处理器任务。每项任务都规定了正确性要求、计时边界、工作负载和允许的修改；智能体可以依据公开测试反复迭代，另有独立验证器对最终提交结果评分。[E010] Why it matters: 如果你要为性能工程选择编码智能体，该基准评估的是模型与工具封装的完整组合在协同程序变更方面的表现，而不是孤立的代码片段。独立的最终验证器也降低了智能体通过改变规定计算内容来提升实测速度的风险。Evidence: E010. High confidence.

authors: Xunkai Li, Kairui Yang, Jiaxi Li, Yuecong Mao, Zekai Chen, Xinle Zhang, Rong-Hua Li, Guoren Wang
evidence_items.summary: Constructing multi-agent system (MAS) applications across domains requires translating diverse requirements into executable systems, involving task decomposition, agent and tool selection, and execution organization. Existing studies have explored individual aspects of MAS construction, including agent generation, architecture design, workflow generation, and component selection. However, these methods are often developed and evaluated independently, using different task specifications, component resources, and execution settings. This makes it difficult to compare their construction capabilities or determine how they can be applied to different domains. To address this problem, we propose OpenMAS-GApp, a One-for-All benchmark for MAS application construction across diverse domains. It standardizes task inputs, component resources, construction interfaces, and execution environments to support MAS construction under consistent conditions. Within OpenMAS-GApp, we provide Graph Harness as a reference construction method that derives task dependencies, selects compatible agents and tools, and organizes their interactions into executable graphs. We evaluate construction methods across 19 benchmark datasets under 20 evaluation settings spanning four application types and four professional domains.
evidence_items.title: OpenMAS-GApp: A Comprehensive Benchmark for Domain-Adaptive Multi-Agent Application Construction

organizations: Iowa State University
evidence_items.summary: Overview MLIRBench: A Benchmark and Dataset for Compiler and Hardware-Aware Reasoning is a research benchmark and reproducibility framework designed to evaluate the ability of large language models (LLMs) to reason about program semantics, compiler transformations, and execution behavior in the Multi-Level Intermediate Representation (MLIR). This release provides the MLIRBench codebase, benchmark dataset, experimental artifacts, and reproducibility infrastructure accompanying the paper accepted at the 2027 IEEE/ACM International Symposium on Code Generation and Optimization (CGO 2027). The benchmark consists of 1,768 original–mutated MLIR program pairs, derived from 40 curated PyTorch seed programs, including 888 linalg pairs and 880 torch pairs across five mutation difficulty levels (L1–L5). MLIRBench evaluates nine language models, producing 15,912 model reasoning records and 15,907 judged evaluation records. Release Contents This software and dataset release provides the components required to inspect, analyze, and reproduce the archived MLIRBench experiments. 1. Benchmark Dataset The dataset includes nine complementary views: Core: Original and mutated MLIR programs with semantic annotations. Master: Consolidated program, mutation, and validation metadata. Reasoning: Model-generated predictions and semantic explanations. Evaluation: Judged predictions, verdicts, and evaluation scores. Errors: Per-model error-related records. Model Arena: Model comparison and evaluation information. Performance: Program-pair runtime measurements where available. Difficulty: Mutation difficulty and aggregated evaluation information. Mutation Provenance: Transformation requirements and validation provenance. The dataset views are distributed in JSONL and CSV formats, accompanied by schema documentation, integrity checksums, and licensing information. 2.
evidence_items.title: Dataset  Open MLIRBench - A Benchmark and Dataset for Compiler and Hardware-Aware Reasoning

evidence_items.summary: NeurIPS accepted 1,898 papers in 2020 and 9,111 in 2026. At that volume, reading the proceedings is no longer how researchers learn the shape of the field. We present Illustrated NeurIPS, an open dataset and browser-based map of all 30,225 papers accepted to NeurIPS from 2020 to 2026. Each paper is embedded from its title and abstract, placed on a two-dimensional map, and assigned to one of 285 fine topics nested in 30 areas, each with a short name and one-sentence description. We link 21,946 papers (72.6%) to their arXiv records, attach citation counts to 26,172, and add 1,035 highly cited "landmark" papers from other venues to the topics they belong to. Against NeurIPS's own subject-area labels, our two-stage clustering (k-means on UMAP features) agrees better than k-means on the raw embeddings (adjusted Rand index 0.086 vs. 0.065; paired-bootstrap 95% interval of the gain [0.018, 0.023]) and much better than TF-IDF clustering (0.056). Title-only search over the deployed embeddings retrieves the correct paper first 83.2% of the time among 26,632 abstracts (MRR 0.876, vs. 0.761 for TF-IDF). The map shows, for example, that LLM agent benchmarks and RL with verifiable rewards went from no NeurIPS papers in 2020–21 to 1.5% and 1.1% of 2025–26 papers, while generative adversarial networks fell from 1.0% to 0.01%. The site, data and code are public. Interactive map: https://vincentychu.com/neurips/ . Code and evaluation: github.com/vinceychu/vincent-chu-website (scripts/neurips/, paper/).
evidence_items.title: Illustrated NeurIPS: A Navigable Map of 30,225 NeurIPS Papers (2020–2026) with Linked arXiv Records, Citations and Landmark Papers

evidence_items.summary: TrustFire-X: Dataset Description This dataset accompanies the TrustFire-X research framework developed for quality-aware spatiotemporal prediction of satellite-detected thermal anomalies in Türkiye and for evaluating model transferability to previously unsampled geographical regions. The dataset integrates satellite-derived thermal activity observations, meteorological variables, vegetation indicators, land-cover characteristics, topographical information, and historical fire-related features. The primary research panel contains 102,305 grid-cell–week observations collected over 2018–2026 from 230 sampled geographical cells at an approximately 35 km spatial resolution. The modelling framework uses 63 predictive features, including original environmental variables and derived temporal and spatial indicators. An additional geographical transfer evaluation contains 2,737 observations from 54 previously unsampled cells in northwestern Iran. This evaluation was conducted using frozen model configurations without retraining on the new geographical samples. The repository provides curated research data, feature documentation, preprocessing and analysis code, trained model files, experimental results, statistical evaluation outputs, and reproducibility information. The predictive experiments include gradient-boosting approaches based on XGBoost and CatBoost, with evaluation using area under the precision–recall curve (AUPRC), area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC), probability calibration, bootstrap confidence intervals, and operational alert-budget measures. Scope and limitations: The dataset represents sampled grid-cell–week observations rather than a complete national wildfire-event inventory. Satellite thermal-anomaly detections are not equivalent to independently verified wildfire incidents. The geographical transfer experiment does not establish full operational validation or confirmed wildfire-event forecasting performance.
evidence_items.title: TrustFire-X: A Multisource Spatiotemporal Pilot Dataset and Model Benchmark for Satellite Thermal-Anomaly Prediction in Türkiye (2018–2026)

evidence_items.summary: Existing autonomous driving datasets and benchmarks provide extensive resources for routine driving, yet real-world data covering safety-critical scenarios and extreme environmental conditions remain limited. To address this gap, we present ExtremeDrive, a real-world dataset and benchmark covering emergency maneuvers, complex traffic interactions, and adverse conditions such as slippery or snow-covered roads, alongside routine driving. The dataset comprises 589 driving scenes curated from a larger pool of real-world driving recordings, with calibrated and aligned multisensor data and reviewed annotations of road structure and traffic participants. We further establish a benchmark to evaluate planned trajectories through simulated vehicle execution, measuring safety-related metrics and driving performance. Experiments at equal training set sizes show that incorporating critical driving data reduces trajectory prediction errors and improves mean critical-success rates in critical scenarios. ExtremeDrive provides a unified resource for learning and evaluating autonomous driving in safety-critical scenarios and extreme environmental conditions.
evidence_items.title: ExtremeDrive: A Real-World Dataset and Benchmark for Critical Driving

evidence_items.summary: As new attack categories emerge, network intrusion detection models need to be updated; however, when fine-tuned sequentially on new classes, previous classes are forgotten, resulting in catastrophic for- getting. The three public datasets we use are UNSW-NB15, ToN-IoT and CIC-IDS2017, and for these datasets, our class-incremental intrusion detection system is built using a CNN with one-dimensional (1D) archi- tecture trained over nine sequential tasks, each of which introduces one attack category. We evaluate sequential fine-tuning without any buffe compared to Elastic Weight Consolidation (EWC) and Learning without Forgetting (LwF), both of which include a class-size-adaptive rehearsal buffer of 20% of all previous classes (from 20 to 300 samples). The hyper-parameters were selected using UNSW-NB15 and fixed for the other two datasets. On UNSW-NB15, replay improves the final accuracy of both regularisers to 73.6% (EWC) and 71.1% (LwF) compared to about 32% (no improvement over fine-tuning). LwF with replay achieves 46.1% and 91.6% final accuracy for the two frozen-configuration datasets (ToN-IoT, CIC-IDS2017) while EWC with replay achieves 23.7% and 61.9%. In order to avoid this, EWC was therefore tuned on one dataset and the other two data sets were used as test sets. It is also demonstrated that the common forgetting measure can be misleading for a model which does not learn the old classes. As the fine-tuning baseline was not re- played and all the results were based on a single seed, it is not claimed hat the regularisers provide any extra support over replay alone.
evidence_items.title: Replay-Augmented Regularisation for Class-Incremental Network Intrusion Detection: A Three-Dataset Evaluation of EWC and LwF

evidence_items.summary: Teams that adopt LLM agents for issue resolution must decide which agent to pay for, and how much to spend finding out. Leaderboard ranks give weak evidence for this decision. Accuracy differences may be statistically unresolved, reported costs may be inconsistent, and evaluating candidate agents can itself be expensive. We investigate budget-constrained agent selection using 58,197 run--task records extracted from the Holistic Agent Leaderboard (HAL), focusing on SWE-bench and six additional benchmarks. Across seven benchmarks, 27 of 35 steps along the accuracy--cost Pareto frontiers are statistically unresolved. On SWE-bench, a run costing $34.16 trails the $170.78 leader by 14.6 percentage points, but the available tasks cannot statistically distinguish their accuracy. Reported costs also differ from standardized token-based estimates by up to 11.7x, while selective task evaluation can bias estimates of full-benchmark execution cost. We therefore compare evaluation strategies under explicit evaluation budgets and deployment-cost caps. Under advance knowledge of task costs, successive halving reaches our uncertainty-aware selection target on SWE-bench using 6.6% of exhaustive evaluation spend, achieving the lowest cost on six of seven benchmarks and tying on the seventh. Its advantage narrows when task costs are unknown before execution or exact-best selection is required. Our findings motivate decision-oriented agent evaluation that accounts for accuracy uncertainty, validates execution costs, and compares complex selection methods against simple adaptive allocation.
evidence_items.title: Beyond Leaderboard Ranks: Selecting Software Engineering Agents Under Budget Constraints

evidence_items.summary: Teams deploying coding agents need benchmarks built from their own code, but curating and validating them by hand is resource intensive, and an unvalidated benchmark can mislead silently. We present Benchmark Factory, an autonomous meta-agent loop with human checkpoints: an LLM agent writes sourcing queries over landed production code changes, runs models of known relative strength on each candidate, diagnoses why a candidate fails, and repairs it by editing its queries, prompts, and configuration until it clears quality anchors that need no per-task human labels. We used Benchmark Factory to build benchmarks for five developer cohorts at our organization. Engineering raters scored a 5% sample 2.3 for task quality and 2.6 for grader verdicts on a 1-to-3 scale. On configurations never used to build them, the benchmarks ranked Claude Opus~4.7 at high reasoning effort above low effort (60.6% vs. 54.4% of tasks passed, $p=0.002$) and GPT-5.5 above GPT-5.4 (65.8% vs. 60.5%, $p=0.004$); 9 of the 10 per-cohort comparisons pointed the same way. A deliberately trivial benchmark failed the anchors; five broken graders failed them, even under a relaxed rule fixed in advance that the real grader passes; and with model labels shuffled so that no true ordering existed, random redraws of a candidate passed in at most 1.4% of simulations. The anchors are necessary, not sufficient, conditions for a valid benchmark, designed to focus human review on what the loop cannot repair.
evidence_items.title: Benchmark Factory: Agentic Benchmark Creation via Dataset Curation and Label-Free Quality Anchors

evidence_items.summary: Despite their success in general question answering, large language models (LLMs) struggle with hallucinations and inaccurate reasoning in scientific domains. A major challenge stems from experimental data, which are often stored in external sources like supplementary materials and domain-specific databases. These tables are large, heterogeneous, and semantically complex, making them difficult for LLMs to interpret. While external tools show promise, current benchmarks fail to assess LLMs’ ability to navigate this data-particularly in locating relevant tables, retrieving key columns, interpreting experimental conditions, and invoking tools. To address this gap, we introduce CataTQA, a new benchmark for Catalytic materials Table Question and Answering. CataTQA features an automated dataset framework and four auxiliary tools. We evaluate tool-enhanced LLMs across five dimensions: table location, column retrieval, condition analysis, tool calling, and question answering, identifying their strengths and weaknesses.
evidence_items.title: CataTQA:A Benchmark for Tool-Augmented LLM Question Answering over Heterogeneous Catalysis Tables.

rationale: Matched: agents~benchmarking, benchmark, dataset, evaluat, training data
evidence_items.summary: Persistent spatial understanding is essential for embodied agents to operate reliably in environments they repeatedly encounter. It requires recognizing revisited places despite viewpoint changes, distinguishing them from similar-looking rooms, and updating memories as environments change. Yet existing evaluations often leave physical place identity across separated visits implicit. We introduce ReSpaceBench, a benchmark comprising 3,244 questions across 590 synthetic and real-home scenes, organized into 9 tasks spanning room association, persistent state tracking, and downstream reasoning. Controlled walkthroughs define visits by physical room entry and deliberately include same-type room distractors and cross-session object changes. Our evaluation of 32 models and 3 agentic video-understanding frameworks reveals substantial limitations: the strongest evaluated zero-shot model achieves 50.5% overall accuracy and 52.2% on a 450-question subset, compared with 90.1% for human annotators. The evaluated agentic frameworks offer no overall improvement over direct inference with the same base model. Analysis of agent execution traces reveals evidence omissions and incorrect cross-visit room associations as major failure modes, suggesting that iterative evidence seeking alone does not ensure consistent spatial memory. Further analyses expose a gap between recognizing familiar rooms and identifying the correct visited room, while annotation-guided sampling highlights the importance of preserving intervening visits and transitions. We also provide RS-30K, a separate training dataset from synthetic sources with no template, scene, route, or video overlap with the benchmark. Fine-tuning Qwen3-VL-8B raises overall accuracy from 35.5% to 60.4%, with the largest gains in association and improvements extending to real-life scenes.

evidence_items.summary: Application optimization requires coding agents to discover useful changes and coordinate them across a complete program while preserving the required computation. We introduce Accelerate Bench, a benchmark of 32 CPU optimization tasks adapted from scientific applications and supercomputing competitions. Each task provides a working program and specifies the workload, correctness requirements, timing boundaries, and permitted edits, leaving agents to choose where and how to optimize. Public testing supports iterative development, and a separate verifier scores the final submission. On benchmark version 1.1, we evaluate 16 coding agents, each pairing a model with a harness. Their Score@1 ranges from 25.5% to 67.4%. Most of their programs are correct, and the size of the speedup separates them: the two leading agents are at least 2x faster on 22 or more of the 32 tasks, while the other fourteen reach 2x on 8 to 17 and leave 125 of their 412 correct outcomes below 1.25x. Controlled replays show why coordination across an application matters: identical source code runs between 0.29x and 2.12x depending only on build and runtime settings, and one code change is worth 1.01x or 6.4x depending on another. Accelerate Bench pairs executable workloads with agents' programs and trajectories to evaluate both their gains and the process behind them.
evidence_items.title: Accelerate Bench: Evaluating Agents for Application-Level Program Optimization

authors: Hongbo Zhang, Liuyang Song, Hang Zhou, Xinchen Liu, Wei He, Kai Han, Yunhe Wang
evidence_items.summary: AI agents are commonly used for everyday information retrieval and coding. We ask whether they can also interpret human requests and turn them into complete videos. We introduce VAHBench, a benchmark that tests this ability through five short-drama briefs specifying story, characters, dialogue and duration. Agents plan and carry out production using shared generation tools. Evaluation combines video completeness and basic quality with checks of production reliability and reporting accuracy. Across 240 runs covering 48 configurations of general-purpose and video-specific agents, higher quality scores do not necessarily mean more complete delivery. Missing episodes, repeated footage and static filler reveal gaps between producing a video file and fulfilling the brief. Added composition tools help some agents but do not consistently improve performance. VAHBench measures how well agents translate user intent into finished video content and helps identify where that process breaks down.
evidence_items.title: VAHBench: A Harness Benchmark for Agentic Long-Video Generation

authors: Yerin Nam, Minkyung Cho, MinKyu Kim, SeungWoo Song, Hangyeol Yoo, Jihyo Kim, KyungTae Lim
evidence_items.summary: GUI agents are increasingly evaluated by whether they complete web tasks, but surface success can hide a critical failure: the final answer may not be supported by evidence observed during navigation. We introduce EVIDENT, an evidence-driven benchmark for evaluating whether GUI agents ground their decisions in observable web evidence. EVIDENT contains 220 real-world English and Korean tasks spanning semantic grounding, contextual inference, and visual grounding, each paired with human-curated evidence metadata specifying what must be verified. We further separate surface task completion from evidence-grounded success using three metrics: TSR, ESR, and GSR, which respectively measure outcome success, required evidence observation, and claim-level evidence support. Experiments on commercial and open-source GUI agents reveal substantial gaps between surface success and evidence-grounded success, especially in contextual and visual tasks. These results show that current evaluations can overestimate agent reliability and highlight the need to assess not only whether agents answer, but whether they verify.
evidence_items.title: EVIDENT: Evaluating Evidence Grounding in GUI Agents

authors: Yuzhu Ling, Jiale Han, Benyou Wang
evidence_items.summary: As LLM agents become increasingly capable of making consequential economic decisions, their safety under economic pressures remains poorly understood. We introduce EconSafeBench, the first benchmark for systematically evaluating the safety of LLM agents in executable economic environments. EconSafeBench contains 828 cases across five economic scenarios and four categories of safety violations. A key design is the matched evaluation of three sources of safety pressure, including explicit user requests, pressure from other actors, and pressure arising from the agent's own pursuit of a performance objective. We further evaluate safety at both static and dynamic scales through 30-period interactions with persistent memory and matched controls. Across eight LLMs, all evaluated models exhibit safety violations on the static benchmark, with overall violation rates ranging from 8.5% to 40.6%. We further find that violations can occur even without an explicit unsafe request, and that initially compliant agents may begin to violate as performance pressure increases over time. These findings highlight the need for stronger safety alignment and rigorous evaluation before LLM agents are deployed in high-stakes economic environments.
evidence_items.title: When Helpful Agents Cause Financial Harm: Evaluating LLM Agent Safety in Executable Economic Worlds

evidence_items.summary: Patient recruitment remains a major barrier in clinical trials, as identifying eligible participants often requires manual screening of complex health records, contributing significantly to trial delays and increased costs. While Large Language Models (LLMs) offer potential to automate this process, existing public datasets are overly simplistic in their patient representation: they pair full criterion lists with single-paragraph synthetic summaries, failing to capture the longitudinal complexity of real clinical records. We introduce MIMIC-CTRL-2026, a dataset of 800 manually labeled patient-criterion pairs grounded in real-world longitudinal EHR data from MIMIC-IV, annotated by clinically trained experts. Each instance pairs one eligibility criterion with a full patient record spanning multiple discharge notes, radiology reports, lab values, and medication histories. While simple prompting achieves a Cohen's Kappa, κ = 0.84 on existing simplified benchmarks, it collapses to κ = 0.06 on our dataset, revealing a substantial benchmark-difficulty gap between simplified and real-world clinical evaluation. Lastly, we present a framework combining structured pre-processing with a clinician-validated expanded prompt that substantially outperforms naive baselines without any model fine-tuning, establishing a realistic benchmark for automated clinical trial screening on real EHR data.
evidence_items.title: MIMIC-CTRL-2026: A Realistic Clinical Trial Dataset to Benchmark LLM Performance

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Language models are revolutionizing the biochemistry domain, assisting scientists in drug design and chemical synthesis with high efficiency. Yet current approaches struggle between small language models prone to hallucination and limited knowledge retention, and large cloud-based language models plagued by privacy risks and high inference costs. To bridge this gap, we introduce ChemCRAFT, a novel framework leveraging agentic reinforcement learning to decouple chemical reasoning from knowledge storage. Instead of forcing the model to memorize vast chemical data, our approach empowers the language model to interact with a sandbox for precise information retrieval. This externalization of knowledge allows a locally deployable small model to achieve superior performance while being highly token-efficient compared to traditional multi-agent systems. To enable small language models for agent-calling ability, we build an agentic trajectory construction pipeline and a comprehensive chemical-agent sandbox. Based on sandbox interactions, we constructed ChemToolDataset, the first large-scale chemical tool trajectory dataset. Simultaneously, we propose SMILES-GRPO to build a dense chemical reward function, promoting the model's ability to call chemical agents. Evaluations across diverse aspects of drug design show that ChemCRAFT outperforms current cloud-based LLMs in molecular structure analysis, molecular optimization, and synthesis pathway prediction, demonstrating that scientific reasoning is not solely an emergent ability of model scale, but a learnable policy of tool orchestration. Furthermore, assessments in real-world drug optimization scenarios, including fentanyl analog optimization and pro-inflammatory GSTO1 inhibitors optimization, reveal that ChemCRAFT generates optimization trajectories mirroring human experts, confirming its reliability as a scientific assistant.
evidence_items.title: Agentic reinforcement learning empowers next-generation chemical language models for molecular design and synthesis

evidence_items.summary: Laboratory dataset and analysis code for 24 hardened concrete mixtures (water/cement ratio 0.40–0.59, three cement types, steel and polyolefin macrofibres, an integral crystalline waterproofing admixture), all tested at an age of about 100 days. The data comprise: drying water-retention points measured from 0.1 kPa to 170 MPa on 18 mixtures by sand and sand/kaolin box, pressure membrane and vapour equilibrium over saturated salt solutions; drying and wetting retention branches measured on four mixtures by chilled-mirror dew-point potentiometry and reported per specimen disc; saturated hydraulic conductivity at every accepted pressure stage of a constant-head triaxial permeameter, with the hydraulic gradient and the Darcy velocity where these were recorded; the depth of penetration of water under pressure of three cubes per mixture, with the standard deviation and the resulting watertightness classification; and the computed output of transient unsaturated seepage analyses of the penetration test, for three permeability-function variants and five initial relative humidities. Also included are the fitted Fredlund–Xing and van Genuchten parameters of every curve with the inflection point and its tangent slope, the figures in PNG and PDF, and the Python scripts that regenerate every derived quantity, table and figure directly from the deposited data. Mixture identifiers M1–M24 are consistent across all files. The conductivities are the values recorded in the doctoral evaluation; for the second group the mean of the listed determinations is given alongside the recorded mean.
evidence_items.title: Water retention, saturated conductivity and pressurized water penetration of 24 mature concrete mixtures: laboratory data and analysis code

evidence_items.summary: Artificial intelligence (AI), particularly large language models (LLMs) and vision-language models (VLMs), is increasingly applied in civil and structural engineering for disaster assessment, structural analysis, and engineering decision support. However, the extent to which current VLMs possess the reasoning capabilities required for reliable engineering judgments remains unclear. In this work, we introduce CivilBench, a comprehensive benchmark for evaluating VLMs in civil engineering and disaster-related scenarios. CivilBench covers three major task families: Sequential Reasoning, Image-based Structural Understanding, and Open-world Understanding, encompassing numerical reasoning, structural damage assessment, risk inference, causal analysis, and repair planning. The benchmark is constructed through a systematic pipeline of domain-specific data collection, engineering-oriented captioning, expert annotation, question design, and quality verification. Evaluation of representative state-of-the-art VLMs reveals substantial limitations in domain-specific reasoning, with Sequential Reasoning emerging as a major bottleneck, particularly when models must infer numerical relationships from sparse structured observations. Further experiments show that numerical priors and external knowledge can alleviate these limitations, although their effectiveness depends on the model's ability to reliably interpret and use the available evidence. CivilBench provides a capability-oriented testbed for identifying reasoning limitations and evaluating progress toward reliable AI-assisted engineering decision-making. The benchmark will be publicly available at https://huggingface.co/datasets/traceuryuan/CivilBench.
evidence_items.title: CivilBench: Benchmarking Vision-Language Models for Multimodal Information Integration in Civil Engineering

evidence_items.summary: We introduce WorldOracle, a benchmark specifically designed to evaluate action-conditioned world models (ACWMs) against paired real-world executions. Given the same initial observation and low-level action sequence, WorldOracle asks whether a predicted rollout reproduces what happens in the real world, including physical consequences and task-state transitions. We evaluate models along four complementary dimensions: physical state correctness, interaction spatial alignment, key interaction area fidelity, and multi-view action coherence. To support this evaluation, we curate real-world training and evaluation suites that cover different interaction dynamics and embodiments. The evaluation suite contains long, multi-segment episodes with both successful and failed executions, enabling evaluation across varied action outcomes and behavior distributions. Experiments on seven representative ACWMs reveal distinct model strengths and failure modes. WorldOracle provides a systematic foundation for measuring and advancing action-conditioned world modeling for manipulation. We release the datasets, evaluation code, and leaderboard: https://worldoracle-benchmark.github.io/.
evidence_items.title: WorldOracle: Benchmarking Action-Conditioned World Models against Real-World Executions

rationale: Matched: benchmark, dataset, evaluat, training data
evidence_items.summary: Audio-visual deepfakes can spread misinformation and enable impersonation, undermining trust in digital media. However, existing datasets provide limited coverage of forgery operations and their combinations, constraining detector development and systematic evaluation. We introduce Mega-MMDF, containing 100,000 real and 1.2 million forged clips across 22 pipelines spanning modality-specific manipulations, stacked forgeries, and joint audio-video generation. To assess its training value and enable fair comparisons, we develop DeepfakeBench-MM, which standardizes training and evaluation across 8 datasets and 10 detectors. Training-based detectors achieve their highest mean AUC when trained on Mega-MMDF, with gains of up to 0.0784 over the best alternative training dataset for each detector. Experiments on data scale and pipeline coverage further support the value of large, diverse training data. Cross-pipeline evaluations reveal bidirectional and asymmetric generalization. Training on composite forgeries does not necessarily enable detection of their constituent operations in isolation. Our analysis of altered inputs shows that modality masking can increase false alarms and missed detections, and temporal misalignment can raise mean predicted forgery probabilities. Together, these resources provide a foundation for understanding and improving multimodal deepfake detection, with publicly available code and dataset access subject to application and usage terms.
evidence_items.title: DeepfakeBench-MM: A Comprehensive Benchmark for Multimodal Deepfake Detection

evidence_items.summary: Description This repository contains the public k-space dataset, reconstructed motion states, validation data, and example code accompanying the publication "Fast ungated five-dimensional cardiac MRI on a 1.5 T MR-linac for MRI-guided radiotherapy" The dataset consists of 10 distinct patient/volunteer files formatted as HDF5 ( .h5 ), plus accompanying example code demonstrating how to load and parse the high-dimensional data arrays. Abstract Background: Stereotactic arrhythmia radio-ablation (STAR) for patients with ventricular tachycardia is currently limited by complex cardiorespiratory motion. Hence, patient-specific five-dimensional magnetic resonance imaging (5D-MRI) motion models are required to overcome this clinical challenge. However, current 5D-MRI methods are hampered by long acquisition and reconstruction times, limiting their clinical availability for STAR treatments. Objective: To develop and validate a fast, ungated 5D-MRI reconstruction method, providing personalized motion characterization to support MRI-guided STAR treatments. Methods: We propose a fast, ungated 5D-MRI reconstruction method based on the previously established cardiac MR-MOTUS framework. The method utilizes a variable-density 3D Cartesian acquisition with a joint optimization framework to reconstruct a motion-corrected reference image and low-rank deformation vector fields (DVFs). By exploiting the low rank structure of the DVFs, we explicitly disentangle respiratory and cardiac motion during optimization. After optimization, the DVFs are used as navigators for cardiorespiratory motion, enabling fast 5D-MRI reconstruction with a retrospectively adjustable number of motion states. Validation was performed using digital and physical cardiorespiratory phantoms. Furthermore, the approach was evaluated in vivo using 10 healthy volunteers, comparing motion consistency with standard 2D cine MRI.
evidence_items.title: Fast ungated five-dimensional cardiac MRI on a 1.5 T MR-linac for MRI-guided radiotherapy - public k-space dataset

evidence_items.summary: Universities require fast, consistent, and traceable academic information services, yet direct use of large language models still poses risks of hallucination, outdated knowledge, and unsupported answers. This study developed an Agentic Artificial Intelligence framework based on Retrieval-Augmented Generation for intelligent academic question answering. The study employed Design Science Research comprising problem identification, requirements analysis, architecture design, prototype implementation, retrieval benchmarking, and evaluation. The framework integrated an agent orchestrator, intent routing, query rewriting, hybrid retrieval, reranking, memory, policy guardrails, a generator, and a verifier to check grounding and answer sources. Controlled testing used 12 synthetic academic-policy documents and 216 questions covering course registration, payments, academic leave, graduation, theses, MBKM, scholarships, library services, LMS, transcripts, academic calendars, and administration. Baseline RAG achieved Hit@1 of 80.6%, Recall@3 of 93.5%, and MRR of 87.6%, whereas Agentic RAG achieved 96.3%, 99.5%, and 97.8%, respectively. The improvement mainly resulted from intent-aware query expansion and combined lexical-character retrieval, which improved handling of paraphrases and overlapping service terminology. The proposed framework offers a more structured, transparent, and auditable implementation pattern for AI-based academic services. Field evaluation using an institution’s official corpus remains necessary before operational deployment.
evidence_items.title: Agentic AI Framework Using Retrieval Augmented Generation for Intelligent Academic Question Answering in Higher Education

evidence_items.summary: AI agents for autonomous scientific discovery must decide which experiments to run under a limited budget. Most benchmarks for science agents provide fixed datasets, while others that support active experimentation largely rely on simulation. We introduce Autonomous Science Bench, an initial release comprising six budgeted design-build-test-learn campaigns grounded in published experiments across biology, chemistry, and materials science. Agents select batches of designs, receive measurements from a lab service, and use the results to guide subsequent experiments before delivering a predictive model. Success requires passing two calibrated gates: a discovery gate, which evaluates the designs the agent measured, and a learning gate, which evaluates its model's ranking of held-out designs. In a pilot evaluation of ten agent-model configurations and 180 trials, the best configuration succeeds in 72% of trials, while the hardest campaign is solved in only five of 30 attempts. The two gates reveal different weaknesses: some agents build accurate rankings but find too few promising designs, while others find promising designs but fail to predict which unseen designs will perform well. These differences are obscured by overall success rates alone. We release version 0.1 of the campaigns, lab runtime, and public leaderboard at https://asb.open-ssi.org/.
evidence_items.title: Autonomous Science Bench: Evaluating AI Agents for Autonomous Scientific Discovery

evidence_items.summary: Building automation systems are increasingly represented as semantic knowledge graphs (KGs) using ontologies such as Brick and ASHRAE 223P, creating a machine-readable substrate for artificial-intelligence applications. One promising application is translating natural-language questions into SPARQL (text-to-SPARQL), which would let building operators query these graphs through language agents, but progress is limited by the scarcity of large natural-language/SPARQL benchmarks. This paper presents Build2SPARQL, a large-scale benchmark for building KGs generated by a KG-grounded pipeline: SPARQL queries are produced and validated entirely by graph-traversal code, while large language models generate only the natural-language questions, keeping query correctness independent of model behavior. The pipeline mines six query-pattern families -- linear chains, branching, UNION, aggregation, OPTIONAL, and attribute-filtered -- and phrases each query across five vocabulary registers. Applied to 201 building KGs (180 Brick, 21 ASHRAE 223P), it yields 6,136 executable SPARQL queries and 30,680 questions. A two-rater human validation of 300 questions found 98.8% semantic fidelity, 98.8% naturalness, and 84.0% operational plausibility. A retrieval-augmented evaluation across three open-weight language models raised exact-match accuracy from 0.2-20% (zero-shot) to 56-65% (three-shot retrieved).
evidence_items.title: Build2SPARQL: A Large-Scale Text-to-SPARQL Benchmark Dataset for Building Knowledge Graph Querying
