evidence_items.summary: Batch job schedulers run the nightly file transfers, scripts and database loads of many organisations, and their administrators spend much of their time on routine repairs: a rotated password, a broken key permission, a held lock, a full disk, a wrong date pattern in a file name. I present SchedOps-Bench, a live benchmark in which a language-model agent acts as the scheduler administrator in a Docker lab with a real scheduler (JS7), two Linux agent hosts, an SFTP server and a PostgreSQL database. Each scenario really breaks the site, gives the agent a ticket that does not name the root cause, and judges the episode only by the end state read from the servers, with separate verdicts for partial, false green and harmful outcomes. The benchmark has 165 scenarios in six sets, each validated in both directions. I also present Vardiya, an open harness that aims to help small and mid-sized models adapt to this work, and compare three rungs: a bare model (zero by construction), a tool-equipped model with only the access layer, and Usta, the same model inside the full harness. The main measured gain is access: with tools, a light hosted model solves 15 of 15 development episodes. The harness adds step efficiency (8.3 against 14.1 steps on average) and, with a weaker model on the hidden test set, 11 of 27 against 8 of 26 correct with 1 against 4 harmful outcomes, a difference that is not statistically significant. With a small local model (qwen3:14b) on the development set, which the harness was tuned on, the harness removed all harmful outcomes (0 against 10 of 16) and raised correct episodes from 3 to 9. On the hard tier there is no correctness gain: on the 17-scenario hard hidden test set both arms are correct in 0 episodes. I release the lab, scenarios, harness, raw episode evidence and analysis scripts under Apache 2.0, and I present the hard tier as an open challenge.
evidence_items.title: SchedOps-Bench and Vardiya: a live benchmark and an open harness for language-model agents in batch job scheduler operations

evidence_items.summary: Large input data for the manuscript "Evaluating LLM-Written Operators in Evolutionary Neural Architecture Search: Acceptance Rules and Search-Configuration Effects". This record holds the 34 pipeline pod logs of the October 2026 search runs that the paper's benchmark, FractalNAS-13, is fitted from: 6 baseline genetic-algorithm runs, 10 frozen-operator runs and 18 runs in which a language model (DeepSeek, Mistral or Qwen) rewrote the search operators. The runs search a 13-gene FractalNet space on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100. The logs are unmodified pipeline output, about 330 MB uncompressed. The logs are published separately because they are too large for the paper's source folder and code repository. They are only needed to rebuild the paper's results from the raw logs (the split of each run into segments, the learning curves and the accuracy-floor truncation rates). The manuscript sources, the analysis scripts and the smaller run logs are in the code repository. Contents of fractalnas13 large input data.zip: - large input data/pod logs/<arm>/<dataset>/seed<N> <uuid>/ : one log per run - large input data/README.md : layout and usage - large input data/SHA256SUMS : checksums of every file To use the logs, unpack the archive into the paper folder so that large input data/ sits next to analysis/ and logs/, then run "sha256sum -c SHA256SUMS" inside it to check the files.
evidence_items.title: FractalNAS-13: Pod Logs of 34 LLM-Guided Neural Architecture Search Runs (Large Input Data for "Evaluating LLM-Written Operators in Evolutionary Neural Architecture Search")

evidence_items.summary: Visual grounding benchmarks usually do not consider the contextual uncertainty of real-world scenarios. In this study, we construct a novel benchmark, the Japanese evaluation for Ambiguous visual Grounding with Dialogue (JAG-D) dataset. It consists of human-robot conversational multimodal interactions covering different types of ambiguity, arising from visual and linguistic categories. We evaluate the capabilities of different state-of-the-art Visual Language Models (VLMs) for ambiguity recognition and resolution. We compare dialogue context grounding performance for visual and linguistic ambiguity resolution. Our experiments show that VLMs can substantially improve the resolution of linguistic ambiguity, especially Japanese zero anaphora, by using dialogue context. We further conduct a comparative analysis to understand whether grounding improvements arise from the semantic content of the dialogue or from its conversational structure.
evidence_items.title: Seeing Isn't Resolving: Visual and Linguistic Disambiguation with Conversational Grounding

evidence_items.summary: While the ability of video generation models to accurately depict scientific phenomena has received growing attention, determining whether these models genuinely understand the underlying principles remains a critical challenge. Existing benchmarks typically evaluate video samples in isolation, making it difficult to expose models that simply fit superficial visual priors. In scientific experiments, a small change in one condition produces a markedly different outcome even when the rest of the setup remains fixed. Capitalizing on this sensitivity, we introduce SciWorldBench, a benchmark comprising paired scientific experiments. Each pair varies a single condition in an otherwise fixed setup, yielding two mutually exclusive expected outcomes. Each generation prompt specifies the condition but omits the expected outcome. We evaluate ten text-and-image-to-video (TI2V) models using an independent vision-language model (VLM) that assesses each video without access to the condition text or the label identifying the correct outcome. A pair is scored as correct only when both videos depict their respective scientifically correct outcomes. Across all ten models, we find that the two videos in an experimental pair frequently depict the same outcome even though the conditions require different results. This recurring failure suggests that current video world models struggle to apply the underlying scientific principles reliably during generation. We will publicly release the benchmark dataset and open-source the evaluation code.
evidence_items.title: SciWorldBench: Do Video World Models Really Understand Scientific Experiments?

evidence_items.summary: Vision-language models (VLMs) have shown strong multimodal capabilities across scientific and biomedical domains, yet their ability to understand electroencephalography (EEG) signals remains unclear. We introduce EEGProbe, a signal-grounded benchmark for evaluating whether general-purpose VLMs can extract and reason from minimally processed, channel-wise EEG without task-specific feature engineering or EEG-specific adaptation. EEGProbe contains 620 EEG-centered questions across 13 subtasks and three capability categories: EEG Signal Classification, EEG Cross-modal Alignment, and EEG Neurophysiological Reasoning. To reduce shortcut-based answering, EEGProbe preserves the temporal structure of the recordings where possible, minimizes benchmark-induced processing, and applies signal-necessity testing followed by expert verification. We evaluate 11 representative open- and closed-source VLMs under a unified zero-shot protocol. The strongest model, GPT-5.6 Sol, achieves an overall score of only 41.63\%, with cross-modal EEG alignment emerging as a major bottleneck. We further examine model behavior from a neurophysiological perspective and analyze how temporal, spectral, spatial, and physiological EEG structure relates to model successes and failures. Inference-time neurophysiological guidance can reshape model predictions by helping models recognize the neurophysiological patterns present in the input and connect them with relevant neurological knowledge, narrowing the gap between general multimodal competence and EEG understanding. EEGProbe provides a testbed for current VLMs and a basis for developing future multimodal models that can interpret EEG evidence more reliably. The EEGProbe benchmark will be publicly available at https://huggingface.co/datasets/2122ZHU/EEGProbe.
evidence_items.title: EEGProbe: Do Vision-Language Models Really Understand EEG? A Benchmark for Signal-Grounded EEG Signals Evaluation

evidence_items.summary: Memory systems address the challenge of context loss in Large Language Models during prolonged interactions. However, as an essential tool for warm companionship and personalized services, the effectiveness of memory systems in processing affective information remains underexamined. To bridge this gap, we propose an emotion-enhanced memory evaluation benchmark to assess the performance of mainstream and state-of-the-art memory systems in integrating and harnessing emotional information. First, we design a benchmark called \textbf{MemEmo} to assess the affective reasoning and tracking capabilities of memory systems across four dimensions: emotional information extraction, emotional memory updating, emotional memory question-answering, and emotional conflict detection. Second, we construct the \textbf{H}uman-\textbf{L}ike \textbf{M}emory \textbf{E}motion (\textbf{HLME}) dataset to provide an empirical foundation for scrutinizing memory systems. Finally, We evaluate five representative memory systems on the HLME dataset, reporting 11 performance metrics across four dimensions. Experimental results reveal that aggregating scores for all tested memory systems is up to 45\%, far below 100\% scale, exposing a profound disparity between memory system and affective intelligence.
evidence_items.title: MemEmo: Evaluating Emotion in Memory Systems

evidence_items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly explored for industrial tasks, yet few benchmarks evaluate their mastery of industrial knowledge across different types of cognitive demand. We introduce IndustrialKnowEval (IndKnow), a benchmark for industrial knowledge and engineering question answering. It contains 43,282 samples covering 21 task types across seven industrial sectors, including aerospace, electric power, and metallurgy, organized into four levels of cognitive demand: memory, comprehension, reasoning, and engineering application. Enterprise-based domain specialists and experienced researchers participate in all stages of dataset construction and quality control. We conduct a series of experiments on 18 representative LLMs, with domain experts deeply involved in the evaluation. Building upon IndKnow, we propose the Industrial Cognitive Capability Gap (ICCG) metric to characterize the performance differential between foundational industrial knowledge and higher-order reasoning and application, and we analyze it alongside absolute performance to provide a more complete view of model capabilities. We anticipate that IndustrialKnowEval will support the benchmarking of LLMs in industrial scenarios and promote the development of robust industrial intelligence. Code is available at: https://github.com/J4cksonLee/IndKnow
evidence_items.title: IndustrialKnowEval: A Benchmark for Evaluating Multi-Level Industrial Knowledge in LLMs

evidence_items.summary: Pixel art is widely used in games and digital content creation, requiring readable forms, coherent spatial relationships, and harmonious colors under limited resolution and palette constraints. Language models show growing promise in visual creation, yet their pixel art creation capabilities lack systematic evaluation. We introduce PixelBench, formalizing text-to-image generation and instruction-guided editing for pixel art and providing a benchmark for these tasks. We further present a creation environment in which language model agents invoke drawing tools through code to generate and edit pixel art. We assess the quality of generated artwork through human evaluation and employ a multimodal large language model as a judge, validating the agreement between its automated assessments and human preferences. We compare language models and configurations across diverse subjects and canvas sizes. In our experiments, GPT-6 Astra achieves both the highest average judge score and the best average human rank, highlighting the potential of general-purpose language models for pixel art creation. We release the tasks, all artworks, the human rankings, and the judge protocol.
evidence_items.title: PixelBench: Evaluating Language Models for Pixel-Art Creation

evidence_items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to build interactive honeypots, yet existing evaluations mainly assess isolated command outputs and cannot determine whether a system remains believable when later commands depend on earlier results. We present ReconPotBench, a multi-round benchmark for Linux reconnaissance honeypots. It contains 1{,}032 three-round reconnaissance interactions across eight reconnaissance categories, with reference outputs collected from a real Linux environment. Under a unified testing protocol, we compare Cowrie, open-source LLMs, and closed-source LLMs along three dimensions: round-level authenticity, cross-round contextual consistency, and hacker-oriented reconnaissance value. Results show that multi-round evaluation exposes failures hidden by single-round testing, as authenticity declines with interaction depth and both open-source and closed-source LLMs struggle to maintain coherent state across rounds. LLM-based honeypots nevertheless outperform Cowrie in authenticity and reconnaissance value, while Cowrie remains more consistent because of its rigid templated behavior. Category-level analysis further shows that tasks requiring systems to preserve network relationships across rounds are harder than tasks centered on explicit entities such as ports. ReconPotBench enables reproducible evaluation of LLM honeypots across authenticity, entity consistency, and hacker-perspective utility in dependent multi-round interactions. The dataset is available at: https://github.com/qianli-wang/ReconPotBench
evidence_items.title: ReconPotBench: Evaluating LLM Honeypots in Multi-Round Linux Reconnaissance

evidence_items.summary: Memory systems allow AI agents to persist information across interactions, making them more personalized and more capable on long-horizon tasks. This persistence introduces new risks: stored information can be disclosed in inappropriate contexts, resist correction or deletion, be retained beyond what users desire, or be poisoned to influence later agent behaviour. Yet memory systems are typically evaluated on task performance and efficiency alone. We argue that a memory system should instead be understood as the custodian of its user's persistent information, with responsibilities that extend beyond helping an agent complete its tasks, and that it should be evaluated holistically against all such responsibilities. We present Holistic Evaluation of Agent Memory Systems (HEAMS), an open-source framework for evaluating agent memory systems in this way. First, we state the responsibilities of agent memory systems as explicit behavioural desiderata spanning performance, efficiency, security, privacy, and user sovereignty. Second, we assemble a benchmark suite that covers these desiderata and acknowledge the gaps that remain. Third, we develop MilaMem, a prototype memory system, and a governance layer that can wrap any memory system, enabling controlled study of memory system design choices. Fourth, we compare memory systems across the full HEAMS benchmark suite. We find that no memory system leads every performance benchmark, and strong performance scores may coexist with poor privacy, user-sovereignty, and security scores. Governance strongly influences results: recall policies can reduce inappropriate disclosure at a cost in helpfulness, while both recall and retention policies improve poisoning resistance. Performance and efficiency benchmarks alone therefore cannot reveal how well a memory system meets its responsibilities. Code: https://github.com/milatechtransfer/heams
evidence_items.title: HEAMS: Holistic Evaluation of Agent Memory Systems

evidence_items.summary: An autonomous vehicle must foresee the consequences of its actions, especially in the rare, time-critical situations where crashes happen. A world model offers this foresight, but only within the coverage of its training data, which poses an exploration-exploitation dilemma. Within this coverage a planner can hardly improve on the data, and beyond it the model's errors mislead it. Logs of competent driving rarely contain the failures that would widen the coverage, and agents that learn from interaction gain them only by failing themselves, without being shown what to do instead. We propose SAFER, a framework that learns offline from failures that others make, judged by an expert, and keeps learning online from its own driving. Offline, partially trained agents and scripted, recoverable perturbations Stage failures in simulation, and an expert Annotates every visited state with its action and value, so that much of what the planner explores is covered before it drives. In planning, a chunked latent world model Foresees the consequences fast enough for real-time use, and a risk-aware sampling-based planner Evaluates candidate maneuvers by their return minus a bounded collision penalty. Online, a loop continuously Refines the model wherever this driving leaves the coverage of the offline data. In closed-loop evaluation against the compared methods, SAFER reaches the highest route completion and reward per step on the CARLA Leaderboard routes, 0.95 and 0.77 from a privileged bird's-eye view, and the highest episode reward in MetaDrive, 53.4 in regular and 49.0 in safety-critical traffic. Project page: https://ys-qu.github.io/safer-website.
evidence_items.title: SAFER: Navigating the Exploration-Exploitation Dilemma in World-Model-Based Planning for Autonomous Driving

evidence_items.summary: Deep research and agentic search agents autonomously retrieve content from the open web and generate reports with citations, and their outputs are often taken directly as research conclusions. This paper systematizes security research in this area along four stages, namely retrieval, planning, evidence integration, and report generation. We present a unified threat model, a taxonomy of attacks and defenses, and a review of evaluation benchmarks, and we align the area dimension by dimension with retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) poisoning, prompt injection, and generative engine optimization (GEO). Coding 34 primary studies shows that only 26.5% of them involve the planning stage, and none performs an end-to-end poisoning evaluation on commercial products. To address this gap, we propose the agenda seeding attack, in which the attacker writes no instructions and only introduces a fictitious evaluation metric. Across 3,520 sandboxed research runs under the same budget, GEO and prompt injection are nearly ineffective, whereas agenda seeding makes the attacker's target the top pick in 16% to 28% of reports. Injection detection and query anchoring fail against it, verification prompting hurts utility, and our proposed provenance tagging preserves utility but can be bypassed by multi-site bait. Finally, we propose eight research directions.
evidence_items.title: Security of Deep Research Agents: Attack Surface, Defenses, Benchmarks, and Agenda Seeding against Research Planning

evidence_items.summary: Offline language models could extend access to maternal-health information where internet connectivity is unreliable, but deployment requires both clinically appropriate responses and feasible local execution. This study presents an offline Android assistant integrating ready-made quantized language models, a clinically validated local knowledge package, conversational context, and model-initiated local retrieval. Gemma 4 E2B and Qwen3.5 0.8B were compared across 45 conversations and 312 turns per configuration, including a dedicated offline agentic benchmark. Gemma achieved higher response-quality, context-retention, and safety scores; Qwen offered faster generation and lower memory use. Clinician assessment of 150 Gemma responses across nine clinical domains yielded a mean quality score of 3.80/4, with 147 responses meeting the acceptance criterion. A paired RAG-on/off experiment evaluated 74 questions: retrieval improved 11 responses, left 56 neutral, produced four adverse response changes, and left three pairs unassessable. RAG-on had descriptively higher mean usefulness, safety, correctness, and actionability in the conditional 70-pair subset excluding the four flagged pairs from both conditions. Physical-device testing demonstrated offline responses on a 6 GB Android handset, with a 14.3 s median latency, alongside successful reconnection synchronization in the integrated application. Together, the findings document clinical response quality and practical performance of the integrated offline maternal-health assistant.
evidence_items.title: Offline-First Quantized AI: Design and Evaluation of an On-Device Maternal-Health Assistant for Low-Connectivity Environments

evidence_items.summary: Hematoxylin and eosin (H&E)-to-multiplex immunofluorescence (mIF) generators predict spatial protein expression from routine histology, yet pixel-level marker reconstruction does not establish downstream utility. We present HEmIF-Bench, evaluating five frozen generators across eight datasets spanning molecular, cellular, tissue, and patient scales. HEmIF-Bench decouples internal encoder features from generated outputs, benchmarking both against the pathology foundation reference UNI2. Mirroring the clinical workflow where pathologists rely on mIF to define cell phenotypes, delineate tertiary lymphoid structures (TLSs) and germinal centers (GCs), and stratify patient risk, we evaluate external CD3 recovery, single-cell classification, dense nuclear segmentation, TLS/GC segmentation, and patient survival prediction. Across the benchmark, foundation-model-based MIPHEI-ViT leads among the generators, while non-foundation models show task-specific strengths. Comparing the two routes reveals that internal encoder features generally outperform generated outputs, and larger output marker panels do not guarantee stronger downstream utility across datasets. Moreover, neither internal encoder features nor generated outputs consistently surpass frozen UNI2. These findings show that pixel-level stain fidelity does not equate to downstream utility, and that generators trained at current paired-data scales have yet to surpass large-scale pure-H&E foundation models. With the expansion of paired translation cohorts and the advancement of foundation-based generative architectures, HEmIF-Bench establishes a definitive benchmark for tracking when H&E-to-mIF generation crosses the threshold to deliver genuine value beyond routine histology for tumor microenvironment analysis and precision oncology.
evidence_items.title: HEmIF-Bench: Benchmarking H&E-to-mIF Models BeyondVirtual-StainFidelity

evidence_items.summary: Agents operating in complex scenarios often face uncertainty due to incomplete information about the environment they operate in, ambiguous user queries, complex business rules and the inherently stochastic dynamics of the governing policy. Several new benchmarks have been proposed to evaluate LLM-based agents on complex tasks in multi-tool environments, including settings with policy constraints and varying levels of intent ambiguity. These conditions make it important to evaluate agentic systems systematically and quantify their performance under different conditions to assess their reliability in production. This need is evident in the recently introduced Thinkingbox benchmark, where even the strongest models struggle to perform consistently across diverse business scenarios. This paper presents a statistical framework for evaluating uncertainty and reliability in agentic systems. We define a hierarchy of scenarios, instances, and samples to assess model performance and variability systematically. We apply this framework to common metrics found in the literature: mean pass rate, $pass@k$, and $passhat^k$, with uncertainty estimates for each metric. Aggregating metrics at different levels of the hierarchy reveals different structures and properties of the policy model; we connect this hierarchical aggregation with the known process of \emph{coarse-graining} as intended in the physics and statistical literature. We independently derive exact finite-sample expressions for the sampling variances of the unbiased $pass@k$ and $passhatk$ estimators; related results also appear in recent submissions. Our central contribution is a constructive derivation of hierarchical uncertainty propagation, making explicit its correspondence with coarse-graining and separating execution noise from task heterogeneity.
evidence_items.title: A Hierarchical Statistical Framework for Evaluating Agent Reliability

evidence_items.summary: When a production issue is reported, engineers get a description and some logs, but no failing test and no way to reproduce the fault. The logs show where the failure was noticed, not where it was caused: in 49% of the real reports we study, the text names none of the files that the fix later changed. We built a benchmark for this setting from two public datasets and 27 open-source projects (Apache, Red Hat, MongoDB, MariaDB, Qt and Sakai). It holds 38,001 resolved issue reports with their pasted logs, the code as it was while the bug was still present, and the files the fix changed. We present INQUEST, an agent that finds the faulty code using a 27B open-weights model. Code, not the model, controls the procedure. It first gathers the evidence, including the files fixed in similar past issues that were resolved before the report was filed. The model then makes only three bounded decisions: which files to open, what role each file plays in the failure, and how to rank them. On 26,544 evaluation reports, INQUEST ranks a changed file first for 68.6% and in the top five for 85.9%, names the correct module for 90.2%, and ranks a changed function first for 53.8%. On the reports that name no faulty file, it reaches 52.8% and 73.6%. A free agent loop with the same model and tools finds files equally well, but names the faulty function 14 points less often. On a 1,000-report sample, INQUEST beats our reimplementations of two published agents by 7 and 20 points of top-1 accuracy (4 and 16 counting only the reports those agents answered), and the same model used as a re-ranker by 6. We report the cost of every system and the results that go against us, and we release the benchmark, both systems and every run transcript.
evidence_items.title: Inquest: Log-Guided Root-Cause Code Localization with a Staged Agent

evidence_items.summary: LoCoMo is a widely reported benchmark for long-term conversational memory, but published scores mix memory quality with choices of answer prompt, judge and baseline layout that are rarely reported together. We measure how much these choices move a score, and evaluate Becos, a team memory system for coding agents, as a black box under all of them: ten conversations (1,540 questions), two answer models (gpt-4o-mini, gpt-4.1-mini), two answer prompts and three LLM judges, against a whole-conversation baseline rerun under identical conditions. Changing only the judge moves a score by up to 7.2 points and changing only the answer prompt by up to 9.3. A blind human check of 150 answers finds the judges reliable when they agree, and the primary judge's errors on disputed answers working against Becos rather than for it. Becos answers from a context with 90% fewer characters than the whole conversation. Its configuration was developed on LoCoMo itself, so there is no held-out set. With gpt-4o-mini answers it scores clearly higher than the whole conversation (79.7 vs 73.0 with the short prompt, paired 95% interval for the difference +3.8 to +9.5; 88.8 vs 77.5 with a step-by-step prompt). With gpt-4.1-mini answers the two score about the same (83.2 vs 83.1; 92.5 vs 92.1). We release every answer and verdict and the scoring script.
evidence_items.title: What Moves a LoCoMo Score? Memory Context, Answer Prompts and Judges

evidence_items.summary: LLM critics increasingly steer iterative search in agentic AutoML, prompt optimization, and self-refinement--evaluated for whether they help, but rarely for whether they can hurt. We isolate the critic's marginal effect through a four-arm audit and characterize the loop's tolerance through controlled fault injection. We show a naive 8B critic drives search below the no-critic random-search floor on 7 of 8 tabular datasets, losing up to 0.245 AUC in the worst case; the magnitude varies strongly with dataset, frontier, and budget. When: stronger critics attenuate the loss on the evaluated suite, without establishing a universal capability threshold. Why: controlled fault injection shows that non-directional errors are nearly costless under best-so-far search, whereas directional errors consume finite search opportunities; an idealized effective-sample calculation yields a necessary condition, $q(m-1) > \beta$, not a deployment certificate. How: a simple observable validation gate and a learned detector can reduce realized loss, but neither is guaranteed to preserve the full-budget no-critic baseline. We will release CRITFAULT, to our knowledge the first benchmark for detecting harmful critic feedback in AutoML. A critic is not a free addition: audit before trusting, and gate when capability or verification is insufficient.
evidence_items.title: The Critic Can Hurt: On the Safety of Critics in LLM-Guided AutoML Search

evidence_items.summary: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have advanced rapidly in image and video understanding, yet their ability to reason over paired aerial electro-optical and infrared (EO-IR) videos remains poorly understood. Such video poses a harder test than standard RGB video QA: targets are often small, evidence may appear only briefly, viewpoints change with the platform, and useful cues may appear in only one stream. We introduce RAVEN-Bench (Reasoning over Aerial Videos with EO-IR aligNment), a paired EO-IR video QA benchmark for low-altitude aerial multimodal understanding. RAVEN-Bench contains 100 temporally aligned EO-IR video pairs and 1,200 human-authored four-way multiple-choice questions, each independently audited for answer keys, modality requirements, evidence intervals, and group validity. It supports EO-only, IR-only, and paired EO+IR evaluation, and uses hierarchical capability levels and structured question groups to diagnose paired-input gain beyond the stronger unimodal condition, unimodal reliance, target consistency, and evidence-chain coherence. We evaluate frontier, open-weight, and remote-sensing MLLMs, showing that aggregate accuracy can overstate evidence-supported EO-IR reasoning. RAVEN-Bench provides controlled modality conditions and group-level diagnostics for auditing whether progress on RGB video benchmarks transfers to aerial cross-spectral understanding. Code and data are available at https://github.com/yuhu990424/RAVEN-Bench and https://huggingface.co/datasets/TerraSenseAnalytics/RAVEN-Bench.
evidence_items.title: RAVEN-Bench: A Paired EO-IR Video QA Benchmark for Aerial Multimodal Understanding

evidence_items.summary: Scaling device-control evaluation requires scaling both the worlds agents interact with and the tasks they must solve. We introduce SynthDCB, a scalable benchmark for environment awareness and device control built through world distillation. World distillation transforms knowledge of device behaviors, interaction constraints, and environmental effects into modular executable components, which are composed into interactive worlds with explicit states, actions, and temporal dynamics. A unified capability representation connects tool discovery, world execution, and task synthesis, allowing new capabilities to enter evaluation through a shared construction pipeline. SynthDCB instantiates Home, Car, and Phone domains with 114 device classes, 1,166 functions, and 95 events, supporting five task families with 32 subtypes. The stateful design enables task validation and agent evaluation through state correctness and tool-call traces. We evaluate seven models on 2,560 test tasks; the best achieves 68.2% Pass@1. Error analysis reveals challenges in answer delivery, feasibility diagnosis, and temporal coordination. Construction experiments demonstrate scalability across domains and token efficiency: world distillation reduces token consumption by 0.9-66.0% and 46.2-92.5% relative to Codex with low and xhigh reasoning effort, respectively, while achieving broader capability coverage. SynthDCB makes executable world construction the basis of scalable device-control benchmarking, connecting an expanding space of capabilities and interactions to verifiable agent evaluation.
evidence_items.title: SynthDCB: World Distillation for Scalable Device Control Benchmarking

evidence_items.summary: Generative image editing models struggle with structured statistical charts when data modifications require geometric synchronization. We formalize this task as Visuo-Logical Cascading Editing (VLCE). However, existing methods remain confined to localized text substitutions and struggle with dependency-aware cascading updates. To systematically evaluate this capability, we introduce ChartSync, an expert-validated benchmark constructed via a programmatic rendering pipeline that guarantees deterministic visuo-logical coupling for the ground truth. ChartSync comprises 870 triplets across 9 chart categories and 4 task types, including 235 geometry-coupled VLCE instances that specifically test cascading text-to-geometry synchronization. We further evaluate these instances via a two-tier framework combining objective visual metrics with a vision-language model judge paradigm to assess low-level fidelity alongside multimodal comprehension and reasoning. Evaluating 14 image editing models and one code-mediated pipeline reveals a nuanced capability gap: most open-source models suffer severe drops in geometric synchronization, while only two frontier proprietary models show emerging VLCE capability, with their residual errors mainly involving semantic isolation and background corruption. Our detailed error analysis deconstructs these failure paradigms to identify core meta-abilities for guiding future multimodal architectures. The ChartSync dataset and code are publicly released at https://github.com/kaka-yjk/ChartSyncCodebase.
evidence_items.title: ChartSync: A Benchmark for Visuo-Logical Cascading Chart Editing

evidence_items.summary: A growing failure mode in agent evaluation and training is that models can achieve high evaluation scores (e.g., test pass rates) by exploiting shortcuts instead of solving the intended task, making these scores deceptive. This makes evaluation scores unreliable as measures of true task-solving ability. We propose CapCode, a framework for constructing coding datasets with randomized tests whose best achievable non-cheating score is deliberately capped below 100%. This capped-score design gives evaluation scores a clearer interpretation: scores substantially above the cap are implausible and therefore provide evidence of cheating. To prevent cheating, we propose CapReward, a reward design based on the CapCode principle to discourage optimization beyond the cap. Experiments across multiple datasets show that CapCode detects cheating while preserving performance ranking of models, and CapReward reduces cheating behavior, yielding models that better follow the intended task specification.
evidence_items.title: Do Coding Agents Deceive Us? Detecting and Preventing Cheating via Capped Evaluation with Randomized Tests

evidence_items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) have shown impressive capability to understand and develop code. However, their capability to rigorously reason about and formally prove the correctness of software systems remains in question. Current benchmarks for formal proof generation focus on isolated tasks, typically algorithmic-style problems utilizing basic data structures. We curate a new benchmark suite for system-level proof generation, VeruSAGE-Bench, which consists of 849 proof tasks extracted from eight open-source Verus-verified Rust systems, covering operating systems, storage systems, memory allocators, and more. These tasks are much more complicated than those in previous benchmarks, containing on average more than 20x the formal specification (in Lines of Code) and requiring a much broader array of verification techniques. We evaluate six LLMs on VeruSAGE-Bench (o4-mini, GPT-5, Sonnet 4, Sonnet 4.5, Opus 4.5, Qwen3.5), and demonstrate that different models and agentic setups lead to vastly different success rates and costs. We also show that the best models possess impressive capability in writing correctness proofs and hence should inspire new ways of developing trustworthy software. Meanwhile, some difficult tasks in VeruSAGE-Bench stress even the best model, forcing long reasoning time (over an hour on the hardest tasks, 15.3 min per task on average), high token cost (USD 13.65 per task on average), and proof failures, which we hope will guide future improvements in models and agents. This is particularly true for a harder no-lemma version of VeruSAGE-Bench, where the helper lemmas written by human experts are removed: there, the best model proves only 41% of the tasks from the hardest project, at USD 96 per task.
evidence_items.title: VeruSAGE-Bench: A Benchmark Suite for Rust System Verification

evidence_items.summary: Reliable 3D reconstruction of field-grown crops is hindered by thin, overlapping structures, wind-driven foliage motion, and changing illumination. Yet longitudinal field datasets and standardized novel-view synthesis (NVS) benchmarks remain scarce. We present an integrated framework for robotic acquisition, dataset construction, NVS evaluation, and agricultural scene reconstruction. AgriChrobot enables web-based teleoperation and repeated multi-view capture along crop rows. Using this platform, we introduce AgriChrono, a longitudinal canola dataset collected over approximately one month, comprising 160 recording sessions, four RGB streams, two depth maps, and estimated camera poses. We define seven NVS scenarios spanning four times of day and three acquisition dates, and benchmark 15 NeRF- and Gaussian Splatting-based methods. In addition to whole-image metrics, we assess fine-detail reconstruction within manually annotated canola regions using gradient- and edge-based metrics. Our results show that strong whole-image scores do not guarantee faithful reconstruction of thin, overlapping crop structures. To address this gap, we propose AgriSplat, which relaxes visibility filtering during initialization and reallocates model capacity through contribution-based pruning and budgeted reinvestment in sub-threshold candidates ranked by existing gradient statistics. After reallocation, asymmetric directional supervision penalizes insufficient contrast along reference image-gradient directions. Relative to Octree-GS, AgriSplat improves mean crop-region gradient-energy ratio from 0.506 to 0.847 and edge F-score from 0.712 to 0.797 across seven scenarios, while also improving whole-image PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS. These contributions provide a dataset, benchmark, and method for systematic crop reconstruction under field conditions.
evidence_items.title: AgriChrono: A Longitudinal Dataset and Benchmark for Novel-View Synthesis of Field-Grown Crops

evidence_items.summary: Predicting 6-DoF grasp poses from a single RGB-D frame has recently achieved impressive accuracy, yet performance can degrade significantly when the target object is heavily occluded by clutter. In this paper, we establish TARGO, the first benchmark dataset for TARget-driven Grasping under Occlusions, and introduce TARGO-Net, a grasp prediction model designed for visual occlusion. Our main contributions are fourfold: 1) We identify the visual occlusion challenge in single-view RGB-D 6-DoF grasping and show that current state-of-the-art models still suffer under severe occlusion. 2) We propose the TARGO dataset, which supports training and testing 6-DoF grasp models across different visual occlusion levels and enables robustness evaluation in real-world scenarios. 3) We devise TARGO-Net, a transformer-based grasping model with a target completion module and target-scene cross-attention, which achieves the most robust performance across all visual occlusion levels. 4) We show that target completion, number of occluders, and target minimum dimension also relate to grasp success in addition to visual occlusion.
evidence_items.title: TARGO and TARGO-Net: Benchmarking Target-driven Object Grasping under Occlusions

evidence_items.summary: SAFFRON benchmark The benchmark tasks from SAFFRON (paper, code): 8 spatial transcriptomics datasets with known, quantifiable spatial variation τ, for evaluating whether the embeddings of a spatial (or single-cell) foundation model capture spatial variation at different scales. Global tasks (Fig. 2a): 1-D spatial gradients of gene expression (global/). Local tasks (Fig. 4a): microenvironments around amyloid-β plaques in Alzheimer's disease brains (local/). These are processed… See the full description on the dataset page: https://huggingface.co/datasets/ChitraLab/saffron-benchmark.
evidence_items.title: ChitraLab/saffron-benchmark

evidence_items.summary: Explicit Edit Benchmark 226 deterministic exact-edit tasks, run by different agents, harnesses, models and configurations. Every observation records what the harness did and whether the resulting files matched byte for byte. Source code and benchmark runner: GitHub — Explicit Edit Benchmark Open the interactive Explorer to compare agents, harnesses, models, versions, reasoning modes, correctness, recovery, time, cost and tokens. Leaderboard by model route Score v2… See the full description on the dataset page: https://huggingface.co/datasets/alexshpunt/explicit-edit-benchmark.
evidence_items.title: alexshpunt/explicit-edit-benchmark

evidence_items.summary: SeisBench v0.13 brings a range of new models, datasets and performance improvements. Now SeisBench can also determine polarities and help you study local earthquakes. And all of that at blazing speed! Major updates SeisBench now includes dedicated models for polarity determination and a tutorial notebook on how to use these models. The new models are EquiPol and RPNet (#405). With a number of PRs (#441, #442, #443, #444, #446, #447), the performance of the annotate and classify has been substantially improved. In addition, SeisBench now supports autocasting. Thanks to @miili for these additions! The CRLBD dataset from the Golf of Corinth provides a new benchmark dataset with a high number of earthquake records at local distances and dense earthquake sequences (#448). Thanks to @ispingos. With SeisT, a new model for earthquake detection and phase picking is available now (#437). Thanks @senli1073! Long requested, finally available: a progress bar for annotate (#435). Thanks to @manduinca! In addition, this release adds many smaller feature additions, performance improvements, updates to newer dependency versions, etc. Thanks to everyone how contributed to this release with feedback, issues, and especially with PRs!
evidence_items.title: seisbench/seisbench: SeisBench v0.13 - Polarity determination, performance improvements, new models and datasets

evidence_items.summary: LeanZero Agentic Benchmarks Aggregated results of LeanZero's agentic coding benchmarks, exactly as ranked on leanzero.net/agentic-benchmarks. One row per model per published benchmark run (a Forge 2.0 cloud baseline row covers its independent builds). Synced automatically from the site's data; the site is the source of truth and every row links back to its run page there, with the checks, screenshots, video and cost. Leaderboard view: Mihai-LeanZero/leanzero-agentic-leaderboard.… See the full description on the dataset page: https://huggingface.co/datasets/Mihai-LeanZero/leanzero-agentic-benchmarks.
evidence_items.title: Mihai-LeanZero/leanzero-agentic-benchmarks

evidence_items.summary: Companion deposit for the manuscript "More Agents Is Not Enough: A Budget-Aware Evaluation of Fine-Tuned Multi-Agent LLM Systems for Hate-Speech Target Categorization", submitted to the Journal of Computational and Cognitive Engineering. The study compares an aggregative ensemble of three fine-tuned persona agents and a compositional three-stage pipeline with a monolithic model and a self-consistency control at measured generated-token budgets, on four-way hate-speech target categorization, across five training seeds (42–46), with one Llama-3-8B base adapted with rationales from a Llama-3-70B teacher, under two readouts (normalized label-continuation scores and generated labels).   The deposit contains: the canonical train/validation/test split (8,180 items, split seed pinned); per-item predictions and aligned test tables for every arm at every seed; measured inference cost and hardware logs; the dual-readout recomputation and the verdict-stripped re-embedding outputs; the external best-of-N probe (ten samples of the frozen seed-42 monolith at temperature 1.2, its reproduction gate and its trained verifiers); the trained LoRA adapters (rank 16, 41,943,040 trainable parameters) for every arm and seed; and the notebooks, audit scripts and verification scripts that recompute the main results from the stored predictions, without retraining or re-inference. Version 1.2.0 adds revision round1.zip, which holds the run configurations, package versions, a table-to-script map, the recovered sample-selection rule, the label rebuild, the regenerated verifier energies, the figure code, and one notebook for the revision's new analyses. It also adds revision code.zip, with that notebook's code and the external test's analysis plan, and revision outputs.zip, with the outputs of that notebook. It also adds supplementary note.pdf, which holds extended methods and results that the revised manuscript cites by section.

evidence_items.summary: In windows environment PowerShell becomes an integral part who’s responsible for system automation, management and configuration tasks. It is very flexible and helps in performing all the operations, which makes it more popular among developers and users. Yet, this flexibility is also the reason for being targeted for criminal activities by implanting PowerShell scripts in the form of File less malware as it doesn’t leave any trace in memory. So detecting these scripts before execution is the best way to counter the filmless attacks. For that, an authentic and reliable dataset with advanced Machine Learning (ML) and Deep Learning (DL) models was required with the most useful feature sets for better detection. This paper implemented a generalized workflow to create a reliable dataset by collecting PowerShell scripts from different repositories and cleaning the obfuscated script by implementing a deobfuscation technique. Then evaluated them with a well-known antivirus (AV) platform, Virus Total, to label those scripts. The extracted meaningful features from those clean and labelled scripts are passed as inputs to ML models for evaluation of those models. Among defined models, Trigonometric Functional Link Artificial Neural Network (TFLANN) performed outstandingly with an accuracy of 97.68%. The proposed reliable dataset offers effective support to future research in PowerShell-based file less malware detection and can be used to create more effective machine learning-based cybersecurity mechanisms.
evidence_items.title: Generation and Evaluation of Reliable Dataset for PowerShell Based Fileless Malware Detection: A Machine Learning Approach

evidence_items.summary: We construct confidence intervals for linear functionals $θ(F m)=\int h\,dF m$ of the empirical law $F m$ of success probabilities $p 1,\dots,p m$, from independent counts $c i\sim\mathrm{Bin}(n,p i)$, as for a language model run $n$ times per problem. Coverage is at least $1-α$ for every $n$, $m$ and fixed $(p i)$, simultaneously for all bounded $h$. The variance-adaptive (VA) region tests each candidate mixing law with the conditional variance of the tail counts it implies. This variance is linear in the law, so the region is a linear program, and cell envelopes keep it valid off-grid. Regions calibrated for iid sampling target a super-population law and are conservative for $θ(F m)$. With all $n$ tail counts, fixed $n$, continuous $h$ and a grid refined as $m\to\infty$, the identification part of VA's width is first-order worst-case optimal, as for any localization with the same index set. Under a rule fixed before the main comparator runs, VA was narrower than a two-stage plug-in band at every $n$ (median width ratio 0.60 at $n=128$), but not than the asymptotic, pointwise AMARI interval at $n=128$; on real rollout pools it was wider than both pointwise and Bonferroni-adjusted AMARI at $n\le128$. For $P(p>0)$ and pass@$k$ with $k\gg n$ the data support only lower bounds.
evidence_items.title: Variance-adaptive confidence regions for fixed-benchmark binomial mixtures, with application to LLM evaluation

evidence_items.summary: Large language model (LLM) trading agents now trade stocks for their users, and benchmarks rank models by their agents' returns. Yet a single run's return says little about skill. In our study, two runs of the same model that differed only in the random seed ended 5.2 points apart on average, so telling skill from luck takes many backtests across markets, models and seeds. However, live arenas trade each day only once, and backtests either use the few months after a model's training cutoff or run on years the model may remember, often with news joined to prices by calendar date. In this paper, we present rta-bench-1, a backtest over three US markets (a rally, a bear market and a crash). It shows each headline only after its publication minute, plays each period blind and named, and checks every run for look-ahead. It also splits each return into factor exposure and alpha and scores every decision against random choices of the same day and sector. In 91 runs of six models from four vendors, no alpha was significant, market and style exposure accounted for a median 78% of the return, and the decisions did no better than random stocks of the same sector. The agents bought the stocks with the most positive news, yet in ablations they earned as much without their headlines. Still, the agents carried out rules reliably, since a single cash rule in the prompt cut a GPT-based agent's share in stocks by 30.3 points in all six pairs. Builders should therefore supply the edge themselves and report exposures and alpha, and benchmarks should replay news by publication time.
evidence_items.title: LLM Trading Agents Earn Beta, Not Alpha: A Look-Ahead-Free Benchmark

evidence_items.summary: VEP DATASET STANDARD3 is a curated clinical dataset of transient pattern-reversal visual evoked potentials (VEPs), developed to support reproducible research in clinical neurophysiology, biomedical signal processing, and automated electrophysiological assessment. The openly released component (Part H) contains 119 averaged VEP responses from 38 adult participants, including 88 normal and 31 pathological responses, recorded at Mohammed VI University Hospital of Tangier, Morocco. Recordings were acquired using two clinical stimulation protocols and harmonized to a sampling frequency of 1,000 Hz, with 400 samples per response covering the 0 to 399 ms post-stimulus interval. Each response is accompanied by two sub-averages, enabling estimation of residual noise, signal-to-noise ratio (SNR), and split-half reliability. The dataset includes pseudonymized participant information, acquisition parameters, response-level clinical labels, documented label provenance, clinician-annotated P100 latencies, and waveform polarity information. Clinical labels distinguish electrophysiologically normal and pathological responses and do not necessarily represent disease diagnoses. The release provides signal recordings in CSV and compressed NumPy (NPZ) formats, structured metadata in TSV files, and predefined subject-grouped cross-validation splits consisting of five repetitions of five folds. These partitions support subject-independent evaluation and reduce the risk of data leakage caused by including responses from the same participant in both training and testing sets. Technical validation includes normative measurements of N75, P100, and N135 components, signal quality assessment, waveform reproducibility, agreement between automatic and clinician-defined P100 latencies, and analysis of age-related effects.
evidence_items.title: VEP_DATASET_STANDARD3: an open clinical dataset of pattern-reversal visual evoked potentials with sub-averages, label provenance and subject-grouped benchmark splits

authors: Zhiyu Zhou, Tianyou Liu, Xinping Yang, Yiyao Liu, Jiayi Dong, Yihan Lin, Haokai Ye, Yifan Lu, Zeyu Dong, Yansong Li, Shengqi Zhang
evidence_items.summary: We developed CAE-Bench, a benchmark to evaluate AI agents on Computer-Aided Engineering (CAE) solver development. A CAE solver is more than a PDE solver; it must be able to generalize across various inputs, such as different boundary conditions, geometries, and material properties. CAE-Bench evaluates the generalizability of AI-developed CAE solvers by providing the same task, such as a heat transfer problem, multiple cases, with each case specifying an input. The AI agent develops a solver for a fixed task using only a few public cases, and the resulting solver is then tested on held-out cases, i.e., cases it has never seen before. We evaluate 12 models across a range of reasoning settings on 80 computational tasks. Our experiments show that even if a solver developed by an AI agent performs well on the public cases, it may even get 0 score on held-out cases. For tasks such as fluid dynamics problems, even the solver developed by GPT-6 Astra performs poorly on held-out cases. A data format and an SDK for task registration are provided, so the researcher can use the benchmark on their own infrastructure. We hope that CAE-Bench will help the community to develop AI agents that can develop reusable CAE solvers that generalize to various inputs.
evidence_items.title: CAE-Bench: Benchmarking AI Agents for Reusable CAE Solver Development

authors: Hanlin Tian, Sihan Zhu, Zhao Yang, Yuxiang Wang, Zhiquan Hu, Yu Mi, Hongquan Zhu, Qiufei Hu
evidence_items.summary: Benchmarks judge language-model agents mainly by whether they reach the correct final state, not by how they got there. Endpoint scoring cannot separate an agent that retrieved exactly the evidence a decision required from one that read most of the environment, nor an agent that never located the evidence from one that stopped a single action short. Settling this needs a reference cost, and authored solutions establish only that a task is solvable, not that no shorter route exists. We present DetourBench, which constrains the environment until that minimum is computable. Each task is a finite, partially observable transition system with unit-cost accesses whose resources become globally addressable after discovery. Exhaustive search yields the full-information minimum action count $L 0$ with a replayable witness; from graph-recoverable terminal states it also yields exact residual work $R T$, which separates an episode that stopped one access short from one that wandered, while an irreversible wrong commitment is recorded as having no finite residual distance rather than assigned one. Success, attainment, residual progress, and normalized detour are reported separately. Across 375 scored episodes --- five model endpoints, 25 integrated tasks, three repeats --- success ranges from 58.7% to 96.0% while conditional attainment ranges from 0.803 to 0.890 and orders the models differently. Among recoverable failures, residual work separates near-complete trajectories from costly incompletion and from irreversible commitment. We open-source the instances, oracle witnesses, and evaluation harness at https://github.com/DatagridsAI/DetourBench.
evidence_items.title: DetourBench: Trajectory-Level Evaluation of Interactive Agents with Exact Minimum-Action Bounds

authors: Yongkang Xiao, Qiyi Deng, Jing Chen, Min Shi, Ju Ma, Ruiying Du
evidence_items.summary: Tamarin-based formal verification of security protocols requires expert-authored multiset rewriting rules and temporal-logic lemmas. Translating a natural-language protocol description into a complete formal model with an LLM is hard because syntactic, reachability, and property-level errors compound across the multi-step modeling process, and a single agent that both authors and self-evaluates cannot reliably localize them. We present MASTA, a multi-agent system that addresses these difficulties through three innovations. First, an operational--evaluative role decomposition assigns rule modeling to an Architect, property modeling to an Auditor, and pure dispatch to a dedicated Arbiter that holds no authoring duties. Second, the Arbiter implements a Tamarin-anchored scheduler that dispatches the next agent based on the latest verifier verdict and routes problem-tagged fixes through a modification list, with a six-class problem taxonomy and an LLM deduplication check preventing routing deadlock. Third, we construct a benchmark of 10 protocols paired with 139 mutation variants and five fine-grained metrics that jointly assess model correctness ($M 1$--$M 3$) and completeness ($M 4$--$M 5$). On this benchmark, MASTA on Qwen 3.5-plus improves over OpenCode on the same backbone by up to $+0.27$ on individual metrics and ranks first on both the correctness and completeness averages, surpassing Codex (GPT-5.5) and Claude Code (Opus 4.7) despite using a weaker LLM. Ablations on five protocols confirm that removing the Arbiter collapses property and verification scores to zero.
evidence_items.title: MASTA: A Feedback-Scheduled Multi-Agent System for End-to-End Tamarin Modeling and Analysis

authors: Xinping Lei, Minghao Liu, Ruijie Zhu, Xiaohui Hu, Xingqiao Li, Ao Zhang, Wenhao Chai, Han Li, Tao Wang, Jingyuan Zhang, Enduo Zhao, Yunfeng Shi, Yiming Liang, Zetao Yang, Xingjian Wang, Yifan Yao, Xinkai Ma, Yingru Li, Tianhan Yang, Huan Zhou, Weiran Shi, Shen Yan, Jiaheng Liu, Stephen Huang, Eli Cheung, Weihao Xuan

evidence_items.summary: A coding agent working within a software organization must establish what to build, collaborate with colleagues, and verify what it delivers. We introduce SWE-CoWork, a benchmark comprising 101 development assignments across 101 real repositories, 11 programming languages, and 12 application domains. Each assignment places an agent in a simulated engineering organization with 26 colleagues who have distinct responsibilities, bounded knowledge, and controlled collaboration behavior. Starting from a brief handoff, agents must recover requirements distributed across colleagues and workplace records, reconcile conflicting evidence, and implement changes evaluated by private executable tests. We evaluate eleven models and find a substantial gap between partial implementation and complete task delivery. The two leading models satisfy approximately 63% of fail-to-pass (F2P) tests but complete fewer than 8% of assignments. Providing complete requirements upfront improves F2P by approximately 16 percentage points for Seed Evolving and GPT-6 Astra, yet leaves complete task success unchanged. Requirement-level trajectory analysis reveals failures throughout the delivery process: Claude-Opus-5.5 directs a mean of 93% of first questions about queried cards to their accountable owners across runs but obtains only 64% of colleague-held requirements. Deferred questions go unfollowed, implementations remain incomplete even after requirements are acquired, and 31% of requirements reported as completed fail their tests. These findings highlight sustained requirement tracking, from clarification through implementation, verification, and handoff, as a key challenge for reliable autonomous software engineering.
evidence_items.title: SWE-CoWork: Benchmarking Coding Agents as Digital Employees in Organizations

authors: Gaytri Jena, Kapil Wanaskar, Aman Chadha, Vasu Sharma, Vinija Jain, Amitava Das
evidence_items.summary: Long-horizon embodied tasks fail in ways that end-task success cannot see. HospitalBench is a diagnostic benchmark of ten hospital chores in NVIDIA Isaac Sim, each two unscored warm-up steps followed by a causal chain of five scored sub-tasks in one continuous simulation: the state one step leaves (an object pose, a choice, a fact seen once) determines what the next step must do, unlike benchmarks that place sub-tasks side by side. Vision-language agents act through skill-level tools from camera images. A scripted robot that makes only the calls a model gets is the solvability check of a chore. From each trajectory the benchmark reads where a chain breaks, what the agent did after a failed call, and how far its own position estimate drifts from the true one. This version reports first results only: 15 of 60 planned runs (three models at high effort, one run each on chores T1 and T10 from both start states and T3 from one), with scripted-robot proofs on three of the ten chores. Of the 15 runs, 2 passed all five sub-tasks. Runs still going after sub-tasks 1 to 5 were 15, 8, 4, 2, 2. Of 189 failed calls, 168 were followed by a different call and 111 by a call that did not fail. These are first results and not a full benchmark. We will release the scenes, task chains, scripted robot, evaluation harness and trajectories.
evidence_items.title: HospitalBench: Diagnosing Where and Why Embodied Agents Fail on Long Hospital Task Chains

authors: Yuhao Wang, Yucheng Zhao, Yiran Zhong, Feida Zhu, Hongcheng Liu, Qichao Wang, Ming Ma, Yu Wang
evidence_items.summary: Omni-modal agents are expected to move beyond multimodal understanding toward completing complex tasks in realistic multimodal environments. In these settings, information is distributed across heterogeneous files and modalities, with cross-file and cross-modal dependencies requiring agents to continually coordinate perception, reasoning, and tool use as newly gathered evidence informs subsequent actions. However, existing omni-modal benchmarks primarily focus on multimodal perception and understanding, leaving complex task completion through sustained interaction with multimodal workspaces underexplored. We introduce Omni-Workspace, a benchmark comprising 380 deep-research-style tasks across four multimodal workspace types and two difficulty levels. These tasks require agents to inspect and process workspace files, retrieve external information when needed, integrate evidence across files and modalities, and produce artifacts satisfying explicit requirements. Evaluating 18 representative models reveals limitations in long-horizon multimodal workspace execution, with the best model scoring only 65.93 on average. Further analysis identifies multimodal context inflation and task-state drift as recurring challenges. Motivated by these findings, we further propose OmniFocus, a lightweight approach combining multimodal working-memory management with explicit task-state tracking to improve performance and efficiency. Omni-Workspace advances the evaluation and development of omni-modal agents toward autonomous completion of complex tasks in multimodal workspaces.
evidence_items.title: Omni-Workspace: Benchmarking Omni-Modal AI Assistants on Multimodal Workspace Tasks

evidence_items.summary: Gloss is a written approximation that bridges Sign Language (SL) and its corresponding spoken language. Despite a deaf and hard-of-hearing population of at least 3 million in Bangladesh, Bangla Sign Language (BdSL) remains largely understudied, with very limited prior work on Bangla text-to-gloss translation and no publicly available parallel dataset at the time of this work. To address this gap, we construct the first publicly available Bangla text-to-gloss dataset, consisting of 1,000 manually annotated and 4,000 synthetically generated Bangla sentence-gloss pairs, along with 159 expert human-annotated pairs used as a test set. Our experimental framework performs a comparative analysis between several fine-tuned open-source models and a leading closed-source LLM to evaluate their performance in low-resource BdSL translation. GPT-5.4 achieves the best automatic metric scores, while open-source models perform competitively despite being much smaller. This work introduces the first publicly available expert-annotated Bangla text-to-gloss dataset, benchmark and trained model for Bangla text-to-gloss translation. It also demonstrates the effectiveness of systematically generated synthetic data for addressing challenges in low-resource sign language translation.
evidence_items.title: Breaking the Silence: A Dataset and Benchmark for Bangla Text-to-Gloss Translation

Changes to this version include updated datasets and results, where a different set of questions was asked of the AI agents.   The questions reflect the additional information added into the knowledge graph.   Additional changes were made to the python files to account for these changes.   The RDF and LPG RAG agent programs were updated to include justifications in the responses, ensure data properties properly reach the agent, database query generations were improved, and a calculator tool was added    to allow for deterministic calculations by the agent.

evidence_items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) suffer from two persistent problems in their parametric knowledge: update lag and factual deviation, which hinder their deployment in professional domains. Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) connects external corpora at inference time, expanding the knowledge boundary without modifying model parameters, and has become the mainstream solution for enterprise knowledge bases, intelligent question answering, and document understanding. This paper divides RAG technology into four stages along its design focus: naive retrieval, precise retrieval, adaptive routing, and agentic reasoning, and examines the principal contradictions and new costs of each stage. On this basis, a hierarchical evolution framework is proposed that cross-compares six levels—retrieval, knowledge, fusion, generation, conflict arbitration, and engineering evaluation—against the four stages, identifying gaps in existing research, especially the unresolved arbitration of multi-source contradictory documents across all stages. The paper also discusses applicable boundaries: when knowledge is already well mastered by the model, when the context window suffices to cover the full corpus, or when the knowledge base is small and sparsely updated, adding a retrieval link only increases latency and noise. Finally, selection guidance is provided along three dimensions: accuracy, computational cost, and robustness, serving as a reference for engineering design and future research.
evidence_items.title: Paradigm Evolution and Engineering Selection of Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Large Language Models

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Calibration and scope choices determine what set-theoretic estimands represent, yet applied studies often treat them as neutral preprocessing. We benchmark the recovery and false-detection behaviour of Necessary Condition Analysis (NCA) and fuzzy-set Qualitative Comparative Analysis (fsQCA) using a public-service measurement framework motivated by five rural services in Vietnam. The evaluation uses 456,000 synthetic datasets from 456 scenarios with 1,000 replications each. Scenarios vary sample size, measurement error, condition correlation, cellwise missingness, outcome resolution, missingness mechanism and two data-generating processes: a two-condition gate and a substitutive non-gate. Across the 432-scenario missing-completely-at-random factorial, fsQCA calibrated with substantive 2/3/4 anchors recovered the programmed gate in 0.749 of replications and falsely detected the pair in 0.015 of non-gate replications. Raw-score NCA yielded rates of 0.673 and 0.087, respectively. NCA applied to 2/3/4 fuzzy memberships was conservative (0.049 recovery), whereas percentile-calibrated fsQCA was less specific (0.519 recovery; 0.162 false detection). In matched scenarios, increasing sample size improved semantic-anchor fsQCA recovery but reduced raw NCA recovery as observations filled the ceiling region. These results show that calibration anchors and NCA scope definitions are part of the estimand. Applied studies should preregister external anchors, report scope and algorithmic non-results, and test recovery against a plausible counterfactual data-generating process. The benchmark evaluates analytical workflows; it does not estimate how Vietnamese residents assess public services.
evidence_items.title: Calibration and Configurational Recovery in NCA and fsQCA: A Monte Carlo Benchmark for Public-Service Research in Vietnam

evidence_items.summary: Indic quality estimation (QE) and automatic post-editing (APE) data is spread across separate releases, so no single resource supports training and evaluation across tasks and language pairs on one footing. We consolidate the WMT 2020-2024 shared-task lineage with an extended English-Malayalam resource into IndicQE-APE: $126{,}754$ instances over nine directional pairs, with up to four label types aligned on the same segment, a direct assessment, a human post-edit, word-level tags and an error explanation, and a test set stratified over four difficulty axes. We benchmark six prompted LLMs and three COMET metrics on segment-level QE, and three systems on APE. Two of the axes are defined partly on direct assessment and select a compressed slice of it. Segments whose segment-level and token-level signals disagree are ranked below equally scored segments of the same language. Four-shot prompting costs every model at or below $3.4$B both correlation and output-format compliance. Unedited MT beats every APE system we run on three of the four pairs. The benchmark https://huggingface.co/datasets/surrey-nlp/IndicQE-APE and code https://github.com/surrey-nlp/IndicQE-APE are released.
evidence_items.title: IndicQE-APE: A Consolidated Benchmark for Quality Estimation and Automatic Post-Editing over Indic Languages

evidence_items.summary: Real-world crisis intervention is inherently conversational, yet existing research largely focuses on static texts. When applied to multi-turn dialogues, current models exhibit significant performance degradation, struggling to track risk signals that emerge as context evolves. To address this gap, we introduce CRADLE-Dialogue, a clinician-annotated benchmark for turn-level crisis detection in conversational settings. The dataset features 600 dialogues with multi-label annotations across clinically grounded risks, including suicide ideation, self-harm, and child abuse, distinguishing past from ongoing risk. We further propose an Alert-Confirm evaluation protocol that distinguishes early warning signals (Alert) from turns where a specific crisis becomes explicitly identifiable (Confirm), reflecting the clinical need to intervene before risk becomes explicit. Experiments show that identifying when risk emerges is much harder than recognizing that it exists: models achieve only mid-40% to high-60% Micro F1. Additionally, we release a synthetic training corpus and a 32B-parameter model that substantially outperforms existing open-source models and achieves competitive or superior results against proprietary models across turn-level, dialogue-level, and confirm-only evaluation settings. We further validate our model on real patient interviews, demonstrating its ability to generalize beyond synthetic conversations.
evidence_items.title: CRADLE-Dialogue: Expert-Level Crisis Detection in Mental Health Conversations

evidence_items.summary: We present an in-depth evaluation of LLMs' ability to negotiate, a central business task that requires strategic reasoning and theory of mind to create and claim economic value. To do so, we introduce PieArena, a large-scale negotiation benchmark grounded in multi-agent interactions over realistic scenarios adapted from MBA negotiation courses at an elite business school. We evaluate language agents across three pairing regimes: mirror-play, cross-play, and human-LM play. We develop a ranking model for continuous negotiation payoffs that yields order-invariant, uncertainty-quantified leaderboards while correcting for systematic experimental asymmetries. We further study the effects of shared-intentionality agentic scaffolding and find asymmetric gains, with large improvements for mid- and lower-tier LMs and diminishing returns for frontier LMs. As calibration anchors, we collect human-human and human-LM negotiation data from trained business school students, finding that a representative frontier language agent matches or exceeds this human baseline in our evaluation settings. Beyond deal outcomes, PieArena provides a multi-dimensional behavioral profile that reveals cross-model heterogeneity in instruction compliance, computation accuracy, as well as judge-assessed deception and reputation, illustrating the value of evaluation beyond outcome-only leaderboards.
evidence_items.title: PieArena: Ranking and Profiling Language Agents in Realistic Negotiation Scenarios

evidence_items.summary: Supporting visual recovery and semantic interpretation within the same communication framework remains difficult when channel quality deteriorates. To address this issue, this paper proposes a large language model (LLM)-guided channel-aware semantic communication framework that jointly supports these two tasks through decoupled transmission streams. An LLM-based channel-aware encoder jointly processes image features and a textual prompt describing the current channel condition. This design allows the semantic representation to adapt to different signal-to-noise ratio levels while retaining an independent reconstruction pathway. A lightweight learnable masking mechanism is also incorporated to scramble the transmitted latent features. The ablation results indicate that this mechanism introduces only a limited impact on reconstruction performance. Evaluation under additive white Gaussian noise shows that the proposed design remains effective across the tested channel conditions. In particular, the framework achieves classification accuracies of 90.58% and 88.23% at 0 dB on the CIFAR-10 and Intel image classification datasets, respectively.
evidence_items.title: Large language model-guided channel-aware semantic communication

evidence_items.summary: Logical reasoning is a highly valued capability in language models. However, high-quality logical reasoning data remain scarce, while manual data creation is costly and time-consuming. We introduce Operations Research Aided Synthesis (ORAS), a solver-verified, two-layer incremental framework for synthesizing logic question-answering data. ORAS leverages operations research techniques to systematically generate high-quality datasets for evaluating large language models (LLMs) and, when used for training, improving their reasoning capabilities. ORAS’s pipeline integrates mathematical programming methods to generate question–answer pairs, and then employs a dual-phase approach: the first phase uses optimization algorithms to construct and evaluate the logic systems by solving the problem using a mathematical solver. The second phase translates the logic system to human-readable problems and generates answers according to the information from the mathematical solver. The fine-tuned model achieves a 22–33% (percentage point) improvement in accuracy on in-sample tests and a 4–22% (percentage point) improvement on similar out-of-sample tests.
evidence_items.title: Synthesis of Reliable Logic Question Answering Data for Large Language Model with the Aid of Operations Research Program

evidence_items.summary: Abstract We mapped clinical translation of large language models (LLMs) evaluated using electronic health record data. PubMed, Embase, Scopus and IEEE Xplore were searched for peer-reviewed empirical reports published between 1 January 2022 and 1 June 2026. LLM agent-assisted screening and profiling, human validation and targeted full-text review produced a descriptive map of 1,870 reports. Primary classifications came from full texts for 181 reports and titles and abstracts for the remainder. Most evaluations were retrospective or offline (92.3%); 56.2% used a single dataset or setting. Integrated, operational, interventional or outcome-impact evaluation occurred in 4.6%; 3.1% combined these evaluations with validation across multiple datasets or settings. Evidence connecting broader validation with clinical use remains limited. Translation into practice requires transportability, accountable human oversight, prospective evaluation in real-world workflows and clinically meaningful outcomes.
evidence_items.title: A systematic review of clinical translation of large language models using electronic health records

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Antifreeze proteins (AFPs) offer promising prospects as biocryoprotectants, yet their discovery remains a great challenge due to the lack of efficient large-scale screening tools. Here, we present a benchmark-optimized, multimodel computational pipeline that integrates property evaluation and structural assessment for high-throughput AFP identification. Through systematic benchmarking on independent testing data set, two optimal strategies were identified: the two-model-based Strategy 8 achieved the highest accuracy of 0.82, while the stricter four-model-based Strategy 18 attained the highest precision of 0.97, making it optimal for initial large-scale screening. Furthermore, this pipeline was applied to screen 153,359 Antarctic krill sequences and discovered 13 novel antifreeze peptides. Dynamic ice shaping assays revealed that four out of 13 peptides significantly inhibited ice crystal growth. Notably, Peptide 10 (SPHSWANTYQQCK) could inhibit ice growth and recrystallization. This study establishes a robust framework for large-scale AFP identification and provides a set of experimentally validated Antarctic krill peptides with strong potential as novel biobased cryoprotectants.
evidence_items.title:
Benchmark-Optimized Pipeline Identifies Experimentally
Validated Antifreeze Peptides in Antarctic Krill
