evidence_items.summary: Abstract Electricity demand forecasting is harder on grids where supply often falls short, because load shedding changes how demand behaves. This study benchmarks one-hour-ahead forecasting on the national grid of Bangladesh from April 2015 to March 2026, a period in which load shedding rose from less than 1% of hours to 44% of hours in 2022 to 2025. Eleven models were compared under a single leak-free protocol: three naive baselines, two linear models, Random Forest, XGBoost and four deep learning architectures (PatchTST, iTransformer, CNN-BiLSTM and BiGRU). All were scored on the same 14,142 test hours from July 2024 to March 2026, 41% of which had load shedding. PatchTST was the most accurate model, with an RMSE of 203.8 MW and a MAPE of 1.26%. Its RMSE was 34% lower than that of a tuned XGBoost and 58% lower than persistence. Diebold-Mariano tests with autocorrelation-robust variance and paired block-bootstrap intervals confirmed that it was significantly better than every other model. The advantage came mainly from load-shedding hours, where the error of XGBoost rose by 36% while that of every deep learning model changed by about 5% or less. Integrated Gradients and TreeSHAP showed that the transformers used the full weekly demand cycle and the recent shedding history, whereas XGBoost could not predict demand above its training range. BatchNorm improved the transformers but not the recurrent models. Forecasting models for energy-constrained grids should therefore be evaluated separately for hours with and without load shedding.
evidence_items.title: Forecasting Electricity Demand Under Severe Load Shedding: An Explainable and Statistically Validated Deep Learning Benchmark

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Post-quantum cryptography migration can depend on the readiness of shared trust, software, control, and recovery services. We evaluate GridPQC-Graph, a temporal relational estimator coupled to constrained migration planning, in a constructed energy-sector benchmark. Six public power-system cases supply physical topology; deterministic cyber-dependency fixtures, archived primitive timings, and a disclosed stochastic label generator supply the remaining evidence. The benchmark contains 769 assets, 5,242 directed relations, and 110,736 controlled trials. Fifty-three time-indexed features feed calibrated histogram gradient boosting. Training, calibration, unseen-topology testing, and later-epoch testing use disjoint rows. Across 20 seeds, the model attains average precision 0.8884 and Brier score 0.1178 on the held-out 300-bus case. Against a newly calibrated logistic comparator, the corresponding paired differences are 0.00415 and − 0.00244; the logistic comparator has lower expected calibration error. Relation-group substitution measures output sensitivity and local ranking stability, without identifying causal effects. A mixed-integer planner enforces maintenance, criticality, privileged-asset, and prerequisite constraints. Its ten-wave mean exposure retirement is 0.3210, with a consequence proxy of 15.895; readiness-first scheduling trades lower consequence for less retired exposure. Optimizer-matched comparisons separate scoring effects from solver choice. These findings establish conditional benchmark performance, not operational effectiveness, field-disruption probabilities, or safe deployment. Formal stochastic models offer complementary assurance when their transition assumptions and probability bounds are independently validated.
evidence_items.title: Explainable temporal relational learning for constraint-aware PQC migration in a constructed energy-sector benchmark

organizations: Department of Emergency, Shijingshan Teaching Hospital, Capital Medical University
evidence_items.summary: Background Biomarkers may show strong outcome associations without adding information to detailed electronic health record (EHR) models. We developed a reproducible benchmark separating association from incremental value for the lactate-to-albumin ratio (LAR) and troponin in older high-acuity patients, with the aim of locating where marker-specific information remains distinct after an information-rich baseline. Methods From 12,000 records in the official CinC 2012 Sets A, B, and C, we included 1,640 patients aged at least 65 years with computable LAR. First-48-h measurements from 37 raw variables produced a transparent 290-feature baseline. Baseline, LAR-augmented, missingness-aware troponin, integrated, and score-enhanced models used L2-regularized logistic regression, random forest, and gradient boosting. Set A supported development, Set B validation and recalibration, and Set C locked internal testing. Evaluation combined discrimination, calibration, paired bootstrap ablation, optimism correction, decision curves, permutation importance, and risk concentration. Results Mortality rose from 18.2% in the lowest LAR max quartile to 36.7% in the highest, with 2.60-fold higher odds of death. The association pointed in the same direction across four ICU categories (odds ratios per stratum-specific LAR interquartile range, 1.30–1.76). The score-enhanced random forest achieved the highest Set C AUROC (0.769; 95% CI: 0.729–0.809). Recalibration improved its Brier score from 0.200 to 0.170 and moved calibration-in-the-large from − 0.652 to 0.078, thereby reducing average overprediction. Paired-bootstrap intervals for LAR or troponin augmentation crossed zero, locating an information-saturation boundary after the 290-feature EHR baseline; decision-curve mean net benefits for baseline and LAR-augmented gradient boosting were 0.120 and 0.122. Troponin-tested patients had higher mortality than untested patients (31.6% vs. 23.6%).
evidence_items.title: Separating biomarker association from incremental EHR value: a reproducible LAR and troponin benchmark in older high-acuity patients

evidence_items.summary: Enterprise data platforms are commonly evaluated through measures such as connectivity, source onboarding, pipeline reliability, processing speed, and latency. Although these measures are important, they do not establish whether the resulting data can actually be trusted for business decisions. A technically successful integration may still produce duplicate customer identities, incorrect record associations, missing consent information, or attributes whose origins cannot be established. This paper proposes a trust-centric architecture in which trust is treated as a first-class property of enterprise data rather than an implicit consequence of integration and data-quality processes. The framework connects customer identity resolution, master data governance, data provenance, confidence assessment, stewardship, policy enforcement, and intelligent data consumption through a common trust substrate. Customer identity is treated as an evidence-based claim rather than an unquestioned fact, while attribute-level survivorship, source reliability, reversibility, and usage rights become explicit architectural properties. The paper further examines the implications of AI agents becoming direct consumers of master data and proposes trust-aware retrieval, external action gating, and closed feedback as essential controls. The resulting architecture moves beyond the traditional objective of making data available and instead focuses on making data explainable, traceable, appropriately governed, and fit for its intended use. The paper argues that an intelligent enterprise data platform should communicate not only what a customer record contains, but why each important value should be trusted, how it was established, and under what conditions it can safely support automated or human decisions.
evidence_items.title: Beyond Data Integration: A Trust-Centric Architecture for Customer Identity Resolution, Master Data Governance, and Intelligent Enterprise Data Platforms

organizations: King's College London

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Conventional measures of imputation quality assess how accurately missing values are reconstructed but provide limited information about preservation of the multivariate structure of the data. We introduce TDAssure, a topological data analysis framework for assessing structural preservation following missing-data imputation. The framework constructs Mapper graphs for complete and imputed cases, summarises their topological features using extended persistence diagrams, and quantifies differences using bottleneck distances. Permutation tests assess the statistical significance of these differences across a predefined Mapper parameter grid, with adjustment for multiple testing. We evaluated the framework on the Fashion-MNIST and Epileptic Seizure Recognition datasets using four imputation methods under missing completely at random, missing at random, and missing not at random mechanisms, with target missingness rates of 20% and 30%. Random imputation consistently produced the greatest reconstruction error and the largest number of Mapper configurations showing significant topological differences. The relative performance of k-nearest-neighbour, autoencoder, and mean imputation varied between datasets and assessment approaches. In particular, lower reconstruction error did not always correspond to fewer detectable topological differences, with disagreements most apparent when data were missing not at random. Interpretation in such settings requires caution because complete cases may provide an unrepresentative structural reference. An interactive. TDAssure, implemented in a Shinny application, provides a complementary assessment of imputation quality by examining structural preservation alongside pointwise reconstruction accuracy.
evidence_items.title: TDAssure: a topological data analysis framework for assessing missing data imputation quality

evidence_items.summary: Security operations capabilities are commonly distributed across security operations centres (SOCs), security information and event management (SIEM), vulnerability assessment and penetration testing (VAPT), security awareness training (SAT), secure software development life-cycle (SDLC) practices, continuous integration and delivery (CI/CD) controls, and AI security testing. Although enterprise platforms increasingly integrate telemetry, detection, response, cloud and identity capabilities, evidence and workflows across these seven capability areas are not necessarily connected through a shared, auditable operating model. This paper proposes a Unified Agentic Security Operations Platform (UASP), a conceptual architecture for coordinating the seven capabilities through specialist agents, a shared telemetry and evidence substrate, risk-context orchestration, and policy-governed human oversight. The framework specifies six illustrative feedback loops, including VAPT findings informing development and pipeline controls, deployment provenance enriching SOC investigations, security incidents informing targeted awareness interventions, and AI security testing events becoming correlated SIEM/SOC telemetry. It distinguishes the operational roles of the SOC and SIEM, and of secure SDLC and CI/CD, while allowing them to be implemented through coordinated agents. The design uses the Open Cybersecurity Schema Framework (OCSF) for event normalization and treats entity, temporal and provenance modelling as a complementary semantic layer. It also defines bounded autonomy, risk-graded approvals, and an evaluation agenda. The paper is a narrative conceptual synthesis of selected standards, research and public vendor materials; it does not report a deployed implementation, original empirical dataset, or measured performance results. Its contribution is therefore a structured architecture and a set of testable design propositions for subsequent implementation and evaluation.
evidence_items.title: Toward a Unified Agentic Security Operations Platform: A Conceptual Architecture for Cross-Domain Cybersecurity Integration

evidence_items.summary: Background: Increasing volumes of heterogeneous digital-health intelligence challenge conventional horizon-scanning methods and their ability to examine how technologies, clinical priorities and innovation pathways evolve over time. This study developed an agentic AI-assisted methodology for longitudinal digital-health horizon scanning. Methods: We analysed 123 NHS horizon scans conducted in 2015 and annually from 2019 to 2026, comprising 4,039 company-year profiles. Horizon-scan records were integrated with policy, clinical, funding and media evidence. Entity harmonisation, transformer-based semantic representations, TF-IDF analysis, machine learning and semantic clustering were used to characterise thematic evolution and estimate next-year corpus reappearance and future documented maturity. Performance was evaluated using nested company-grouped and rolling-origin validation, and candidate themes were contextualised through human-reviewed multi-agent synthesis. Results: The corpus shifted from enterprise, workforce and operational technologies towards condition-specific clinical applications, including oncology, women’s health, cardiovascular care, cognitive assessment, neurodevelopmental conditions and imaging artificial intelligence. Under nested company-grouped validation, XGBoost estimated next-year corpus reappearance with an F1 score of 0.67, ROC-AUC of 0.89 and average precision of 0.72. Extra Trees estimated future documented maturity with R2=0.40and RMSE =0.96, compared with R2=0.27and RMSE =1.05for direct carry-forward. Chronological performance was more variable across annual cohorts. Conclusions: The framework provides a structured and traceable approach for transforming historical horizon scans into longitudinal thematic intelligence, company-level estimates and candidate areas for further investigation. It is intended to augment expert-led horizon scanning rather than replace clinical, regulatory, procurement or commissioning judgement.
evidence_items.title: Mapping the Evolution of Digital Health Innovation Using an Agentic AI-Assisted Longitudinal Horizon-Scanning Methodology

evidence_items.summary: Agentic Artificial Intelligence (AI) coding tools have the potential to democratise the development of teacher-facing learning analytics dashboards by enabling educators to generate complete applications from natural language specifications. In this study we evaluate Claude Code (Fable) and OpenAI Codex (GPT-5.5 High) across three dashboard specifications of increasing complexity using realistic educational datasets typically available to educators. Both AI systems successfully generated functional dashboards that accurately implemented the required visualisations and interactions. However, they also independently introduced additional analytical functionality, including student risk classifications and AI-generated insights, despite these features not being requested. These implicit inferences raise important concerns regarding transparency, bias and student data privacy, particularly where educators may be unaware of the analytical models or external AI services embedded within generated applications. The findings suggest that while agentic AI can significantly reduce the technical barriers for end user educators developing learning analytics tools, careful review of generated analytical logic and data flows is essential to support responsible and trustworthy use in educational settings.
evidence_items.title: Where did that student risk model come from? Hidden inference in agentic AI-generated teacher-facing dashboards

evidence_items.summary: Benchmark contamination is not new, but recent model releases show it in a sharper form. We use the term benchleaking for the case in which a benchmark's own test examples enter training data, so that a score reflects recall rather than capability. This differs from benchmaxxing, which optimizes toward a benchmark without seeing its test set. We document two escalations over the past month. First, in post-training, the traces have become explicit: recent audits show an agent stating hidden test requirements it was never given in 23% of its attempts, where its predecessor did so in none, and continuing to follow them after the task is changed to contradict them (Schaeffer and R\"auker, 2026; Lo and Lo, 2026). Second, the problem has reached pre-training. Using few-shot continuation on 20 benchmarks across four public base models, we find that some base models write out other test examples---complete questions, options, and answers---that appear nowhere in their input. For the recently released ERNIE-5.5-Flash-Base, 96% of HumanEval problems leak with their reference implementations and 85% of OpenBookQA questions leak with their answers, against 9% and none for DeepSeek-V4-Flash-Base. To quantify what a reported score owes to such examples, we define an Anti-Hack score: the benchmark score recomputed with every leaked example marked wrong and the number of examples unchanged. Averaged over the suite, it costs DeepSeek-V4-Flash-Base 1.5 points and Hy3-preview-Base 1.3, against 5.0 for MiMo-V2.5-Base and 16.6 for ERNIE-5.5-Flash-Base. Open base models are the foundation of much downstream research, so benchleaking now affects more than leaderboard rankings. We call for decontamination reports and contamination-adjusted scores to become standard practice.
evidence_items.title: Benchleaking Is Accelerating: Benchmark contamination has worsened sharply in the past month -- from post-training down to pre-training base models

evidence_items.summary: The same molecule can be expressed in multiple, syntactically distinct representations, yet it remains unclear whether large language models (LLMs) can recognize and relate these equivalent encodings. We introduce MolReps, a pipeline that generates 9,600 question-answer pairs across ten representations for conversion, normalization, and 2D structure recognition. Post-training on MolReps improves text-only and multimodal models, MolQwen3-4B-Instruct (MQ3-4B-I) and MolQwen3-VL-4B-Instruct (MQ3-VL-4B-I), from $4.01\%$ to $75.13\%$ and from $7.11\%$ to $73.14\%$ (InChIKey match) on the molecule-overlap test set, respectively. On the molecule-disjoint test set, post-training increased validity from $20.35\%$ to $58.12\%$ for MQ3-4B-I and from $17.19\%$ to $59.34\%$ for MQ3-VL-4B-I. However, InChIKey match remained low, decreasing from $3.86\%$ to $3.09\%$ and from $6.44\%$ to $2.29\%$, respectively. Furthermore, the resulting models achieve a relative $27.84\%$ improvement in average over their base model on MolRepBench, a comprehensive benchmark for evaluating molecular property prediction. These results show the effectiveness of targeted post-training for enhancing molecular representation understanding and its potential to improve downstream molecular tasks.
evidence_items.title: MolReps: Taking SELFIES, Making SMILES, Teaching LLMs

evidence_items.summary: Text-to-image (T2I) safety evaluation typically assigns each prompt or image a single culture-blind harm label, so content that is harmful only within a particular culture can pass as benign. We introduce CultureCraft, an agentic framework that constructs T2I prompts that appear benign under a general-purpose rubric yet carry a latent harmful meaning in a target culture, and use it to build CuRSE-Bench: 10,709 culture-specific prompts and 2,648 culture-general controls over six regions and ten harm axes, each drawn from a predefined knowledge base of documented harm vectors and traceable to at least two independent sources. Scoring every prompt under six region persona judges and a paired culture-blind judge, we find that the culture-blind judge under-rates culture-specific latent harm while matching the persona judges on the controls. Each persona judge, in turn, chiefly decodes its own region's latent harm under our instrument: a selective cultural blind spot that persists in deployed moderators.
evidence_items.title: CuRSE-Bench: A Benchmark for Probing Cultural Blind Spots in Text-to-Image Safety Evaluation

evidence_items.summary: Callers to Arabic customer-service lines speak their own dialect, while speech recognizers are built and evaluated mainly on Modern Standard Arabic (MSA). A recognizer that mishears the dialect breaks the call before anything else can help. We present Sada-ASR, the speech recognizer of EchoNova's production Arabic voice agent. On a 120-hour test set of MSA and eight dialects, it has the lowest word and character error rates of twelve systems, against eleven from Microsoft, ElevenLabs, Google, OpenAI, Speechmatics, IFM, Cohere, NVIDIA and Audar: 11.69% word error rate against 13.51% for the strongest, Microsoft's MAI-Transcribe-2 (a lead of 0.74 points on clips unaffected by that system's fixed number and script conventions), and 15.52% against 16.96% averaged over varieties. Its largest margins are on Omani (4.30 points), Egyptian (3.78) and Saudi (2.19) speech; it is level on Syrian and loses on Lebanese (24.96% against 23.05%), mostly because it writes Lebanese words in MSA forms and is less verbatim. On six public test sets its average word error rate under the leaderboard's current scoring is 17.17%, below every published figure we found, among them Falcon-ASR (20.92%), Jais-ASR (22.85%) and Audar-ASR-V1-Turbo (23.17%), though none of these states that it used that scoring, so the comparison is indicative. We describe the data pipeline and methodology behind Sada-ASR and release a 20-hour subset of the test set with our scoring code.
evidence_items.title: Sada-ASR: A Production Multidialectal Arabic Speech Recognition System

evidence_items.summary: For a low-resource language, one public leaderboard is often the only shared measure of progress, so optimizing toward it means optimizing toward a test distribution. Our low-rank fine-tune of whisper-large-v3-turbo ranked first on MediaSpeech, Common Voice 17 and a five-set Turkish community board, at 9.02% word error on MediaSpeech against 11.93% for the best baseline. On its private split it lost to unmodified whisper-large-v3. We treat that split as an alarm, not evidence; the main finding does not depend on it. On a twenty-condition FLEURS-TR benchmark built independently of our model selection, the unmodified base beats every fine-tune in every condition, and all five deficits clear zero under paired bootstrap. We call this acoustic narrowing: fine-tuning contracts the acoustic range a model serves well. The central finding is methodological: our in-house proxy for detecting narrowing concealed it instead, ranking the narrowed fine-tune above the sturdier base. Model selection needs a proxy from an independently produced distribution; more of the same source will not do. A rebuilt pipeline reduces the narrowing: a larger mixture with disclosed provenance, a higher-capacity base, and base-referenced selection with trajectory averaging. It wins three same-provenance axes and draws level on FLEURS-TR, 8.16% against 8.26%, interval spanning zero. Parity holds under a second inference stack and a full epoch, decoder fixed. The recovery is one trajectory, a demonstration rather than a validated recipe. In Kazakh the inversion reappears on corpora we did not build. With matched trainable-parameter shares, fine-tuning raised out-of-pool error by 2.23 points for an attention encoder-decoder and lowered it by 3.46 for a CTC encoder-only model, across three seeds each. Narrowing thus depends on the system adapted. We release TurkSpeak Bench, a robustness-first Turkish ASR leaderboard.
evidence_items.title: Winning the Leaderboard, Losing the Distribution: Diagnosing and Mitigating Acoustic Narrowing in Low-Resource ASR

evidence_items.summary: We present K2-Horizon, a fleet of six fully open language models, from a 0.9B dense model to a 375B-A23B MoE, built for general-purpose reasoning and agentic work across math and science, software engineering, deep research, office automation, and beyond. The models lead or are competitive with strong open models of their size on agentic and coding benchmarks. On the modeling side, to strengthen reasoning, we introduce Mixture-of-Value Attention (MoVA), applying MoE to attention value projections, and softplus attention gating, a more flexible, theoretically motivated gate. Our 36B-A4B model uses both and nearly matches a 32B dense model trained on the same data, with one-seventh the active parameters. We also introduce Uno, lossless diffusion adapters that speed up decoding by up to 2.2x without a separate draft model. Our release follows the LLM360 definition of open source for transparency and reproducibility: the full development history, including intermediate checkpoints from every training stage, pre-training data, training logs, and all training, evaluation, and infrastructure code, notably our production-scale xLLM framework for dense and MoE training and the RL360 reinforcement-learning stack. Beyond the data itself, we release and document in detail every pipeline that built it, the part of model development that open releases most rarely disclose. These pipelines produced roughly 10T synthetic pre-training tokens, showing that synthetic data can be a major ingredient of pre-training at scale. Four of the models share one 22T-token pre-training corpus and recipe, revealing consistent scaling behavior and enabling controlled studies of scale and sparsity. All artifacts are available at https://ifm.ai/k2/
evidence_items.title: K2-Horizon: A Frontier Fleet of Open Source Language Models

evidence_items.summary: Mid- to long-term supply chain risk management requires proactively identifying how disruptions such as natural disasters and geopolitical risks may affect the network and preparing countermeasures in advance. In practice, such planning integrates knowledge from multiple disciplines and stakeholders and evolves through iterative scenario exploration rather than one-shot analysis. While recent work shows that large language models (LLMs) can detect causal relations, most approaches are noninteractive and do not reflect how users iteratively introduce novel factors during planning. This limits practical exploratory analysis and hinders alignment between diverse domain expertise and model structure in dynamic supply chain contexts. This study introduces an interactive decision-support framework for causal inference using LLMs that supports transdisciplinary risk analysis. Users propose new factors and specify their placement within the current causal narrative, enabling incremental incorporation of knowledge from different domains. The framework updates causal relationships while enforcing structural consistency constraints and supports repeated edits to explore relationships and compare scenarios. We demonstrate the framework on a supply-chain-motivated case and evaluate it on benchmark causal datasets against representative baselines. Results indicate that the framework preserves coherence and interpretability while enabling transparent and repeatable model updates, providing a practical foundation for transdisciplinary engineering decision-making under uncertainty.
evidence_items.title: Interactive Causal Inference with Large Language Models for Supply Chain Risk Management

organizations: Computer Science and Engineering Department, College of Applied Studies, King Saud University, 11451 Riyadh, Saudi Arabia
evidence_items.summary: Network intrusion detection plays a crucial role in cybersecurity, aiding in the detection of malicious traffic and the ability to distinguish between attacks and normal network traffic. This paper compares a Transformer-based model for network intrusion detection on the NSL-KDD benchmark dataset with a binary classification approach. The architecture proposed uses a 41-input-feature projection to 64 dimensions, followed by two Transformer encoder blocks with 4 attention heads processing the 64-dimensional features. The confusion matrix for the resulting model on the evaluation set of 30,000 records is 98.72% accuracy, 98.56% precision, 98.78% recall, and 98.67% F1-score. The false-positive and false-negative rate are 1.34% and 1.22%, respectively. When compared with conventional classifiers, the reported accuracy of the Transformer is lower than the accuracy of XGBoost (99.44%) and Random Forest (99.31%) while being superior to the reported accuracy of the multilayer perceptron (98.56%) and close to the reported accuracy of Gradient Boosting (98.80%). These findings demonstrate that the evaluated Transformer model can achieve a high classification performance on the selected NSL-KDD records, although it does not outperform all conventional classifiers. The study provides a benchmark-based assessment of the model and highlights the importance of consistent evaluation procedures when comparing intrusion detection approaches. Further research may investigate feature-tokenized Transformer architectures and evaluate their performance on datasets representing industrial control system networks.
evidence_items.title: Transformer-Based Intrusion Detection on the NSL-KDD Benchmark: A Performance Assessment Against Conventional Classifiers

evidence_items.summary: Sindhi is a low-resource Indo-Aryan language written mainly in an extended Perso-Arabic script. Several Sindhi tokenizers have been released on public model hubs, but they have not been compared with one another on shared data. We train SentencePiece Unigram tokenizers with byte fallback at four vocabulary sizes (32k to 150k) on about 1.10 million Sindhi sentences and a smaller, repeated Urdu, Persian and Arabic slice, from four public sources, and compare them with fourteen existing tokenizers on four evaluation sets: FLORES+, Sindhi Wikipedia, a news-derived sentiment corpus, and a contemporary news corpus. The metrics are fertility, single-token retention, UNK rate, byte-fallback rate, and round-trip character loss. At 64k, our tokenizer averages 1.147 tokens per word, against 1.208 for the best existing tokenizer and 1.512 for XLM-RoBERTa, and keeps 88.6% of words as single tokens. On fertility, single-token retention and UNK rate it is best or tied for best in all four evaluation sets at 64k and above; at 32k it trails one baseline on FLORES+. Margins over the best Sindhi-adapted baselines are small (0.002 fertility on FLORES+ at 64k), and we report no significance tests. A round-trip check finds no character loss for our tokenizer and silent character deletion (up to 0.85% of characters) in two existing ones; seven others lose less than 0.1%. We evaluate intrinsic metrics only, so effects on downstream tasks remain untested. Code and tokenizer files are public (DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23962474).
evidence_items.title: A Corpus‑Driven SentencePiece Unigram Tokenizer for Sindhi: Design and Benchmark Against Fourteen Existing Tokenizers

evidence_items.summary: Machine-learning models of groundwater levels are usually reported with a single accuracy score, yet that score depends on how data are split and on what a trivial predictor achieves. We assembled an analysis-ready dataset of more than 90,000 monthly depth-to-water observations from 644 monitoring wells across continental Chile (1982–2021), paired with 37 environmental and location predictors. Using a fixed modeling pipeline, we evaluated three tree-based learners under five train–test splitting designs (one random, two that withhold whole wells or regions, and two that withhold later records) and compared each with applicable baselines on the same test data. The best random-split model achieved R2 = 0.91, but a lookup of each well’s mean performed nearly as well, while temporal interpolation at the same well performed better. At withheld wells, the best learner roughly matched interpolation from neighboring wells; when whole regions were withheld, all learners had negative mean R2. Under a common calendar split, carrying forward each well’s last observation outperformed every learner at every evaluated horizon, although the learners’ R2 exceeded 0.8. Shuffled cross-validation also substantially understated chronological test error. These results show that a high accuracy score can reflect recognition of monitored wells rather than useful prediction at new locations or later times. Herein, we release the dataset, split assignments, predictions, and code as an open benchmark for evaluating groundwater models against validation designs and baselines matched to their intended use. Those results will help water managers judge when groundwater predictions are reliable enough to inform decisions.
evidence_items.title: Matching Validation Design to the Prediction Task in Groundwater Machine Learning: An Open National Benchmark for Chile

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Background Missing values are pervasive in high-throughput proteomics data from mass spectrometry-based experiments. They can compromise statistical power and mislead downstream inference, necessitating proper imputation as a key preprocessing step. While previous efforts, such as the 2017 National Cancer Institute-Clinical Proteomic Tumor Analysis Consortium (NCI-CPTAC) DREAM Proteogenomics Challenge, established benchmarks for imputation on isobaric labeling-based data-dependent acquisition (DDA) profiles, the applicability of these strategies to the increasingly popular label-free data-independent acquisition (DIA) experiment data remains unverified. This is a critical gap, given the distinct differences in instrument settings and acquisition modes between the two experiments. Methods To address this gap, we systematically benchmarked seven individual algorithms and four ensemble strategies on label-free DIA data, using a unique dataset comprising paired label-free DIA and tandem mass tag (TMT)-DDA global proteomics profiles from 162 melanoma tumors. By leveraging the matched TMT measurements as an independent external reference, we evaluated DIA imputation accuracy under realistic conditions. Results & Conclusion Building on these benchmarking results, we introduce DreamAI2, a DIA-optimized ensemble imputation integrating complementary strategies to achieve superior performance. This study clarifies the transferability of existing imputation methods and delivers DreamAI2 as an open-source tool (https://github.com/WangLab-MSSM/DreamAI2) alongside a rigorous validation framework for future research.
evidence_items.title: DreamAI2: An Imputation Tool for Data-Independent Acquisition Proteomics Data

evidence_items.summary: ABSTRACT Molecular simulation workflows based on the GFN family of semiempirical methods (GFN1‐xTB, GFN2‐xTB, GFN0‐xTB, and GFN‐FF) are benchmarked as geometry engines against the original BP86/def2‐SVP DFT level of theory of the Harvard Clean Energy Project (CEP) database for high‐throughput organic photovoltaic (OPV) molecule screening. Two representative datasets are evaluated: a 73‐molecule subset of the CEP database of extended ‐conjugated systems and a 56‐molecule subset of the QM9 database of small organic molecules, selected via variance‐based Neyman allocation from stratified and clustered chemical spaces. Structural fidelity is assessed through heavy‐atom RMSD, radius of gyration, equilibrium rotational constants, bond lengths, and bond angles, and topological consistency via the VF2 graph isomorphism algorithm. GFN1‐xTB and GFN2‐xTB achieve the highest structural fidelity for both datasets, with mean hRMSD values of 0.765 and 0.771 Å for CEP and bond length MADs of 0.018 and 0.021 Å, respectively. GFN2‐xTB achieves the best angle accuracy (MAD = 0.70°) among all methods. VF2 topological failure rates are minimal for CEP (1.4% for both GFN1/2‐xTB workflows) but substantial for QM9 with GFN0‐xTB (26.8%) and GFN‐FF (16.1%), indicating that self‐consistent‐charge methods (GFN1/2‐xTB) provide substantially higher topological reliability than non‐self‐consistent methods for chemically diverse molecular spaces. Meanwhile, GFN‐FF provides the largest computational speedup (up to ∼177× relative to BP86/def2‐SVP) with an empirical ‐like apparent scaling over the sampled molecular size range. Sensitivity analyses across solvation environments, basis sets (def2‐SVP vs. def2‐TZVP), and DFT levels of theory (BP86/def2‐SVP vs. B3LYP/6‐31G(2df,p) for QM9) confirm that method rankings are preserved in all cases (rank correlation ρ > 0.98), validating the primary benchmark as robust for relative method comparison.

                    /def2‐
                    <scp>SVP</scp>

evidence_items.summary: Automated diagnostic report generation lies at the core of clinical diagnosis and can alleviate clinician shortages. Existing diagnostic report generation methods have two major limitations: they rely on unimodal inputs (e.g., images), ignoring textual biomarkers like medical history, and lack proactive dialogue capabilities to elicit personalized clinical information. To address those issues, we propose a ProActive Multimodal Agentic (PAMA) system, which performs a comprehensive disease analysis by examining biomarkers in diverse sources, including multi-view medical images, medical histories, and diagnostic conversations. Built upon a knowledge graph and recommendation-based dialogue architecture, PAMA actively initiates adaptive, multi-turn conversations with patients, which is integrated with visual data for robust and reliable report generation. Specifically, PAMA actively generates adaptive multi-turn questions to collect clinically relevant background information and then fuses the resulting dialogue context with visual representations for robust diagnostic report generation. We validate our approach on two real-world benchmark datasets, MIMIC-CXR and IU-X-ray, through extensive quantitative evaluations and comparisons with state-of-the-art baselines. Furthermore, we conduct user studies to assess the realism and clinical quality of the generated reports. Finally, we present real-world case studies to examine the performance of our system across diverse scenarios, demonstrating its robustness on scalability, complexity, and data variability.
evidence_items.title: Diagnostic Report Generation via a ProActive Multimodal Agentic System

evidence_items.summary: While language-model agents excel at long-horizon coding and terminal tasks, this success relies on two conditions: explicit text specifications and immediate execution feedback. However, neither condition holds in real-world problems where critical information exists only in images, leaving it unclear whether long-horizon capability transfers from text to visual reasoning. In such visual settings, because rules and clues resist text transcription and lack test-case feedback, agents must repeatedly inspect images, simulate spatial transformations, and autonomously cross-check clues. Despite this challenge, existing evaluations fail to capture such capability: visual reasoning benchmarks largely reduce tasks to single-turn, short-chain question answering, whereas agent benchmarks focus on text-based environments or interactive states that permit trial-and-error. To bridge this gap, we introduce Visual Cipher Bench, a collection of 40 original visual puzzles across four categories: spatial manipulation and simulation, logical constraints and planning, rule induction, and knowledge-based decoding. Each puzzle provides only one to three black-and-white line drawings and a minimal submission instruction, requiring agents to discover the underlying solving mechanism entirely from the images. Across 29 reasoning-effort configurations of eight frontier models, even the strongest model, GPT-6 Astra (max), achieves only 26.7% accuracy, while five of the eight models score below 1%. Yet on a ten-task subset, providing a single non-spoiler mechanism hint boosts accuracy from 12.2% to 51.1%. This sharp contrast shows that the primary bottleneck of current agents lies not in executing multi-step plans, but in autonomously discovering rules from visual evidence. Visual Cipher Bench thus provides a rigorous benchmark for measuring long-horizon visual reasoning in agents.
evidence_items.title: Visual Cipher Bench: Benchmarking LLM Agents on Long-Horizon Visual Reasoning

evidence_items.summary: Video generation models produce visually realistic videos but still struggle with physical dynamics and causal consistency. Learning from generated videos requires fine-grained physical supervision, yet reliable quality judgments, correction pairs, and controlled variations are difficult to obtain. Large language models (LLMs) possess physical knowledge, but struggle to reliably guide video generation models in producing their training videos. We present PhysLoop, a unified harness designed to support physically grounded self-improvement in video generation models. The harness guides and constrains LLMs throughout video generation, selection, and correction, distilling their physical knowledge into physically consistent videos. The framework supports controllable training-data construction and inference-time video repair. By identifying and correcting failures, PhysLoop marks a key milestone toward recursive self-improvement (RSI) in video generation models with limited human intervention. We release 100K videos spanning diverse, realistic indoor and outdoor scenes, along with generation tools and two evaluation datasets: PhysLoop-Gen and PhysLoop-Repair. We evaluate controllable generation and localized repair on these datasets, respectively, and assess physical behavior on the external Physics-IQ Verified benchmark.
evidence_items.title: PhysLoop: Harnessing LLMs' Physics Awareness for Self-Improving Video Generation Models

evidence_items.summary: Frontier AI agents increasingly succeed on realistic, long-horizon tasks and are beginning to improve the systems through which they operate. Yet existing benchmarks often restrict agents to narrow action spaces, use simplified environments, or rely on verification methods that are unreliable for evaluating arbitrary agent-generated systems. We introduce Singularity-Bench, an open-ended benchmark for autonomous AI development with six end-to-end tasks spanning pre-training, mid-training, post-training, inference, the agent harness, and cluster orchestration. Each task requires agents to implement core systems from a minimal starting point and evaluates them against mature human-engineered baselines on identical hardware. Additionally, through extensive red-teaming covering 9 of the 10 categories in the OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications, we expose reward-hacking vulnerabilities in the conventional Harbor framework and develop Breakwater, an extension of Harbor that blocks all attacks tested in our study. Across 11 agents built from 7 frontier models and 2 harnesses, Opus 5.5 with Claude Code matches or outperforms the human baseline on all six tasks with a Singularity-Index of 1.25, suggesting it may have the skills needed to reach the singularity. The remaining agents average only 0.60. Our vision is for Singularity-Bench to track how much of AI development agents can already automate and when they may transition from assisting to taking end-to-end responsibility for building stronger successors.
evidence_items.title: Singularity-Bench: Can Agents Build Agents?

evidence_items.summary: Physical AI aims to learn transferable physical knowledge from real-world experience to understand, predict, and act in the physical world. Internet videos and embodied demonstrations provide complementary observations of motion, interaction, and state evolution. A foundational data challenge is to measure and preserve this physical information as training supervision. In video-language pretraining, captions express observed processes in language, yet a semantically correct description can omit the interactions and transitions that define those processes. Rich physical experience in video does not automatically translate into sufficient language supervision. This gap calls for a yardstick to assess annotation quality, compare captioning strategies, and guide training-data refinement. Motivated by our data construction for world-model pretraining, we introduce PhysCapBench, to our knowledge the first unified physical-caption benchmark spanning all three domains: third-person scenes, egocentric manipulation, and handheld-gripper demonstrations. It provides human-verified annotations for 1,500 video sequences and evaluates accuracy and coverage through seven physical dimensions. We examine downstream utility through video reconstruction and manipulation-policy fine-tuning. Physical captions reduce reconstruction LPIPS by 8.6-9.5% on third-person videos and 26.9-30.9% on egocentric videos relative to metadata captions. Training-instruction enrichment improves both PhysCapBench scores and policy success, including a 7.5-percentage-point gain for pi0.5 on a RoboTwin 2.0 subtask. PhysCapBench makes the physical content of language supervision inspectable and comparable, providing a cross-domain basis for its evaluation and improvement.
evidence_items.title: PhysCapBench: A Cross-Domain Benchmark for Physically Grounded Video Captioning

evidence_items.summary: Automated harness optimization improves agents by learning from trajectories and task feedback. Existing offline methods use reference answers to optimize harnesses for reuse on held-out tasks. However, many real-world tasks are open-ended, while long runs expose new difficulties that offline-optimized harnesses may not address. To study harness optimization in these settings, we introduce PerfRace, a benchmark for long-running performance optimization of software projects, and investigate whether agents can use task-specific experience to recursively improve their harnesses during an ongoing task. To this end, we introduce BOXBOX, which enables agent-triggered harness revision and kernel-managed hot reloading while preserving execution context. We evaluate BOXBOX on PerfRace under matched test-time budgets, comparing it with Frozen Harness, offline Harness Evolution, and Harness Scaling. BOXBOX achieves higher speedup with more efficient use of task time and model cost, reaching a Speedup@4h of 1.70x, compared with 1.54x for the strongest baseline.
evidence_items.title: BOXBOX: Recursive Harness Self-Improvement for Long-Running Performance Optimization

evidence_items.summary: Analogical reasoning is widely considered a fundamental component of human intelligence. Few benchmarks are designed to explicitly test far analogical reasoning - reasoning between domains that are superficially dissimilar yet share deep relational or structural similarities. In this work, we introduce an analogical reasoning benchmark called Abstraction and Reasoning Corpus of ANAlogy (ARCANA). The tasks of ARCANA require performing far analogical mappings from real-world objects or physical phenomena to abstract grid-based transformations, different from the well-known ARC-AGI benchmark which primarily emphasized innate human priors. We validate ARCANA through a human study, demonstrating that humans solve these tasks reliably. In contrast, evaluations across a range of large language models show a distinct performance gap compared to humans, revealing systematic failure modes that remain challenging for current models. To address this gap, we propose ConceptSIR, a reasoning framework based on concept slippage, introspection, and reflection. Experiments demonstrate that ConceptSIR enables standard LLMs to solve several challenging ARCANA tasks that were unsolved by direct prompting in our evaluation. Overall, our results suggest that far analogical reasoning remains an open problem for contemporary LLMs. All the materials are available at sites.google.com/view/arcanacogtest. The complete codebase, including benchmark, and ConceptSIR, is publicly available at https://github.com/density-11/arcana-test. All ARCANA data and task instances can be accessed and explored at https://arcanacogtest.org/.
evidence_items.title: ARCANA: A Benchmark for Abstraction and Analogical Reasoning

evidence_items.summary: Satirical news is a unique form of misinformation: it is intended to be humorous by the original publication source but can be misinterpreted. Explanation of satirical news articles is challenging because recent and local context needs to be incorporated. This is a pilot study that explores explanation generation for satirical news articles from Australia and compares them alongside those from USA. We show that framing explanations with unreliable narrator theory on open-weight models can be a feasible, cost-effective alternative to frontier models. We find that models identify the satirical tropes more accurately on the American source than the Australian one. This work results in a novel dataset and an evaluation benchmark for satire explanation.
evidence_items.title: Unreliable Narrator Framing as a Cost-effective Mechanism for Satire Explanation of Australian and American Satirical News

evidence_items.summary: Benchmarks for coding agents typically assess implementation from explicit specifications, leaving open whether agents can discover and reproduce systems whose rules are undocumented and accessible only through interaction. We study this capability in web games, which offer controlled environments with observable actions and outcomes, and introduce GameReplica, a benchmark for end-to-end black-box game replication. It comprises 125 instances spanning 25 web games and five core mechanism families, with each game instantiated at five difficulty levels. Under container isolation, an agent accesses the target game only through an action--screenshot interface, may iterate between probing the game, implementing a replica, and checking it, and delivers a self-contained runnable replica together with a rule checklist. A reference-grounded evaluation then scores the deliverables separately on rule consistency, implementation consistency, and visual fidelity. Experiments across six models and five agent runtimes show that black-box replication remains challenging: Claude Opus 4.8 achieves the highest Overall score, 71.6%, while the other models obtain 4.0%--43.0%. Every model scores highest on visual fidelity and lowest on rule consistency, suggesting that reproducing appearance is easier than recovering mechanics. Difficulty widens the gap: from L1 to L5, the four lower-scoring models show relative Overall score declines of 33%--63%, whereas the strongest model declines by less than 5%. In the evaluated configurations, outcomes vary more across models than across agent runtimes, and most attributed failures of weaker models arise during exploration, before replica code is written. Resources and interactive demonstrations are available at https://qqqqqqby.github.io/GameReplica/.
evidence_items.title: GameReplica: A Benchmark for Black-Box Visual Game Replication by Vision-Language Agents

evidence_items.summary: Visual place recognition (VPR) is a key enabler of accurate localization and long-term autonomous navigation in robotics applications, such as loop closure detection for simultaneous localisation and mapping (SLAM). However, real-world VPR deployment relies on selecting an image matching threshold that balances precision and recall. These thresholds are typically tuned using labeled validation data and fixed during deployment, making them unreliable under environmental changes where ground truth is unavailable. This is particularly problematic in safety-critical robotics, where accepting a false loop closure can corrupt the estimated trajectory and map. In this work, we introduce Visual Place Recognition Auditing, an independent post-retrieval verification framework that leverages Vision-Language Models (VLMs) to assess retrieved matches by reasoning jointly over query and candidate images. Unlike conventional verification methods, our approach performs instance-level verification without requiring architecture-specific confidence measures, dataset-dependent thresholds, or prior knowledge of the deployment environment. We evaluate our method on six benchmark datasets using five state-of-the-art VPR methods and four VLMs. Results show that VLM-based auditing improves recall@1 by 13.6% on average as compared to state-of-the-art methods while reducing false acceptance rates to 12%, maintaining precision above 95% and coverage above 75%.
evidence_items.title: Breaking D\'ej\`a Vu: Independent Auditing of Visual Place Recognition through Vision-Language Reasoning

evidence_items.summary: Globally consistent semantic digital twins require centimeter-accurate and geographically transferable 3D facade segmentation. However, progress in facade parsing is limited by the lack of large-scale, standardized benchmarks for evaluating cross-domain generalization. Existing datasets are geographically narrow, semantically inconsistent, or insufficiently precise. We introduce UnderOneFacade, the largest cross-country and cross-continent 3D facade benchmark to date, comprising centimeter-accurate point clouds with hierarchical, harmonized, and architecturally grounded semantic labels totaling 2.7 billion annotated points. Through a systematic evaluation of representative point-, graph- and transformer-based architectures, we show that current methods struggle to recognize fine-grained architectural elements and degrade significantly across geographic domains, with the best models achieving only up to 33 IoU on the fine-grained LoFG3 benchmark. By combining geometric precision with standardized semantics at unprecedented scale, UnderOneFacade establishes a rigorous benchmark for developing robust and transferable 3D segmentation models. The dataset, evaluation scripts, and pretrained models will be released upon publication.
evidence_items.title: UnderOneFacade: Worldwide Facade Semantic Segmentation Benchmark Dataset

evidence_items.summary: Frontier model evaluations are shifting from foundational capabilities (e.g., instruction following and reasoning) toward compositional, agentic ones, but Korean agentic benchmarks remain scarce. We introduce K-BrowseComp, a web-browsing agent benchmark grounded in Korean contexts, consisting of 400 problems. The 300-problem K-BrowseComp-Verified subset is manually constructed and validated by native Korean speakers. On this subset, frontier LLMs, including GPT-5.5, DeepSeek-V4-Pro, and GLM-5.1, reach only 30.00--45.67\%, a substantial drop from BrowseComp, while Korean LLMs released through Korea's Proprietary AI Foundation Model program obtain only 0.00--10.33\%. We further construct a 100-problem synthetic split using hard few-shot exemplars and failure-mode-targeted generation to exploit the asymmetry between solving and creating web browsing problems. On the adversarially filtered synthetic diagnostic split, the strongest model reaches only 26.00\%, and we report this split separately as a targeted stress test. We publicly release our data and code.
evidence_items.title: K-BrowseComp: A Web Browsing Agent Benchmark Grounded in Korean Contexts

evidence_items.summary: As large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed to users around the world, they are integrated into everyday tasks across diverse cultural contexts, from drafting personal communications to brainstorming creative ideas. These tasks are inherently cultural: they require contextual appropriateness, symbolic resonance, and tacit cultural expectations that native speakers draw on instinctively, meaning that a response can be factually plausible yet unmistakably wrong to a local reader. Existing cultural benchmarks have treated culture as a flat set of facts via fact verification or norm entailment methods, and have adopted LLM-as-a-Judge without examining whether they can capture such thick cultural errors. To address this gap, we present JuICE (Benchmark for LLM-Judge in Identifying Cultural Errors), a multilingual dataset of 7,470 span-level annotations of cultural and linguistic errors in long-form LLM responses. It covers 1,050 query-response pairs from four countries (the United States, South Korea, Indonesia, and Bangladesh), in both English and their countries' main languages. Using JuICE, we find that even the strongest LLM-judge achieves only an F1 of 0.51 in the erroneous span detection task. Furthermore, LLM-judges consistently miss thick cultural errors that local residents readily identify. Our findings suggest that robust cultural evaluation must move beyond surface-level detection toward frameworks that account for the depth and situatedness of cultural meaning.
evidence_items.title: JuICE: A Benchmark for Evaluating LLM-Judge in Identifying Cultural Errors

evidence_items.summary: PDE-to-solver code generation aims to automatically synthesize executable numerical solvers from partial differential equation (PDE) specifications. This task requires not only understanding the mathematical structure of PDEs, but also selecting appropriate discretization schemes and solver configurations, and correctly implementing the resulting formulations in finite-element method (FEM) libraries. Existing code generation benchmarks mainly evaluate syntactic correctness, or success on predefined test cases. To our knowledge, there is currently no publicly available benchmark specifically for PDE-to-solver code generation, and general-purpose code benchmarks do not fully capture the unique challenges of numerical PDE solution, such as ensuring solver accuracy, efficiency, and compatibility with professional FEM libraries. We introduce PDEAgent-Bench, to the best of our knowledge, the first multi-metric, multi-library benchmark for PDE-to-solver code generation. PDEAgent-Bench contains 645 instances across 6 mathematical categories and 11 PDE families, with common FEM libraries for DOLFINx, Firedrake, and deal.II. Each instance provides an agent-facing problem specification, a reference solution on a prescribed evaluation grid, and case-specific accuracy and runtime targets. PDEAgent-Bench adopts a staged evaluation framework in which generated solvers must sequentially pass executability, numerical accuracy, and computational efficiency checks. Experiments with representative LLMs and code agents show that models can often produce runnable code, but their pass rate drops substantially once accuracy and efficiency requirements are enforced. These results indicate that current agents remain limited in producing numerically reliable and efficient PDE solvers, and that PDEAgent-Bench provides a reproducible testbed grounded in the practical requirements of numerical PDE solving.
evidence_items.title: PDEAgent-Bench: A Multi-Metric, Multi-Library Benchmark for PDE Solver Generation

evidence_items.summary: AI agents are increasingly used to diagnose and mitigate failures in production systems, known as agentic Site Reliability Engineering (SRE). Current SRE benchmarks are limited to oversimplistic SRE tasks and are unfortunately hard to extend due to bespoke designs. We present SREGym, a high-fidelity benchmark for SRE agents. SREGym exposes a live system environment built atop real-world cloud-native system stacks, where high-fidelity failure scenarios are simulated through fault injectors. SREGym models the complexity of production environments by simulating (1) a wide range of faults at different layers, (2) various ambient noises, and (3) diverse failure modes such as metastable failures and correlated failures. SREGym is architected as a modular, extensible framework that orchestrates fault and noise injectors across stacks. SREGym currently includes 90 realistic, challenging SRE problems. We use SREGym to evaluate frontier agents and show that their capabilities varies significantly in addressing different kinds of failures, with up to 40% differences in end-to-end results. SREGym is actively maintained as an open-source project and has been used by researchers and practitioners.
evidence_items.title: SREGym: A Live Benchmark for AI SRE Agents with High-Fidelity Failure Scenarios

evidence_items.summary: Language model (LM) agents have driven substantial progress in automated software engineering (SWE), yet building and testing software repositories at scale remains a largely manual and labor-intensive bottleneck. In this work, we introduce RepoLaunch, a novel agentic framework that automatically resolves dependencies, compiles source code, and extracts test results across diverse programming languages and operating systems. RepoLaunch achieves a 78% build success rate, outperforming the Python/Linux-only prior system by 18%. To demonstrate its application, we further present a fully automated pipeline for SWE dataset creation driven by RepoLaunch, which only requires human input at the task-design stage. RepoLaunch is open-sourced, and its automated task-generation pipeline has been adopted by several recent works on agentic benchmarking and training.
evidence_items.title: RepoLaunch: Automating Build and Management of Code Repositories across Languages and Platforms

evidence_items.summary: In this work, we introduce MediX-R1, an open-ended Reinforcement Learning (RL) framework for medical vision language models (VLMs) that enables free-form answers beyond multiple-choice formats. MediX-R1 fine-tunes a baseline vision-language backbone with Group Based RL and a composite reward tailored for medical reasoning: an LLM-based accuracy reward that judges semantic correctness with a strict YES/NO decision, a medical embedding-based semantic reward to capture paraphrases and terminology variants, and lightweight format and modality rewards that enforce interpretable reasoning and modality recognition. This multi-signal design provides stable, informative feedback for open-ended outputs where traditional verifiable or MCQ-only rewards fall short. To evaluate performance, we employ a unified evaluation framework for both text-only and multimodal (image+text) tasks that uses a Reference-based LLM-as-judge in place of brittle string-overlap metrics, capturing semantic correctness, clinical accuracy, and contextual alignment. Our results show that open-ended RL with comprehensive reward signals can effectively strengthen medical reasoning in multimodal models. Despite using only $\sim51$K instruction examples, MediX-R1 achieves strong performance across standard medical LLM (text-only) and VLM (image + text) benchmarks, outperforming existing open-weight medical VLMs, with large gains particularly on open-ended clinical tasks. These improvements remain consistent across multiple RL algorithms and VLM backbones and are further supported by blinded evaluations with medical experts. Our trained models, curated datasets and source code are available at https://medix.cvmbzuai.com
evidence_items.title: MediX-R1: Open Ended Medical Reinforcement Learning

evidence_items.summary: Environmental, social, and governance (ESG) criteria are essential for evaluating corporate sustainability and ethical performance. However, professional ESG analysis is hindered by data fragmentation across unstructured sources, and existing large language models (LLMs) often struggle with the complex, multi-step workflows required for rigorous auditing. To address these limitations, we introduce ESGAgent, a hierarchical multi-agent system empowered by a specialized toolset, including retrieval augmentation, web search and domain-specific functions, to generate in-depth ESG analysis. Complementing this agentic system, we present a comprehensive three-level benchmark derived from 310 corporate sustainability reports, designed to evaluate capabilities ranging from atomic common-sense questions to the generation of integrated, in-depth analysis. Empirical evaluations demonstrate that ESGAgent outperforms state-of-the-art closed-source LLMs with an average accuracy of 84.15% on atomic question-answering tasks, and excels in professional report generation by integrating rich charts and verifiable references. These findings confirm the diagnostic value of our benchmark, establishing it as a vital testbed for assessing general and advanced agentic capabilities in high-stakes vertical domains.
evidence_items.title: Advancing ESG Intelligence: An Expert-level Agent and Comprehensive Benchmark for Sustainable Finance

evidence_items.summary: Data and trained checkpoints for the AptaLM manuscript on inverse-folding distillation for foldable RNA (Bhat, Ul-Kabir, Islam, Caulfield; Digital Ether Computing LLC). Sequences are 10–80 nt over A, C, G, U. Restricted : the metadata is public and the files are shared by the depositor. This record holds data and checkpoints only, with no source code and no third-party model weights. File-level detail is in docs/DATA.md of the code repository. Files aptalm synthetic cohort.tar.zst : the screened synthetic pool (about 3.8 million sequences) and the training corpora built from it. aptalm natural cohort.tar.zst : the natural reference (1,735,854 sequences) and the natural training corpora, from RNAcentral. aptalm aptamer references.tar.zst : 637 published aptamers, used only as an evaluation reference (583 from the UTexas Aptamer Database, 54 from RNAapt3D). aptalm checkpoints.tar.zst : 19 trained checkpoints, each the epoch with the lowest validation loss. aptalm quantitative analysis.tar.zst : precomputed quantitative analysis JSON (headline/GC strata, ablations, mutation robustness and GC-neutral mutscan stats, pool stats.npz). No figure PDFs or scored-draw JSONL. SHA256SUMS.txt : checksums of the archives. Sources Natural : RNAcentral active collection, release 26.0 (September 2025), clustered with MMseqs2 at 90% identity (Steinegger & Söding, Nat. Biotechnol. 2017). Cite RNAcentral Consortium, Nucleic Acids Res. 49:D212–D220 (2021), doi:10.1093/nar/gkaa921. Synthetic : the authors' pipeline. Scaffolds from stochastic and multiple context-free grammars (Knudsen & Hein 1999; Pfold 2003; Kato, Seki & Kasami 2006), sequences from gRNAde, checks with KnotFold, RibonanzaNet, ViennaRNA 2 and JAX-RNAfold. A small share of rows is sampled from GenerRNA and yakRNA and passed through the same screen. Aptamers : UTexas Aptamer Database, Askari et al., Nucleic Acids Res.
evidence_items.title: AptaLM: synthetic and natural RNA cohorts, aptamer references, and model checkpoints
