evidence_items.summary: Recent advances in video generation call for reliable detection grounded in explicit forensic evidence. However, current methods primarily depend on single-pass chain-of-thought reasoning that overlooks brief or localized artifacts, or on predefined multi-agent workflows that offer limited flexibility in selecting relevant inspections. Even with adaptive investigation, optimizing the investigation policy alone does not directly improve the forensic capabilities of fixed experts. We introduce WeVisForensics, an agentic framework in which a main investigator agent coordinates a self-evolving library of forensic inspector sub-agents spanning visual and audio cues. The investigator learns which artifact type to examine, over which window, and when to conclude, and these interactions provide shared feedback for both levels of agents. Our dual-timescale policy optimization strategy, DTPO, closes this loop through fast reinforcement learning of the investigator and slower refinement of the inspectors, guided by annotated artifact intervals, to report subtle artifacts they once dismissed. Furthermore, we curate ForenCue-30K, combining role-specific forensic annotations and interaction trajectories to supervise individual inspections and their coordination, with an accompanying reinforcement-learning pool. Experiments show that WeVisForensics averages 95.2% detection accuracy across in-domain, out-of-domain and agentic benchmarks, 9.0% above the strongest prior detector, while grounding its verdicts in localized evidence.
evidence_items.title: WeVisForensics: Self-Evolving Agent for Omni AI-Generated Video Detection

evidence_items.summary: Existing Large Vision-Language Model benchmarks primarily evaluate visual understanding in general everyday scenarios, leaving historical consistency with a specified era and country largely underexplored. To address this gap, we propose AnachroBench, a controlled discriminative benchmark for evaluating historical consistency in visual scenes. It contains 1,600 image pairs from eight countries spanning the late 19th to the early 20th century, each pairing an original historical image with an anachronistic version containing a seamlessly inserted modern object. AnachroBench evaluates three aspects: Inserted Object Perception, which tests whether models detect the inserted modern object; Era-Country Consistency, which assesses whether the scene is consistent with the specified era and country; and Conditional Era-Country Consistency, which measures consistency judgments only when the inserted object is correctly perceived. A false consistency judgment occurs when a model perceives the modern object but still judges the scene as historically consistent. Overall, AnachroBench reveals a gap between inserted object perception and era-country consistency judgments, providing a targeted evaluation of this behavior.
evidence_items.title: AnachroBench: Evaluating Historical Consistency in Large Vision-Language Models

evidence_items.summary: After a large language model (LLM) agent generates an artifact, users often send edit requests for it. This paper studies whether an LLM can anticipate these requests before they are sent. Such anticipation is useful in practice because it reduces the effort of user review and feedback. We formalize this task as edit recommendation and build EditRecBench, a benchmark for evaluating the performance of LLMs on this task, from real-world conversation logs in WildChat-4.8M. Through benchmarking and failure analysis, we identify a practical challenge that some cases are inherently difficult to predict in real-world settings. To address this, we introduce decision model-based gating to filter out cases where predictions are unlikely to be correct before they are presented to the user. Our trained model outperforms existing decision models and raises pass@5 among shown suggestions by 12--25 points at a gating threshold. Our code is available at https://github.com/ntt-dkiku/llm-edit-recommendation.
evidence_items.title: Edit Recommendation: Can LLMs Anticipate Edit Requests from Users, and When?

evidence_items.summary: Source-free domain adaptation (SFDA) adapts a model trained on a labelled source domain to an unlabelled target domain without access to the source data. Almost the entire SFDA literature assumes mutually exclusive classes, yet many deployed settings are multi-label. This paper formulates SFDA for multi-label classification and establishes the first benchmark for it: five adaptation tasks over six datasets spanning remote sensing, natural, clipart-style and driving imagery, with four single-label SFDA methods extended to provide the first baselines and a published multi-label method run alongside them, over three seeds. The benchmark shows that extending a single-label method is unreliable rather than merely suboptimal: half of the extended baselines fail to improve on the unadapted source model at all, and on two of the five tasks none of them does. The failures are not incidental. Nearest-centroid pseudo-labelling, softmax-based confidence, the diversity term of information maximization and confidence-weighted prototype construction each rely on mutual exclusivity, and each fails differently without it, so replacing the softmax with per-class sigmoids is a valid but insufficient extension. Multi-label Prototype Alignment with Contrastive Teaching (MPACT) is proposed in response, a mean-teacher framework whose objective, prototype construction and alignment term are each reconsidered for overlapping label sets. It attains the best average on every reported metric and is the only method that improves on the unadapted source model on all five tasks. The analysis further introduces a prototype-agreement diagnostic separating feature-space alignment from self-reinforcing agreement with the classifier, and reports a negative result for confidence-based pseudo-label filtering.
evidence_items.title: Source-Free Domain Adaptation for Multi-Label Image Classification: A Framework, Baselines, and Benchmark

evidence_items.summary: AI agents are being deployed on Indian workflows such as payments, tax, forms, travel and customer support in Hindi and Hinglish. Public agent evaluations rarely cover these workflows, and many score with another language model. We present Navital Gym, a set of six open environments with 321 public tasks in five task families: trip planning, UPI payments and disputes, GST invoicing and returns, form filling (including a multi-document split) and customer support in Hindi, Hinglish and three experimental Indian languages. Every task is graded by named, deterministic rules that recompute the outcome from a synthetic sandbox world. No language model judges any score. We report one run per task for three models on all six environments, Claude Opus 5.5, Claude Sonnet 5.5 and Claude Haiku 4.5, and for Gemini 3.1 Flash-Lite on two (UPI and the Support core). Opus solves 315 of 321 tasks, Sonnet 302 and Haiku 205. Trip planning and Hindi/Hinglish support separate the models most. We also describe a private held-out set that is not published, and a 7B adapter trained in the gym. Code is Apache-2.0 and task data is CC BY 4.0. The rules are a documented simplification of Indian practice, not the live systems.
evidence_items.title: Navital Gym: Rule-Graded Agent Environments for Indian Workflows

evidence_items.summary: Tool-handover interaction calls for preparation before a response is warranted. The model waits until interaction cues appear, then prepares while assessing whether the accumulating evidence supports a response or calls for cancellation. We introduce EviBridge, a framework that integrates predictive visual representations into a vision-language interaction model for joint state and tool prediction. A trainable evidence interface maps features from a frozen V-JEPA 2 encoder into the language decoder alongside native visual inputs, preserving their temporal context and using only observations available at each decision time. The framework has two instantiations. EviBridge-E distinguishes recent from historical evidence and encodes the timing and spatial location of each observation. EviBridge-I preserves the temporal order of pooled V-JEPA 2 features and interaction turns and generates dedicated interaction tokens. We evaluate on FuGIBench, a streaming-video benchmark for preparation, response, and cancellation in tool-handover assistance. The best-performing variants of EviBridge-E and EviBridge-I achieve Overall scores of 0.6448 and 0.5892, compared with 0.2178 and 0.5327 for their respective task-adapted native baselines. These gains span target handovers, long waits, and cancelled requests, demonstrating the value of predictive visual evidence for interaction decisions.
evidence_items.title: EviBridge: Encoding Predictive Visual Evidence for Proactive Interaction

evidence_items.summary: Shadows are a ubiquitous radiative attenuation phenomenon in remote sensing images and can severely affect high-resolution remote sensing interpretation tasks. In shadow removal, although introducing a mask prior provides explicit positional information for the restoration network, it also causes non-shadow regions to be modulated by the shadow prior, producing a systematic brightness shift; notably, this phenomenon is independent of whether the mask is accurate. In remote sensing images, non-shadow regions usually occupy a larger proportion, so a small shift over these regions incurs a much higher cost on whole-image metrics than an equal gain in shadow regions. Adopting a task-decoupling perspective, we therefore decompose shadow removal into two tasks, shadow-region restoration and non-shadow-region identity, within a cascaded architecture, and handle them sequentially. Based on this insight, we propose STARS, a cascaded shadow removal framework that separates regional responsibilities across stages. The method retains the advantages of the shadow mask while resolving the degradation of non-shadow regions, without requiring a complex parallel dual-branch structure. Meanwhile, to introduce large-model prior knowledge into remote sensing tasks, we further design a Feature Selection and Fusion Adapter (FSFA). We conduct extensive experiments on three benchmark datasets, UAV-SC+, ISTD+ and WSRD+ 2026, demonstrating the superiority of STARS. The framework shows that decoupling regional responsibilities can resolve the intrinsic contradiction of mask priors, providing a new direction for image restoration with region heterogeneity.
evidence_items.title: STARS: Stage-Adaptive Responsibility Separation for Shadow Removal in Remote Sensing Images

evidence_items.summary: Agent evaluations report task success and rarely say what an agent did at each decision. We score every decision node of three 12B to 14B instruct-tuned language models (LMs) playing five zero-sum imperfect-information games against four opponents on eight properties from decision and game theory, five of them against a CFR+ equilibrium reference. At each node, the LM also states a belief about the opponent's hidden state in a separate call. Without memory and at temperature 0, stated beliefs sit 0.250 to 0.288 in total variation distance from the equilibrium posterior, and where the action responds to the state its agreement with that belief exceeds chance by -0.04 to 0.19. The two calls frame the opponent differently, so the result is a behavioural inconsistency and makes no claim about internal beliefs. Under one prompt and greedy decoding, the LM's action never varies with the state in 10 of the 38 cells where the reference varies its own. Memory lowers the constant-action share in 9 of 13 testable ladders at temperature 0; at temperature 0.2 the cells at 1 fall from 16 to 5 of the 46 informative cells, while the belief results hold. A gate withholds, with a stated reason, any belief score the run cannot support, and seven of the eight non-zero defect rates are attributable to the instrument, a representation, or the LMs.
evidence_items.title: Instrumenting Failure: Scoring Language Model Agents at Every Decision Node in Imperfect-Information Games

evidence_items.summary: Drug combination therapy has become a mainstream of modern medicine, with the potential to enhance efficacy, reduce toxicity, and overcome drug resistance. However, identifying synergistic drug combinations remains challenging, as it requires modeling complex interactions across multiple biological scales---from atom-level molecular structures to entity-level relations in biological networks. Existing approaches typically model these levels in isolation, overlooking complementary signals and long-range dependencies. To address these limitations, we propose BiGSyn, a Bi-level heterogeneous Graph contrastive learning framework for drug Synergy prediction. Specifically, BiGSyn leverages heterogeneous graph transformers to extract high-order dependencies from molecular graphs and biological networks, and introduces a bi-level contrastive learning objective to bridge the cross-level semantic gap. Extensive experiments on two benchmark datasets show that BiGSyn consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines. Moreover, its attention mechanism highlights key molecular substructures and biological interactions driving synergy, providing interpretable insights.
evidence_items.title: BiGSyn: A Bi-Level Heterogeneous Graph Contrastive Learning Framework for Interpretable Drug Synergy Prediction

evidence_items.summary: We introduce The Logic Chain Breaking Point, a controlled-variable benchmark for deductive reasoning in open-weight language models. It spans three phases: (i) pure modus-ponens chain scaling, (ii) distractor resilience with a fixed core chain, and (iii) contradiction detection under primacy versus recency placement. Independent variables follow a powers-of-two sequence $v \in \{1,2,4,8,16,32,64,128\}$, with ground truth known by construction. We evaluate sixteen open-weight models across instruction-tuned and reasoning-tuned panels, including a small-model suite and a larger local-model extension. All models are evaluated with greedy decoding under model-appropriate context and output budgets, while context- and length-limited trials are quarantined from the valid accuracy denominator. Our results reveal a sharply non-monotonic difficulty surface: pure deductive chains up to $L=128$ remain near saturation for most models, and distractor noise causes only model-specific degradation at high $D$, while the inconsistent premise condition has the lowest accuracy. Instruction-tuned models, including larger 24B--27B baselines, score essentially zero on inconsistent premise sets, while reasoning-tuned models recover only partially and remain below reliable accuracy. Within this benchmark, inconsistent premise sets are associated with the strongest degradation under the benchmark's abstention-based scoring rule.
evidence_items.title: The Logic Chain Breaking Point: A Controlled-Variable Benchmark for Reasoning Degradation in Open-Weight Language Models

evidence_items.summary: Prediction of drug-target interaction (DTI) has become a very crucial part of drug discovery. With the increase in the data volume, it has become very important to improve prediction accuracy by integrating multiple data sources. In this regard, utilising multiple resources in the form of heterogeneous information network to address DTI prediction can be rewarding. In this work, we propose a heterogeneous information network based multi-task DTI prediction model which leverages the advantages of relation graph convolutional network (RGCN). To achieve this, the model employs drug-target interaction network, drug-drug similarity network and protein-protein similarity network to construct a heterogeneous information network. Moreover, we use a knowledge graph embedding scoring functions to model interactions between drug and targets, specifically DistMult and ComplEx as decoders over the learned node representations. We performed extensive experiments on multiple benchmark datasets and compared with state-of-the-art methods. We observed that the proposed model shows competitive performance, thereby confirming the effectiveness of our approach. The codes and datasets are available at https://github.com/Dheeran-S/MT-RGCN-DTI/.
evidence_items.title: MT-RGCN-DTI: A Multi-Task Relational Graph Convolutional Network for Drug-Target Interaction Prediction

evidence_items.summary: Human motion prediction (HMP) aims to forecast future movement from an observed motion sequence, and recent methods have incorporated 3D scene geometry and object semantics to improve long-term plausibility. However, the destination of future motion remains ambiguous in cluttered scenes: the same observed motion can lead to different interaction targets or navigation modes. Existing methods either handle this ambiguity implicitly or rely on auxiliary signals like gaze that are hard to obtain in practice. To address this, we propose SGIP, which explicitly predicts where in the scene future motion will be grounded across both objects and open navigation regions, and uses it to condition future trajectory and full-body pose prediction. This scene-grounded interaction prior is learned via intent distillation: at training time only, a teacher model scores candidate scene regions by combining an LLM prompted with a textual description of the person's intent with geometric motion-scene features. A student model learns to reproduce these scores from only the observed motion and 3D scene, making intent and LLM unnecessary at test time. Across multiple benchmark datasets, SGIP outperforms prior scene-aware baselines on both trajectory and pose accuracy in a realistic deployment setting where neither gaze nor intent is available at inference, demonstrating the effectiveness of the proposed framework. The project page is available at https://sgip2026.github.io.
evidence_items.title: SGIP: Learning Scene-Grounded Interaction Priors for Scene-Aware Human Motion Prediction

evidence_items.summary: Panoramic multi-object tracking (MOT) requires reliable identity association across a 360{\deg} field of view, yet bandwidth-constrained operation forces a trade-off between low-resolution (LR) identity ambiguity and costly high-resolution (HR) transmission. We propose HIVE-ECIA, an identity-aware framework that selectively retrieves historical HR evidence to recover fragmented identities without modifying detection boxes or the underlying tracker. An ECIA Base-Guided query policy determines when additional HR evidence is warranted; HIVE ranks historical LR observations to select an informative retrieval timestamp; and ECIA Full integrates the retrieved HR crop through learned gated fusion and conservative identity safeguards. We further introduce DualPano-MOT, a real-world dual-fisheye panoramic evaluation dataset featuring controlled pedestrian interactions, panorama-seam challenges, and occlusions, with model-assisted, manually verified tracking annotations. On held-out QuadTrack sequences and zero-shot DualPano-MOT, HIVE-ECIA improves identity association across four MOT trackers without tracker-specific retraining. Across these trackers, identity switches decrease by up to 21.8% and 23.4%, while the largest IDF1 gains reach 3.81 and 6.74 percentage points, respectively. Under an offline JPEG-based acquisition model, our framework reduces encoded data volume by 89.2% and 79.3% relative to continuous Full-HR acquisition.
evidence_items.title: HIVE-ECIA: Identity-Aware Historical Evidence Acquisition for Bandwidth-Efficient Multi-Object Tracking

evidence_items.summary: Autonomous coding agents (such as Antigravity, Claude Code, Cursor, and OpenHands) rely on third-party tools to inspect files, run commands, and call external APIs. Today's security auditors evaluate these tools almost entirely in isolation: static linters and AST checkers verify that each individual tool contains no malicious code at installation time. In this paper, we show that isolated tool auditing is fundamentally flawed. We expose compositional exploits in autonomous coding agents, an emergent vulnerability class where an agent chains individually harmless tools to execute an unauthorized attack. Much like code-reuse attacks in binary exploitation, this threat requires no malware; instead, the agent stitches together legitimate tool operations across turns over shared workspace files, environment variables, and chat memory. Across a 560-task benchmark suite (360 exploit tasks across 8 hazard classes and 200 benign developer and cloud workflows), unprotected frontier models (Gemini 3.5, 3.7, and 3.8 Flash) execute compositional exploit chains with a 72.9% to 84.5% success rate, while five leading single-tool pre-distribution scanners exhibit a 0% detection rate across all constituent tools. To eliminate compositional exploits, we present CompGuard, an OS-grounded defense uniting two planes: (1) a Cognitive Control Plane that issues single-skill capability leases and tracks dataflow provenance, and (2) an OS Kernel Enforcement Layer using Linux Landlock LSM v4, seccomp-BPF socket filters, and an ephemeral loopback proxy to close the invocation gap. CompGuard achieves a 100% Defense Block Rate (0.0% to 0.8% pre-teardown Net ASR) at 61.4 microseconds interposition overhead, preserves a 98.0% solve rate on benign developer workflows, and triggers zero false alarms across 615 real cloud diagnostic calls.
evidence_items.title: Compositional Exploits in Autonomous Coding Agents: Attack Mechanics and Ephemeral Defense

evidence_items.summary: Singapore offers a distinctive testbed for legal reasoning by large language models (LLMs). Its legal system combines inherited English common law with jurisdiction-specific statutes, requiring models to distinguish local doctrine from generic common-law intuition. This setting also highlights the challenge of recognizing underspecification in lay legal queries, because the facts material to a legal outcome depend on the governing doctrine. Yet legal benchmarks rarely cover Singapore law or test this form of ambiguity recognition. To address these gaps, we introduce SG-LegalClarify, a large-scale benchmark for open-ended legal reasoning and ambiguity recognition in Singapore law. SG-LegalClarify contains 1,100 lawyer-authored source questions spanning 10 legal domains, including 340 fully specified and 760 underspecified questions. Each underspecified question has a fixed hidden-fact assignment and a fully specified counterpart, yielding 1,860 evaluation instances. Responses are graded with lawyer-authored Issue, Rule, Application, and Conclusion (IRAC) rubrics. We evaluate 19 LLMs, closed-book and with web search, using a multi-turn pipeline in which models decide whether to answer or clarify, and a user simulator reveals hidden facts only when asked. We find the benchmark far from saturated: the best models satisfy only 69.8% of mandatory rubric items closed-book (average 53.8%) and 77.8% with web search (average 63.0%). Models also struggle to recognize when clarification is necessary. We will release the public split of our benchmark, the model outputs on it, and the evaluation pipeline to support future research.
evidence_items.title: SG-LegalClarify: A Large-Scale Benchmark for Legal Reasoning and Ambiguity Recognition in Singapore Law

evidence_items.summary: The rapid development of multimodal large language models (MLLMs) has highlighted the need for comprehensive benchmarks to assess their capabilities and limitations in remote sensing (RS). However, evaluating MLLMs in large-size synthetic aperture radar (SAR) scenarios remains challenging, as understanding complete scenes requires both global semantic interpretation and fine-grained target perception. Existing SAR benchmarks predominantly rely on small image patches, limiting their ability to assess these capabilities jointly. To address these limitations, we present XLSAR-Bench, a comprehensive benchmark for evaluating the perception and reasoning capabilities of MLLMs in large-scene SAR imagery. XLSAR-Bench comprises 405 images with an average size of 7153$\times$7153 pixels, ten tasks spanning visual question answering, visual grounding, and detailed image captioning, with all evaluation samples meticulously annotated manually, assisted by a semi-automatic captioner. Experimental results from general-purpose and domain-specific MLLMs reveal persistent challenges in understanding large SAR scenes and accurately perceiving small targets. We have open-sourced XLSAR-Bench to support further research in developing more powerful MLLMs for complete large SAR scenes.
evidence_items.title: XLSAR-Bench: Towards Extremely Large SAR Imagery Understanding of MLLMs

evidence_items.summary: Legal reasoning in civil-law systems is not rule-lookup: the German state examination asks for a structured opinion (Gutachten) that names the governing norms, applies them to the facts, and argues to a conclusion. We introduce GPBam (German Public Law Bar-style Exam), 81 public-law examination cases with reference solutions, paired with a recitation task over 200 statutory provisions. Drawn from state examination preparation, the cases are broad and rarely repeat, and are not publicly available - we find no evidence of exact-solution memorisation in the models we evaluate, and keeping them private limits contamination. Because each reference solution's cited norms form a retrieval gold set over the very instances the essays are graded on, GPBam scores retrieval and long-form generation jointly, which makes it a benchmark for legal retrieval as well as for legal writing and lets us ask how much retrieval quality a legal opinion actually needs. Across 32 open-weight and proprietary models evaluated without retrieval, scores span 4.81-76.42 out of 100. Supplying the law helps modestly: across seven models and eight retrieval configurations, retrieval performance varies nearly threefold and buys at most 4.1 essay points, and nothing significant for three of the seven, while an oracle with 91% gold-norm recall improves scores by 2-6 points. Essay quality strongly tracks prior knowledge: verbatim statute recall, measured in a separate task, correlates at $\rho = 0.92$ over 32 models.
evidence_items.title: GPBam: A Retrieval-Aware German Public Law Exam Benchmark

evidence_items.summary: Paired unretouched/retouched face videos are costly to produce because professional editing must remain consistent over time, while releasing identifiable face footage raises privacy, consent, and governance concerns. We present DeepVFR, an initial controlled synthetic benchmark-not a new retouching architecture-for paired face video retouching. Starting from paired synthetic DeepFRR images, Wan2.2 generates mild-motion source clips, and backend-specific face transfer constructs synchronized proxy retouching targets, followed by automatic validity screening and manual visual inspection. DeepVFR contains 1,024 pairs of 150-frame clips at 30 fps, evaluated under an identity-disjoint protocol with explicit frame correspondence; release metadata will record the construction route. Within-benchmark baselines, external checkpoints applied to DeepVFR, qualitative analysis, and a 17-participant ranking study establish reference behavior in the controlled domain. The constructed targets exhibit a substantial low-preference tail in the human study. Because both streams inherit synthetic content and the targets additionally inherit commercial-API or face-transfer artifacts, the benchmark neither replaces artist-retouched captured video nor establishes synthetic-to-real generalization. DeepVFR provides a starting point for paired supervision and controlled evaluation. Data, individual study rankings, and training logs will be made publicly available upon acceptance. Broader motion coverage and real-video validation remain future work.
evidence_items.title: From Retouched Images to Paired Videos: A Synthetic Benchmark for Face Video Retouching

evidence_items.summary: A query-based multi-view 3D detector can transfer well to a new calibrated camera network and still produce badly fragmented tracks: on the AI City Challenge 2026 Track 1 validation set, the frozen Sparse4D detector behind the official challenge winner splits each Person identity into a median of eight fragments, and half of the gaps between fragments exceed the horizon of a causal tracker. We show that most of the remaining headroom of such a system lies after detection. Keeping the public detector frozen, we add (i) class-wise source selection between two input scales, which recovers small and distant people from a 0.75x pass while leaving large objects at the scale the detector was trained for; (ii) a geometry-to-appearance bridge that projects every 3D box into all calibrated views, matches it to 2D person detections, and aggregates robust track-level re-identification descriptors; and (iii) constraint-aware consolidation, which combines a causal short-gap stitch with offline centroid-linkage clustering under two hard constraints, temporal exclusion and metric 3D reachability, plus class-aware long-gap stitching for rigid objects. Every association stage changes object identities only. On the challenge evaluation server the system scores 62.3947 3D HOTA (DetA 57.4501, AssA 56.8131, LocA 80.1272), first on the general leaderboard snapshot of 30 October 2026 (second at the time of writing, after a competitor's detector update) and 5.63 points above our reproduction of the official winner; the constrained association stage alone contributes +3.73 HOTA through a +5.49 AssA gain at unchanged DetA. Controlled fixed-box validation studies, a constraint ablation, sensitivity curves, and a catalogue of negative results support the design.
evidence_items.title: Detection Is Not the Finish Line: Multiscale Decoding and Constraint-Aware Global Association for Multi-Camera 3D Tracking

evidence_items.summary: Relation extraction systems often identify what a relation is, but not the condition under which it holds. This can collapse condition-bound claims into unsupported generalizations, a failure we call relation overgeneralization. We introduce CondRelBench, a mixed-domain benchmark for evaluating condition-scoped relation understanding. Each claim is represented as (E1, R, E2 | C), where C is the condition licensing the relation. Using 3,000 synthetic paragraphs, 200 PubMed full-text papers, and 695 Reddit posts, we construct five probe variants per tuple that preserve, replace, remove, or contradict the condition, or contradict the relation itself. Models classify each probe as Supported, Not Supported, or Not Enough Evidence. We also introduce Overgeneralization Rate (OGR) and Scope Preservation Score (SPS) to measure false support for altered claims and consistency across probe families. Across prompted LLMs, fine-tuned LLMs, and encoder models, we find that Accuracy and Macro F1 often hide scope failures. Models frequently support the original scoped claim but fail when its condition is removed or altered. Domain-specific encoders achieve the strongest scope preservation, while instruction-tuned LLMs often show higher overgeneralization. Synthetic supervision helps but does not close the gap to real-world PubMed and Reddit performance.
evidence_items.title: CondRelBench: A Mixed-Domain Benchmark for Condition-Scoped Relation Understanding

evidence_items.summary: Empirical research on software architecture maintenance and evolution is hindered by the scarcity of large-scale, validated, and richly annotated model datasets. Existing benchmarks are limited in scale, provide only model-level annotations, or lack alignment with reference architectures, thereby restricting reproducible studies of architectural reuse, conformance, and AI-driven analysis. To address this gap, we present A3D, a curated dataset of 1,115 Architecture Analysis and Design Language (AADL) models mined from public GitHub repositories and validated with the OSATE tool. The dataset spans 7 generic domains and 52 specific-problem clusters, and provides two annotation layers: (i) domain- and problem-level labels, which capture different model aggregation criteria, and (ii) component-level mappings to three reference architectures, which have been externally validated through a user study. Models are released in AADL and JSON formats with full provenance, a reproducible mining pipeline, and the validation protocol.
evidence_items.title: Mining Architectural Models in the Wild: A Curated Dataset of AADL Models

evidence_items.summary: Coding and computation remain major bottlenecks in Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) workflows, especially as modern sampling algorithms have become increasingly complex and existing probabilistic programming systems remain limited in model support, extensibility, and composability. We introduce AI4BayesCode, an extensible LLM-driven system that translates natural-language Bayesian model descriptions into runnable, validated MCMC samplers. To improve reliability, AI4BayesCode adopts a modular design that decomposes models into modular sampling blocks and maps each block to a built-in sampling component, reducing the need to implement complex sampling algorithms from scratch. Reliability is further improved through pre-generation validation of model specifications and post-generation validation of generated sampler code. AI4BayesCode also introduces a novel recursively stateful coding paradigm for MCMC, allowing modular sampling components, potentially developed by different contributors, to be composed coherently within larger MCMC procedures. We develop a benchmark suite to evaluate AI4BayesCode for sampler-generation. Experiments show that AI4BayesCode can implement a wide range of Bayesian models from natural-language descriptions alone. As an open-ended system, its capability can continue to expand with improvements in the underlying AI agent and the addition of new built-in blocks. The software is available at https://ai4bayescode.com/.
evidence_items.title: AI4BayesCode: From Natural Language Descriptions to Validated Modular Stateful Bayesian Samplers

evidence_items.summary: Electronic Health Records (EHR) contain rich longitudinal patient information and are widely used in predictive modeling applications. However, effectively leveraging historical data remains challenging due to long trajectories, heterogeneous events, temporal irregularity, and the varying relevance of past clinical context. Existing approaches often rely on fixed windows or uniform aggregation, which can obscure clinically important signals. In this work, we introduce EHR-RAGp, a retrieval-based framework that dynamically integrates the most relevant patient history consisting of diverse clinical event types. We propose a prototype-guided retrieval module that acts as an alignment mechanism and estimates the relevance of retrieved historical chunks with respect to a given prediction task, guiding the model towards the most informative context. Across multiple clinical prediction tasks and two benchmark datasets, EHR-RAGp consistently outperforms state-of- the-art EHR-based and transformer-based baselines. Furthermore, EHR-RAGp is model-agnostic, as integrating it with various backbone models yields substantial performance gains. Overall, EHR-RAGp establishes a novel direction for modeling long-range clinical context to improve downstream performance via retrieval.
evidence_items.title: EHR-RAGp: Prototype-Guided Retrieval of Longitudinal Electronic Health Records for Clinical Prediction Models

evidence_items.summary: Generative medical event models use tokenized sequences of patient timelines as input, but practical guidance on the many decisions around tokenization is limited because most studies keep the tokenizer fixed while scaling architecture or data. We benchmark quantization granularity, reference-range anchoring, code--value fusion, numeric and temporal encodings, and schema harmonization across 156 models. Using both Llama-3.2-style and Qwen3-style architectures, all models were trained on full MIMIC-IV hospitalizations from three initialization seeds under a shared training recipe, and linear probes evaluated frozen 24-hour representations across eight binary and regression outcome families during hours 24--48. Fused tokens pairing codes with value deciles produced statistically significant gains in six of eight families over unfused deciles, including all four regression families ($+0.032$ to $+0.114$ Spearman correlation) and vital-signs classification ($+0.033$ AUROC), with 38 of 48 comparisons significant across all six quantization schemes (seven of eight families). Next-token training organized unfused and fused centile embeddings into ordered trajectories and made clinical reference ranges linearly decodable in unfused centiles (93--97\% accuracy). Neither reference-range anchoring nor finer quantization consistently improved 24-hour probes. Event order and admission-relative RoPE shortened inputs while marginally raising all eight family means over explicit time tokens (five and four statistically significant). Mapping native input to the Common Longitudinal Intensive Care Unit Data Format (CLIF) cut training tokens by 71.4\% and vocabulary size by 97.8\%, with statistically significant gains in four of eight families. These findings show that compact, expert-curated tokenizations can outperform more granular and continuous alternatives under a shared training recipe.
evidence_items.title: Representation Before Training: A Practical Benchmark for Generative Medical Event Model Tokenization

evidence_items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) have achieved strong performance on code completion in general-purpose programming languages, but existing repository-level benchmarks focus almost exclusively on software code and largely overlook hardware description languages (HDLs). We present \textbf{MHRC-Bench}, consisting of \textbf{MHRC-Bench-Train} and \textbf{MHRC-Bench-Eval}, the first benchmark for multilingual hardware code completion at the repository level with functional evaluation. MHRC-Bench covers three major hardware design coding styles and annotates each completion target with code-structure-level and hardware-oriented semantic labels derived from concrete syntax tree (CST) analysis. Post-training billion-scale code LLMs on MHRC-Bench-Train enables smaller open-weight models to outperform much larger general-purpose models under matched context windows. Beyond aggregate accuracy, our analysis surfaces four findings that distinguish hardware from software code completion: \emph{(i)}~performance varies sharply across HDLs, with high-level synthesis (HLS) easiest and VHDL hardest in most settings across functional pass rate, exact match (EM), and edit similarity (ES); \emph{(ii)}~hardware accuracy is non-monotonic in code-structure depth, in contrast with the monotonic depth--accuracy curve known for software; \emph{(iii)}~accuracy plateaus once the input context exceeds 2{,}048 tokens, while software completion continues to benefit from longer context; and \emph{(iv)}~certain repository-level retrievers tuned on software underperform a no-retrieval baseline on HDL repositories because their structural and dependency assumptions are violated by hardware code.
evidence_items.title: MHRC-Bench: A Multilingual Hardware Repository-Level Code Completion benchmark

evidence_items.summary: Oversteer, wherein a vehicle's rear tires lose traction and induce unintentional excessive yaw, poses critical safety challenges. Failing to control oversteer often leads to severe traffic accidents. Although recent autonomous driving efforts have attempted to handle oversteer through stabilizing maneuvers, the majority rely on expert-defined trajectories or assume obstacle-free environments, limiting real-world applicability. This paper introduces a novel end-to-end (E2E) autonomous driving approach that tackles oversteer control and collision avoidance simultaneously. Existing E2E techniques, including Imitation Learning (IL), Reinforcement Learning (RL), and Hybrid Learning (HL), generally require near-optimal demonstrations or extensive experience. Yet even skilled human drivers struggle to provide perfect demonstrations under oversteer, and high transition variance hinders the accumulation of sufficient data. Hence, we present Q-Compared Soft Actor-Critic (QC-SAC), a new HL algorithm that effectively learns from immature demonstration data and adapts rapidly to new conditions. To evaluate QC-SAC, we introduce a benchmark inspired by real-world driver training: a vehicle encounters sudden oversteer on a slippery surface and must avoid randomly placed obstacles ahead. Experimental results show that QC-SAC attains near-optimal driving policies, significantly surpassing state-of-the-art IL, RL, and HL baselines. Hardware-in-the-loop simulation (HILS) validation with physical steering hardware further demonstrates that QC-SAC can operate beyond a software-only simulation, providing an intermediate validation step toward real-vehicle implementation. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first work that achieves safe autonomous control of vehicles in oversteer while simultaneously avoiding obstacles.
evidence_items.title: Learning-based Autonomous Oversteer Control and Collision Avoidance

evidence_items.summary: This dataset accompanies the paper “Seeing is Believing: The Case for Hardware-Centric Inefficiency Detection and Remediation,” published in the ACM Symposium on Cloud Computing (SoCC 2026). It provides the evaluation data for Unveil, a hardware-centric observability framework designed to detect, identify, and remediate silent performance inefficiencies in machine learning workloads. Unveil operates using host-visible telemetry without requiring guest-side instrumentation or modifications to applications and their software environments. The dataset covers controlled microbenchmarks and large language model (LLM) serving workloads, including experiments involving NUMA misplacement, interrupt locality issues, reduced transparent huge-page coverage, and GPU power throttling. It includes hardware telemetry traces, anomaly detection results, inefficiency fingerprints, performance measurements, and supporting data for reproducing the evaluation presented in the paper. The dataset is intended to facilitate reproducibility and further research into hardware-centric observability, online anomaly detection, inefficiency fingerprinting, and performance diagnosis in machine learning systems. A detailed description of the dataset structure, file formats, and correspondence to the paper's evaluation is provided in the accompanying README. Associated Publication Ziji Chen, Steven W. D. Chien, Peng Qian, and Noa Zilberman. 2026. Seeing is Believing: The Case for Hardware-Centric Inefficiency Detection and Remediation. ACM Symposium on Cloud Computing, Volume 2 (SoCC 2026). evidence_items.summary: Long-range Saharan dust transport affects radiation, clouds, and air quality, yet its vertical structure and entrainment into the boundary layer remain challenging to simulate. We investigate four contrasting dust events over southwestern Germany using ground-based lidar, sun-photometer and in situ aerosol measurements, satellite observations, backward trajectories, and ICON-ART simulations. The events represent diverse atmospheric conditions, including a six-day cloud-free 5 episode, a cloudy episode involving dust–cloud interactions, and an intense outbreak with aerosol optical depth approaching 1.4. A depolarization-based lidar method separated dust backscatter from contributions by other aerosols, enabling a like-forlike evaluation of the dust represented by ICON-ART and providing a useful approach for evaluating dust models in mixed aerosol layers. ICON-ART reproduced the large-scale transport and arrival of the dust layers, with mean differences of approximately 20 min in arrival time and 50 m in layer height. Daily re-initialization of the global simulations improved correlations 10 with observed near-surface particulate matter concentrations from 0.65–0.69 to 0.86–0.88 and better reproduced the timing and persistence of boundary-layer dust. The benefits of higher resolution (2 and 1 km) become more apparent when combined with model reinitialization. However, ICON-ART consistently overestimated particles of 0.5–2 μm and underestimated particles larger than 2 μm. These results demonstrate the complementary benefits of accurate meteorological initialization and convection-permitting resolution while identifying size-dependent emission, sedimentation, and deposition as priorities for 15 model development. By distinguishing errors in dust transport from those arising from aerosol size representation, this study provides an observation-constrained framework for evaluating and improving convection-permitting dust forecasts.

evidence_items.summary: What's new in 1.14.0 ProvSQL 1.14.0 computes exact probabilities faster. When a lineage splits into parts that share no input tuple, each part is now evaluated separately. And the d-DNNFs compiled in a session are kept: a later lineage with the same structure, over other tuples or with other probabilities, reuses them instead of being compiled again. Both are on by default, with no change to queries. The choice of a probability method is also more robust: a method that takes longer than expected is retried later with a larger budget instead of being abandoned, and an external compiler that runs far too long is stopped. The splitting and the cache were contributed by Aryak Sen (#111). Splitting independent parts When a lineage is an AND or an OR of parts that share no input tuple, the parts are grouped by the tuples they share and each group is evaluated separately. The probability of an AND is then the product of those of its groups, and that of an OR is one minus the product of their complements. A group with a single part is split again. A query whose answer combines many unrelated groups, such as the lines of each order, is then as fast to evaluate as its hardest group. With the default method, splitting is tried when independent fails, and a method is chosen for each group. The new setting provsql.idp fold (default auto ) can turn it off , or on for a method called by name, which then runs on each group. provsql.last eval method and Studio report such an evaluation as fold , followed by the methods used on the groups. Reusing compiled d-DNNFs Each session keeps the d-DNNFs built by tree-decomposition and compilation , indexed by a canonical form of the circuit, which records its structure but not its input tuples. A circuit is looked up piece by piece (first its independent parts, then the rest), and only the pieces not found are compiled. The answers of a single query often have the same structure, so most of them need no compilation.
evidence_items.title: ProvSQL: Semiring Provenance and Probability Management for PostgreSQL

evidence_items.summary: Frame-wise indoor mobile LiDAR dataset to support research on semantic segmentation of indoor 3D point clouds. The dataset was collected in the ITC building (Langezijds) at the University of Twente. Data acquisition was conducted outside working hours to avoid the presence of people. The scanned areas include classrooms, corridors, meeting rooms, shared offices, and study areas. Private offices, restricted laboratories, server rooms, and control rooms are excluded. The dataset contains 52 indoor sequences, 79,108 frame-wise MLS point clouds, and 1.23 billion labeled points covering 16 semantic classes. The labeled point clouds are stored in binary format, with (x, y, z), intensity, and semantic label recorded for each point. Both the original LiDAR-frame and gravity-aligned coordinate representations are provided. Synchronized and undistorted RGB images are stored in .png format with a resolution of (1280 x 1024) pixels. The RGB images were used to assist the semantic annotation process and can also support research on 2D–3D cross-modal semantic segmentation. During dataset construction, BIM data of the building were used to assist the annotation process. However, the BIM data are not included in the released dataset. The dataset is publicly released to support research on frame-wise indoor MLS semantic segmentation and related indoor 3D scene understanding tasks.

evidence_items.summary: Analysis code and processed dataset for a market-scale empirical benchmark of 310 European-market production battery electric vehicles, using manufacturer specifications certified under the Worldwide Harmonised Light Vehicle Test Procedure (WLTP). CONTENTS The deposit contains the analysis dataset (478 vehicles, of which 310 carry complete certified figures) and four Python scripts that reproduce every table and figure in the accompanying article. Running run all.py regenerates the full set of results in roughly two minutes. WHY THE DATASET CARRIES TWO VARIABLE SETS The upstream specification source publishes both manufacturer-certified type-approval figures and its own modelled estimates of real-world performance. A field-identification audit established that three widely used columns hold the modelled estimates rather than the certified values. The choice is consequential: on the same 310 vehicles, the fleet-level correlation between energy consumption and certified range is -0.31 using certified figures and +0.02 using the modelled estimates, and the multivariate consumption elasticity is -0.886 against -0.393. Both variable sets are retained side by side in certified dataset.csv so this comparison can be reproduced directly. KEY RESULTS REPRODUCED Useable battery capacity is the dominant correlate of certified range, with an almost exactly proportional multivariate elasticity (1.013, 95% CI 0.985 to 1.041). Energy consumption carries a partial elasticity of -0.886. Raw energy consumption differs across drivetrain layouts, but the difference tracks vehicle size and mass and no layout term survives conditioning; the drivetrain result is reported as a bounded null, with any residual association confined to roughly 2% of certified range.

evidence_items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly applied to finance, creating a need for benchmarks that evaluate their capabilities across financial systems with different regulations and practices. However, existing financial benchmarks provide limited coverage of country-specific financial systems, and they are difficult to keep up to date as released questions leak into training data. We introduce JFinBench, a Japanese financial benchmark comprising 321 examples from the 2026 editions of six regularly administered certification exams covering accounting, tax, financial planning, and banking. To construct it, we develop a human-in-the-loop agentic pipeline in which a coding agent writes exam-specific conversion code and a review page, while a human verifies every example and feeds corrections back to the agent. This pipeline adapts to heterogeneous exam formats and reduces the effort of incorporating new exam editions, enabling periodic refreshes that mitigate data contamination. Evaluating 12 recent LLMs, we find that Claude Fable 5 and GPT-6 Astra exceed 93% overall, while even the best open-weight model, Kimi K3.1 Pro, trails Claude Fable 5 by 12 percentage points. When models can additionally use a terminal and web access, they retrieve the knowledge they lack and every model improves. The gap narrows but about 4 points remain, and the ranking of models stays largely the same, suggesting that knowledge held in the model itself remains valuable even with tools. We release the dataset, the evaluation code, and the construction pipeline.
evidence_items.title: JFinBench: A Continuously Refreshable Japanese Financial Benchmark from the Latest Certification Exams

evidence_items.summary: Standard coding-agent benchmarks primarily evaluate binary task success, treating execution as a black box and obscuring the behaviors that produce those outcomes. We analyze a large corpus of 143,209 execution trajectories from 125 agent configurations spanning 117 unique models. To enable comparisons across heterogeneous agent interfaces, we develop a rule-based parser that maps raw execution traces to high-level actions such as repository search, file editing, and test execution, and audit its predictions against a six-model consensus reference on 500 events. We find that agents with similar solve rates can nevertheless differ substantially in how they explore, modify and verify code. Moreover, without using task outcomes, token counts, or tool names as features, aggregate behavioral profiles retrieve the corresponding agent stack across disjoint repository sets and programming languages, although task composition is not fully controlled in the cross-repository setting. Through analyses of frontier models and agent scaffolds, we further show that scaffold choice and reasoning effort systematically shift agents' search, editing, and testing behavior. We release the deterministic parser together with the full annotation and analysis pipeline alongside an annotated trajectory subset.
evidence_items.title: Interpreting Coding Agents Through Their Behavioral Trajectories

evidence_items.summary: While large language models (LLMs) have captured global attention for their linguistic abilities, our work harnesses their power to overcome traditional barriers in querying Linked Data (LD) and Resource Description Framework (RDF) triplestores. This article presents an innovative framework that integrates LLMs into conversational user interfaces (UIs), enabling the dynamic generation of precise SPARQL queries without the necessity for constant retraining. Most conversational UI models struggle with adaptability as they require frequent retraining whenever datasets are updated or expanded. This limitation impedes their effectiveness as general-purpose extraction tools. To address this challenge, our approach 1 seamlessly incorporates LLMs into the conversational UI process, fostering a more sophisticated understanding and interpretation of user queries and enhancing overall responsiveness. By leveraging the advanced natural language processing capabilities of LLMs, our method improves RDF entity extraction in web systems that utilise conventional chatbots. Furthermore, it extends the functionality of these chatbots, allowing them to respond directly to queries based on the RDF schema while providing an assistive interface that deepens understanding of the dataset and its underlying domain. This facilitates the extraction of more meaningful information. By adopting this approach, interactions become more refined and context-sensitive, a crucial advancement for managing the intricate query structures commonly found in RDF datasets and Linked Open Data (LOD) endpoints. We have evaluated our approach in practical settings by assessing the tool’s ability to address complex queries and to answer general ecological queries, with the outputs evaluated by human experts. The results demonstrate a notable improvement in system expressiveness and response accuracy, showcasing the potential of LLMs to transform information retrieval.
evidence_items.title: Dialogue Meets Data: A Large Language Model Approach for Efficient Linked Data Retrieval

evidence_items.summary: This study examined the role of counselors in modifying hyperactive behaviours among upper primary school pupils in Oshimili South Local Government Area of Delta State. Hyperactive behaviour, characterized by excessive restlessness, impulsiveness, poor attention span and disruptive classroom conduct, has become a major concern in primary schools because of its adverse effects on pupils' academic achievement, classroom participation and social adjustment. The study sought to identify the causes of hyperactive behaviours, examine the roles performed by school counselors, determine the behaviour modification techniques employed, assess their effectiveness and identify the challenges encountered by counselors. The study adopted a descriptive cross-sectional survey research design. The population comprised teachers in selected public primary schools in Oshimili South Local Government Area, while a sample of 330 teachers was selected using an appropriate sampling technique. A structured questionnaire titled Role of Counselors in Modifying Hyperactive Behaviours Questionnaire (RCMHBQ) was used for data collection. The instrument was validated by experts in Guidance and Counselling and Measurement and Evaluation, while its reliability was established using the Cronbach Alpha method. Data were analysed using frequency counts, percentages, mean and standard deviation, while the hypotheses were tested using appropriate inferential statistical techniques at the 0.05 level of significance. Findings revealed that genetic, neurological, environmental and parenting factors were major causes of hyperactive behaviours. Counselors played significant roles through behavioural assessment, individual and group counselling, consultation with parents and teachers, and behaviour modification techniques such as positive reinforcement, modelling, behaviour contracts and cognitive behavioural counselling.
evidence_items.title: THE ROLE OF A COUNSELOR IN MODIFYING HYPERACTIVE BEHAVIOURS AMONG UPPER PRIMARY SCHOOL PUPILS IN OSHIMILI SOUTH L.G.A, ASABA DELTA STATE.

evidence_items.summary: Disclaimer: This is an author-accepted manuscript of a paper accepted for publication in the Proceedings of the 20th International Conference on Human Interaction & Emerging Technologies: Future Systems and Design Applications (IHIET-FS 2027), June 24-25, 2027, Cambridge, United Kingdom. Please cite the final published version when available. Abstract: Public health surveillance infrastructures and clinical decision-support dashboards routinely ingest discrete, aggregated, and non-harmonized health data streams. While conventional software validation in medical informatics focuses on network throughput and volumetric scalability, analytical engines frequently suffer severe operational degradation, manifesting as false-positive alert storms, denominator-shift drift, and alert fatigue, when processing sparse, zero-inflated, or heavily skewed event counts. To address this vulnerability, we introduce a deterministic, trace-driven load-testing paradigm that repurposes exact statistical confidence limits and non-linear asymptotic transformations into an active heuristic perturbation engine (P). Specifically, the framework integrates Garwood’s exact Poisson lower confidence bounds, Wilson–Hilferty cube-root saturation thresholds, and Cornish–Fisher skewness corrections to systematically deform the uncertainty floor of aggregated surveillance matrices without requiring synthetic big-data generation. Using multi-state European West Nile virus surveillance records (2019–2023) across human, avian, and equid compartments as an empirical workload benchmark, we evaluated a hardened analytical pipeline against standard asymptotic Gaussian thresholding.
evidence_items.title: Heuristic Uncertainty Floor Perturbations for Big Health Data: Engineering a Load-Test Paradigm in Medical Informatics

On the Behnke-Geiger flexible job shops, an agent-written tabu search improved 11 of 32 open instances. With two transport robots, an agent-written solver improved seven of ten MKT instances. evidence_items.summary: Background Acute kidney injury after cardiac surgery (CSA-AKI) is common yet detected late. Risk stratification at the end of surgery could enable timely renal protection, but most machine learning (ML) models either use postoperative data or lack a transparent, pre-specified evaluation. Methods In a retrospective single-center cohort of 1,352 adult cardiac surgery patients (211 AKI, 15.6%), we predicted AKI from 32 routine preoperative and intraoperative (up to end-of-surgery) variables. We benchmarked 210 combinations (five feature-selection strategies × seven algorithms × six class weights) by repeated stratified 5-fold cross-validation (10 repeats) on a fixed development set ( n = 1,081), selected the final model by a pre-specified two-stage rule, and evaluated it once on a fixed test set ( n = 271). A screening-oriented threshold (sensitivity ≥0.80) was pre-specified. We additionally tested the few-shot transformer TabPFN, stability selection, bootstrap optimism correction, and simple ensembling, with SHAP for interpretability. Results The selected random forest (positive-class weighting, isotonic calibration) achieved a test-set AUC of 0.722 (95% CI 0.634–0.799), sensitivity 0.762, and specificity 0.515. No model family was decisively superior; penalized linear models generalized comparably, and none of the small-sample strategies or ensembling improved discrimination. Bootstrap correction reduced the apparent AUC from 0.965 to a corrected 0.724. Homocysteine ranked first in SHAP importance and was among ten independent factors in multivariable logistic regression. Conclusion Routine perioperative variables support a screening-oriented, interpretable prediction of AKI at the end of cardiac surgery, with modest discrimination. The lack of model superiority argues for parsimony, and homocysteine merits prospective study; external validation is required before clinical use.
evidence_items.title: Prediction of acute kidney injury at the end of cardiac surgery using routine perioperative variables: a pre-specified benchmark of 210 machine learning combinations

evidence_items.summary: Text simplification has been a long-standing research topic to make complex information more accessible to a wider audience, yet high-performance Large Language Model (LLM) fine-tuning remains computationally expensive. This research proposes a cost-effective alternative: a multi-agent framework utilizing Small Language Models (SLMs) to achieve high-fidelity simplification for educational knowledge management. Our methodology frames simplification as an iterative, multi-stage reasoning process rather than a single-step transformation. Specialized agents perform sequential semantic analysis, linguistic simplification, and factual verification to minimize information loss and ensure interpretability. To validate the framework, we applied the system to a scientific corpus regarding Robotic Mobile Fulfilment Systems (RMFS). Performance was evaluated using BERTScore, SARI, and Flesch–Kincaid Grade Level across three SLM backbones (Llama3.2 3B, Gemma3 4B, and Qwen3 4B). Results show that the multi-agent pipeline consistently outperforms zero-shot baselines in edit quality, with Qwen 3 achieving SARI of 51.82 while maintaining strong semantic fidelity (BERTScore up to 0.94). The contributions of this work are twofold: (1) a novel, iterative SLM-based multi-agent architecture for scientific text simplification; and (2) a domain-specific RMFS dataset featuring simplifications validated by both human expert and LLM judges with substantial inter-rater agreement (κ = 0.703).
evidence_items.title: Minimal Lossiness Agentic AI for Scientific Text Simplification Leveraging Multi-Agent SLMs for Effective Knowledge Transfer

evidence_items.summary: Law changes over time. A court decides a case under the law in force on that day, and legal QA benchmarks grade answers against today's law. We checked 156,650 decisions of four Thai courts. Up to 67% of them cite law that has since been amended or repealed. We introduce Nitibench+, the sequel of our NitiBench, a Thai legal QA benchmark with 1,670 items across 17 domains, built from decisions of three courts. For each cited section it holds both the text in force on the decision date and the current text, and its retrieval corpus holds every dated version of every Thai statute section. Answers are graded on the Thai Bar Council rubric, the Bar-standard score, and on the overlap between the cited sections and the court's. The report has two parts. Part I measures the cost of the wrong text on 13 open-weight models. Reading the current text of amended law drops the Bar-standard score by 0.25 and missing repealed law drops it by 0.79. The penalty comes from rule changes, 0.45 on the 428 rule-changed items and none on the 331 wording-only items, and Citation F1 does not see it. The text in force is the fair setting. Part II benchmarks today's models on that setting. A public leaderboard ranks 33 models on a held-out test split of 500 items stratified by domain, with a validation split of the same shape released for public use, from memory alone, with the court's sections provided, and as a retrieval agent over the law in force, with the cost per item and the hallucinated citations. The best model scores 7.78 out of 10 and the best open-weight model 6.39. Without a search tool only five open-weight models recall any Thai law, and with it 27 of the 33 models gain and six lose. Leaderboard will take new models as they are released. Legal benchmarks must track dates, and on the right text today's models still leave a wide gap on Thai law.
evidence_items.title: NitiBench+: A Temporal Thai Legal Question Answering Benchmark Across 17 Domains

evidence_items.summary: Parsons problems have been widely recognised to support novice learners by reducing the cognitive demands of writing code from scratch through rearrangement of provided code blocks. A common variation includes distractors – erroneous blocks of code which do not belong to the correct solution. While Parsons problems have been widely studied for introductory programming, they remain underexplored in various domains including in data science education, where students may possess statistical knowledge but limited programming experience. Developing distractors is also time-consuming for educators. This study investigated the feasibility of using a large language model (LLM) to generate semantic distractors for data science Parsons problems. A set of distractors was generated for 315 Python-based data science Parsons problems and was evaluated for pedagogical plausibility, compilability, and output divergence. Validated distractors were then incorporated as exemplars in a refined prompt to generate a second set of distractors, which were evaluated using the same criteria. The findings demonstrate that LLMs can be used to develop semantic distractors for data science Parsons problems and refining the prompts using validated exemplars further improved the quality. This study contributes to the limited literature on data science Parsons problems, distractor design and LLM-supported development of these problems.
evidence_items.title: Large language model generation of plausible semantic distractors for data science Parsons problems

evidence_items.summary: We evaluated Jev, a non-generative decision model, for title and abstract screening using 4527 records from two systematic reviews of bipolar disorder treatments previously used in our 2024 Journal of Medical Internet Research study. Human decisions to retain records for full-text assessment served as the reference. In the primary analysis, Jev answered yes-or-no questions (Noul); at a prespecified 50% cutoff, sensitivity and specificity were 99.6% and 98.9% for light therapy and 93.2% and 93.5% for adjunctive pharmacotherapy. For direct model comparison, Jev used explicit include/exclude options (Choice) and the same prompts as GPT-5 mini and GPT-6 Astra. Jev Choice achieved sensitivity and specificity similar to or higher than those of GPT-5 mini and GPT-6 Astra, while API charges per 1000 records were US$0.043 for Jev, US$0.57 for GPT-5 mini, and US$7.39 for GPT-6 Astra. Jev retained all reports ultimately included in both reviews across all tested conditions and runs. Although these findings do not establish that decision models can replace human reviewers, they support Jev as a promising, low-cost alternative to the tested generative LLM configurations for assisting human title and abstract screening. Independent validation across diverse review topics is needed to assess Jev’s generalizability and utility in human-supervised screening workflows.
evidence_items.title: Title and Abstract Screening for Systematic Reviews with Jev, a Decision Model: Comparison with Generative Large Language Models

evidence_items.summary: Mobile manipulators can move between storage locations and handle goods, but transferring the semantic capabilities of foundation models to dependable warehouse operations remains constrained by execution interfaces, data coverage, and operating conditions. This thematic critical review examines perception, reasoning, planning and execution, and data and generalization. It compares hierarchical approaches with vision-language-action models and assesses their relevance to warehouse tasks using representative studies. Its distinctive value lies in relating model interfaces and transfer limits to warehouse order fulfillment, where stock-keeping unit (SKU) verification, shelf access, and onboard resource limits must be considered together. The evidence indicates that foundation models reorganize selected interfaces between observations, task descriptions, and actions; they do not remove the need for geometric feasibility checks, low-level control, or failure recovery. Open-vocabulary recognition must be connected to item-level verification, while semantic generalization should be distinguished from the acquisition of new motor skills. Reported transfer gains also depend on the task, embodiment, and adaptation budget. The review identifies order completion, coordinated base-arm motion, and measurable adaptation costs as priorities for research and evaluation. These conclusions support method selection and experimental design rather than a claim of validated warehouse deployment.
evidence_items.title: Warehouse Mobile Manipulation with Large Language Models and Foundation Models

evidence_items.summary: Abstract As large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to gather, process and disseminate scientific information, concerns have grown about their identity-related biases. However, national-background biases in scientific evaluation remain insufficiently understood. Existing studies are limited to a narrow range of countries, abbreviated materials and/or simplified evaluation criteria, and have reported inconsistent findings. Moreover, differences in the textual evaluations generated by LLMs have seldom been quantified. Here, we used four popular LLMs to evaluate 292 full-text manuscripts from 28 journals across 8 research fields under 12 assigned national backgrounds, yielding 14,016 manuscript assessments, each covering 28 evaluative dimensions. Further comment-based rescoring tests were conducted to quantify differences in their textual evaluations. The results showed systematic differences in both scores and comments despite unchanged scientific content, with the magnitude and statistical significance these differences varying across national backgrounds. Under different national backgrounds, LLMs could offer different views on the same issue, and give different scores alongside similar textual evaluation. Researchers and decision-makers should be aware of these biases associated with source identity, including national background, when using LLMs for information gathering and processing.
evidence_items.title: National-background bias in scientific evaluation based on large language models

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly being considered as tools for computational social science, yet their implications for survey and public-opinion research remain insufficiently understood. This study examines whether and how they can serve as methodological instruments for estimating aggregate public opinion under out-of-sample conditions. Across three studies, commercial and open-source LLMs are evaluated against recent Pew Research Centre surveys. Study 1 shows that GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 can approximate national-level response distributions more accurately than uniform, normal-distribution, and historical-average baselines, with GPT-4 achieving mean absolute errors of approximately 4–8.5%. However, the models also exhibit important threats to validity, including underrepresentation of Republican viewpoints, underestimation of uncertainty, and, in some cases, overly homogeneous response distributions. Study 2 extends the analysis to GPT-4o, GPT-4o-mini, and Llama 3.3, showing that aggregate predictive accuracy generalises across models but that partisan alignment and distributional fidelity are model- and topic-dependent. Study 3 demonstrates that collective-level estimation is more valid than aggregating persona-based individual simulations, which produce substantially higher error and stronger homogeneity bias. Ablation tests further indicate that predictions are relatively robust to role prompts and temperature settings but sensitive to survey-item context. These findings suggest that LLMs may be useful as exploratory and supplementary tools in public-opinion research. However, the responsible use of LLMs requires explicit validation against human data, attention to bias and uncertainty, and careful integration with established principles of survey design.
evidence_items.title: Public opinion surveys with large language models: methodological opportunities and validity risks

evidence_items.summary: Automatically generating complete and reliable Planning Domain Definition Language (PDDL) models from natural-language task requirements remains challenging because large language models (LLMs) may produce incomplete domain knowledge, inconsistent symbolic definitions, and models that cannot support valid planning. This paper proposes OntoPDDL, an ontology-guided method for automatically constructing complete PDDL Domain–Problem models. OntoPDDL uses a domain ontology to provide explicit knowledge constraints and organizes Domain construction according to the structural dependencies among PDDL components, followed by Problem instantiation within the generated Domain. Layered validation checks formal correctness and domain-semantic consistency, while validation and planner feedback guide targeted repairs to improve planning usability. Experiments on 24 earthquake-rescue tasks show that OntoPDDL achieves final Domain and Problem validation success rates of 100.0% and 91.7%, respectively, and increases planning success from 58.3% to 70.8% after planner-feedback repair, compared with 33.3% for LLM+P. Ablation results further support the roles of ontology constraints, dependency-aware generation, and feedback-based repair under the evaluated configurations. A separate task-semantic evaluation based on information correctness and rule-based information completion yields fidelity rates of 45.8% (11/24) for OntoPDDL and 8.3% (2/24) for LLM+P, indicating that OntoPDDL achieves higher task-semantic fidelity under the evaluated configurations. These results highlight improvements in model reliability and planning usability, alongside remaining challenges in task-semantic fidelity.
evidence_items.title: OntoPDDL: A PDDL Generation Method Based on Domain Ontologies and Large Language Models

organizations: Capital University of Economics and Business
evidence_items.summary: This paper investigates cost-aware adaptive prompt selection for large language models by modeling four prompt strategies as arms in a multi-armed bandit. Standard UCB and Thompson Sampling are compared with contextual extensions, LinUCB and Linear Thompson Sampling (LinTS), on GSM8K. The study evaluates accuracy, cumulative reward, cumulative regret, average token usage, tokens per correct answer, and budget satisfaction. On the held-out evaluation set, the Global Best prompt achieved 96.8% accuracy with a cumulative regret of 3.00, while the Oracle upper bound reached 97.4%. LinUCB achieved 95.47% accuracy with an average of 200.18 tokens per question, reducing token use by approximately 9.9% relative to the Global Best prompt (222.14 tokens). Under the medium normalized token budget B = 0.2893, cost-constrained LinUCB maintained 95.47%-95.49% accuracy and 93% budget satisfaction, compared with 30%-35% for LinTS. In addition, 92% of evaluation questions produced identical binary rewards across all four prompts, indicating limited prompt-specific heterogeneity. The results suggest that contextual prompt selection may provide greater value for resource control than for accuracy improvement in homogeneous, high-accuracy reasoning settings.
evidence_items.title: Cost-Aware Adaptive Prompt Selection for Large Language Models Using UCB and Thompson Sampling
