evidence_items.summary: Artificial intelligence (AI), machine learning (ML) and, more recently, generative AI (GenAI) models are becoming increasingly prevalent in the healthcare setting. For microbiology professionals, these technologies create opportunities to improve diagnostic workflows, analyse complex laboratory data, support education and professional development, summarise evidence, and assist with quality improvement. They also introduce risks, including automation bias, data leakage, poor generalisability, hallucinated or unverifiable outputs, privacy breaches, and unclear accountability. This article proposes a practical curriculum framework for microbiology professionals that treats GenAI as a distinct educational priority rather than a minor extension of conventional data, statistics or ML training. The curriculum framework is organised around six domains: (1) foundations of AI, ML and GenAI; (2) microbiology data and knowledge literacy; (3) critical appraisal, validation and evaluation; (4) responsible use of GenAI in microbiology practice and education; (5) implementation, governance, regulation and professional accountability; and (6) communication, collaboration and lifelong learning. The goal is not to train every microbiology professional as a data scientist. The aim is to develop AI-literate practitioners who can critically evaluate tools, use GenAI safely, participate in governance, communicate uncertainty, and ensure that AI-enabled practice remains grounded in microbiological expertise and patient safety.
evidence_items.title: Artificial intelligence literacy for microbiology professionals

organizations: Department of Hospital Therapeutic Dentistry, Tashkent State Medical University, Tashkent, Uzbekistan
evidence_items.summary: Artificial intelligence (AI) has emerged as one of the most influential technological developments in modern healthcare, creating new opportunities for improving diagnosis, treatment, patient monitoring, clinical decisionmaking, and healthcare management. The increasing availability of electronic health records, medical imaging, genomic information, wearable devices, and other forms of digital health data has created an environment in which AI-based systems can identify complex patterns that may be difficult to recognize through conventional approaches. Machine learning, deep learning, natural language processing, and generative AI are currently being investigated and implemented across multiple medical specialties. In clinical practice, AI can support radiological image interpretation, early disease detection, risk prediction, personalized treatment selection, drug development, clinical documentation, and remote patient monitoring. These applications may contribute to earlier diagnosis, improved clinical efficiency, reduced workload, and more individualized patient care. AI-enabled medical devices have also increasingly entered clinical practice, particularly in radiology and cardiology. However, the successful integration of AI into healthcare requires careful attention to data quality, algorithmic bias, patient privacy, transparency, cybersecurity, clinical validation, and professional accountability. AI should therefore be regarded as a clinical support technology rather than a replacement for healthcare professionals. This review examines the major clinical applications and potential benefits of artificial intelligence in modern healthcare and discusses the principal challenges that must be addressed to ensure safe, ethical, effective, and patient-centered implementation.
evidence_items.title: Artificial Intelligence in Modern Healthcare: Clinical Applications and Benefits

organizations: Central University of South Bihar, India
evidence_items.summary: Alzheimer's Disease (AD) is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder that requires accurate and early diagnosis for effective management. Recent advances in Artificial Intelligence (AI), Machine Learning (ML), and Deep Learning (DL) have significantly improved AD prediction through the analysis of complex biomedical and healthcare data. This chapter reviews AI- and ML-based approaches for AD prediction, highlighting deep learning models, Natural Language Processing (NLP), multimodal data fusion, wearable sensors, and IoT-enabled healthcare systems for continuous monitoring and intelligent assistive care. Emerging technologies such as Explainable AI (XAI), transfer learning, federated learning, and edge AI are also discussed. Despite promising results, challenges including limited datasets, data heterogeneity, interpretability, privacy concerns, data leakage, and computational complexity remain significant barriers to real-world deployment.
evidence_items.title: Artificial Intelligence, Machine Learning, and IoT in Alzheimer's Disease Prediction

evidence_items.summary: Environmental contamination is increasingly recognised as a human rights issue engaging State obligations under the European Convention on Human Rights (ECHR). In Cannavacciuolo and Others v Italy , the European Court of Human Rights held that prolonged environmental exposure may trigger positive obligations under Article 2 ECHR, requiring public authorities to identify, monitor and mitigate foreseeable risks to life. Implementing these obligations depends on the integration of environmental, clinical and epidemiological evidence. This paper argues that legal medicine can provide the methodological bridge between legal principles and scientific assessment. We propose an Integrated Environmental Medico-Legal Assessment Framework (I-EMAF), a conceptual model supporting transparent, multidisciplinary and evidence-based evaluation of environmental contamination. Rather than introducing new investigative methods, I-EMAF organises established scientific approaches within a coherent medico-legal structure to assist courts, public authorities and healthcare systems to implement their Article 2 obligations.
evidence_items.title: Environmental contamination, human rights and medico-legal responsibility after Cannavacciuolo and Others v Italy (ECtHR)

evidence_items.summary: Physical unclonable functions (PUFs) authenticate a device by its manufacturing variation, but cryptographic verification cannot tell whether a live, honest device produced a reading, letting replays, clones, and faults pass. We benchmarked our deployed detector, UnifiedPUFNet, against six baselines on 24 static random-access memory (SRAM) PUF tokens, holding out each attack family in turn. Test clones were real readings from other chips; replays and faults were simulated. Most detectors scored known attacks near-perfectly (area under the receiver operating characteristic curve, AUC, at least 0.999), yet five degraded on unseen families, UnifiedPUFNet included. We traced this to its input normalization, which removes each reading’s scale, where most of the attack signal lies. Our dual-signal variant restores it with a raw-magnitude input, holding AUC above 0.99 on unseen families and 1.000 on unseen chips, and rejecting clones and faults rebuilt from real readings. Two baselines and a training-free score ranked attacks as well, but the score collapsed under session drift, and the best baseline rejected more genuine readings on unseen chips; our variant did neither. Exact replays of older readings passed every detector, leaving replay to the protocol layer. Detectors should preserve each reading’s scale and be validated on unseen families.
evidence_items.title: A Leave-One-Attack-Out Benchmark and a Dual-Signal Architecture for Liveness Detection in SRAM Physical Unclonable Functions

evidence_items.summary: Indiscriminate municipal solid waste disposal in unlined open dumpsites poses a serious threat to underlying unconfined and semi-confined crystalline basement aquifers in developing nations. This study integrated Two-Dimensional Electrical Resistivity Tomography (2D ERT) and hydrochemical analysis to delineate subsurface leachate plume migration pathways and evaluate groundwater quality surrounding the Fagbohun dumpsite in Ado-Ekiti, Southwestern Nigeria. Four 2D ERT profiles (300 m in length each) were acquired using a dipole-dipole electrode configuration, complemented by physico-chemical, major ion, and trace heavy metal analyses of five shallow groundwater samples (S-1 to S-5) collected from adjacent hand-dug wells. Smoothness-constrained least-squares inversion of geoelectrical data delineated three principal geoelectric units: a low-resistivity topsoil/refuse layer (5–5,098 Ωm), a weathered/fractured basement overburden unit (79–58,386 Ωm), and a fresh crystalline basement bedrock (563–35,825,996 Ωm). Distinct anomalous low-resistivity zones (< 20 Ωm) within the topsoil and saprolite layers directly trace conductive leachate plume accumulation and deep vertical infiltration through structural bedrock depressions, lineaments, and interconnected basement fracture networks. Hydrochemical facies characterization using Piper trilinear and Schoeller diagrams identified a single predominant water type: Sodium-Bicarbonate-Chloride (Na - HCO3 - Cl), with cationic abundance following Ca2+ or Mg2+ > (Na++ K+) and anionic abundance following Cl}- > HCO3- > SO42.
evidence_items.title: Integrated Geophysical and Hydrochemical Assessment of Leachate Plume Migration and Groundwater Contamination Around Fagbohun Dumpsite, Ado-Ekiti, Southwestern Nigeria

evidence_items.summary: Aims: Agentic artificial intelligence (AI) systems plan, call tools, hold credentials, and act with little human supervision, yet their security is still assessed mostly after incidents occur. This study forecasts vulnerability disclosures in a selected set of open-source agentic AI components to 2030 and proposes a security framework that responds to those forecasts. Methodology: Four public datasets were assembled: (i) 943 unique, dated vulnerability disclosures (April 2023 to October 2026) in 87 open-source agentic components from PyPI and npm, enriched with CVE records, CVSS vectors, and CISA SSVC decisions; (ii) the CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalogue; (iii) a census of 30,054 Model Context Protocol (MCP) and agent projects on PyPI; and (iv) MITRE ATLAS. Six forecasting models were backtested from four origins, and the identifiable models were combined in a quantile-averaged ensemble. Results: Annual disclosures rose from 19 in 2023 to 164 in 2025 and reached 705 by mid-October 2026, with an April 2026 changepoint that lifted the monthly mean from 8.9 to 94.5. Agent platforms contributed 54% of disclosures, and access-control flaws overtook code injection as the largest weakness family. Nine agentic platform flaws entered KEV in 2026, with a median interval of 30 days between publication and listing; because KEV listing follows confirmed exploitation, this interval is an upper bound on the time to first exploitation. Saturating models were not identifiable because discovery has not reached its inflection point. The ensemble projects a median of 5,334 disclosures in 2030, but the 80% interval (495 to 53,088) is very wide, so this figure indicates a planning range rather than a point prediction. This estimate is bracketed by a diffusion-bounded plateau near 1,200 disclosures per year and an acceleration envelope.
evidence_items.title: Forecasting the Cybersecurity Vulnerabilities of Agentic AI Systems toward 2030: A Framework for Autonomous AI Security

evidence_items.summary: Background Effective patient education is essential in pediatric neurology but challenged by time constraints and variable health literacy. Large language models (LLMs) offer a potential solution, yet their accuracy and safety in this specialized field remain incompletely evaluated. Methods In a prospective, blinded benchmarking study, LLM-generated responses to ten standardized pediatric neurology prompts were evaluated. Responses were assessed for factual accuracy, safety, and perceived usability; the study did not assess real-world clinical decision support or caregiver comprehension. A blinded panel of seven consultant pediatric neurology evaluators assessed the outputs using an expert-developed rubric measuring factual accuracy, safety, clinical appropriateness, and usability. The unit of analysis was the scenario-model pair ( n = 40), with median scores across raters used for primary comparisons. Results Linear mixed-effects models revealed significant performance variation across models (F(3,27) = 8.76, p &lt; 0.001). DeepSeek achieved the highest overall composite score (4.01 ± 0.61) and zero safety flags. ChatGPT scored moderately (3.72 ± 0.75) but accounted for most safety issues (5/8), including a contraindicated medication recommendation. Gemini and Perplexity scored lower (3.45 ± 0.77 and 3.38 ± 0.71). The overall composite difference between DeepSeek and ChatGPT was not statistically significant ( p = 0.087). DeepSeek had the highest System Usability Scale score (74.2/100). Presence of any consensus safety flag drastically reduced the odds of expert approval for caregiver-facing use after clinician review (OR: 0.08, p &lt; 0.001). Conclusions DeepSeek produced no consensus safety flags in this benchmark and had the highest expert-rated usability score, but its overall composite score was not statistically different from ChatGPT.
evidence_items.title: Comparative benchmark of four selected large language models for generating patient education content in pediatric neurology: a prospective study

evidence_items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly accessible to patients with cancer as sources of immediate information about diet, symptoms, supplements, and treatment-related nutritional concerns. Their conversational fluency may create an illusion of clinical adequacy: a response can be well written, plausible, and apparently personalized while remaining incomplete, poorly contextualized, or clinically unsafe. This problem is particularly relevant in oncology nutrition, where advice about restrictive diets, fasting, supplements, malnutrition, sarcopenia, cachexia, and treatment tolerance may have direct implications for patient safety. Existing approaches to evaluating LLM-generated health information use heterogeneous criteria, including accuracy, completeness, readability, usefulness, personalization, evidence support, trust, safety, and potential harm. Classical instruments such as DISCERN, the Patient Education Materials Assessment Tool, and the JAMA benchmarks address selected dimensions of health information quality, whereas contemporary LLM-specific frameworks increasingly account for conversational, clinical, and safety-related features. However, these approaches are not specifically designed for oncology nutrition and do not consistently operationalize a non-compensatory logic in which clinically serious safety concerns are assessed separately from otherwise favorable response qualities. We propose a conceptual and operational framework for evaluating patient-facing LLM-generated oncology nutrition responses. The framework treats scientific, clinical, and nutritional appropriateness; clinical and nutritional safety; communication quality and patient utility; transparency; and system-level robustness as conceptually distinct and non-substitutable evaluation dimensions. It also introduces critical safety flags intended to identify veto-level concerns that should not be averaged with favorable performance in other domains.
evidence_items.title: Evaluating large language model-generated oncology nutrition responses: a conceptual framework and validation roadmap

evidence_items.summary: Background Large language model (LLM)-based chatbots are increasingly used for health information, but their suitability for melanoma public education requires evaluation across accuracy, information quality, transparency, and readability. Methods We compared ChatGPT-5.6, DeepSeek-V4, Claude Sonnet 5, and Gemini 3.5 Flash. Validity was assessed using 200 melanoma-related single-best-answer multiple-choice questions administered in three independent trials. Fifteen core public-education questions were developed from worldwide Google Trends data and clinical experience. Responses were evaluated using DISCERN, EQIP, GQS, and JAMA benchmarks, and readability was assessed using ARI, Coleman–Liau, FKGL, FRES, GFI, and SMOG indices. Results Mean MCQ accuracy was highest for ChatGPT-5.6 (94.0% ± 0.5%), followed by Gemini 3.5 Flash (92.5% ± 1.3%), Claude Sonnet 5 (87.2% ± 1.4%), and DeepSeek-V4 (79.3% ± 0.3%; p &lt; 0.001). ChatGPT-5.6 achieved the highest DISCERN (52.07 ± 9.48), EQIP (81.67 ± 4.08), and GQS (4.40 ± 0.51) scores. JAMA transparency scores were low across models. Gemini 3.5 Flash showed the most favorable overall readability profile; however, mean grade-level indices for all models exceeded the sixth-grade benchmark, and all mean FRES scores were below the recommended range. Conclusion Current LLM chatbots show substantial potential for melanoma education, but performance varies across validity, quality, transparency, and readability. Their use should remain supplementary, with improved source transparency and health-literacy–appropriate language required before broader patient-facing implementation.
evidence_items.title: Validity, reliability, and readability of large language model chatbots for melanoma public education: a cross-sectional comparative study

organizations: Huazhong University of Science and Technology, China
evidence_items.summary: The rapid advancement of large language models (LLMs) has redefined artificial intelligence (AI), pushing the boundaries of AI research and enabling unbounded possibilities for both academia and industry. However, LLM development faces increasingly complex challenges throughout its lifecycle, while existing research has not systematically investigated these challenges and solutions from the perspective of software engineering (SE) approaches. To fill the gap, we systematically analyze the research status throughout the LLM development lifecycle, which is divided into six phases: requirements engineering, dataset construction, model development and enhancement, testing and evaluation, deployment and operations, and maintenance and evolution. We conclude by identifying the key challenges in each phase and presenting potential research directions to address them. In general, we provide valuable insights from an SE perspective to facilitate future advances in LLM development.
evidence_items.title: Software Engineering for Large Language Models: Research Status, Challenges, and the Road Ahead

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Climate change is increasing temperatures and worsening extreme heat[1–5]. Heat threatens human and natural systems[2,3,5–7]. In cities, urban heat islands and concentrations of people, infrastructure, and economic activity amplify risks[6,8–12]. Cities are adapting to heat, yet evidence remains fragmented and difficult to compare because adaptation is multidimensional, context-specific, and scale-dependent[3,6,7,12–18]. Here we introduce and apply the Heat Adaptation Benchmark, a multi-criteria framework for evaluating heat adaptation through structured expert judgment. Twenty-four expert evaluators assessed a purposive sample of 46 cities spanning six global regions and differing in three city characteristics: metropolitan area population, country-level economic resources, and historical climate. Across all cities, the mean total score suggested considerable scope to strengthen documented heat adaptation (36.1 out of 72). Of the six criteria, risk assessment had the highest mean score (8.4 out of 12) and monitoring and evaluation the lowest (3.4). In every city, the combined score for risk assessment, planning, and actions exceeded that for strategy, monitoring and evaluation, and governance. Higher-scoring cities had different combinations of strengths and gaps and were found in every region and city characteristic category. Our results highlight challenges in translating documented assessment, planning, and identified actions into sustained implementation and demonstrated heat risk reduction. We anticipate that the benchmark will support cross-city comparison and learning by illustrating a range of heat adaptation approaches and identifying practices that cities facing similar conditions or challenges could draw on. Across contexts, our findings point to the importance of durable institutions that can implement heat adaptation plans, sustain action through long-term strategies and reliable funding, and assess whether those actions reduce heat risk.
evidence_items.title: A global benchmark of urban heat adaptation

evidence_items.summary: Artificial intelligence (AI) systems used in anesthesia and intensive care are evolving from prediction tools toward agentic systems that can plan and execute actions, such as titrating drugs, adjusting ventilator settings, or modifying orders in electronic health records. Such systems are expected to recognize when an instruction would breach safety, ethical, or legal boundaries, which requires a functional capacity for contextual normative evaluation. Recent experimental reports from AI developers, based on deliberately constructed simulations, have documented frontier language models converting such evaluations into unauthorized actions, including covert sabotage and consequence-driven mislabeling by AI evaluators. The purpose of this conceptual paper is to provide clinicians with a framework for analyzing these behaviors. We distinguish the capability to evaluate a situation from the authority to act on that evaluation, and define agentic overreach, an authority-related form of agentic misalignment, as the conversion of an evaluation into action beyond prospectively delegated authority. The framework specifies how authority is granted, scoped, made conditional, and revoked within a hierarchy of principals; separates evaluative functions (detect, judge) from response options graded by the authority they require (recommend, refuse, escalate, override); treats concealment as a cross-cutting transparency property; and maps behavior on a Judgment × Authority grid that explicitly incorporates uncertainty. We apply the framework to closed-loop ventilation, vasopressor titration, sepsis alerts, medication decision support, and AI-supported triage. The framework is conceptual and has not been empirically validated, and part of the evidence it draws on consists of developer reports and preprints that have not been peer reviewed. Its central principle is that the capability to judge does not confer the authority to act.
evidence_items.title: From Boundary Evaluation to Agentic Overreach: A Judgment–Authority Framework for Clinical Artificial Intelligence

evidence_items.summary: The increasing demand for clean and sustainable energy has accelerated the adoption of solar photovoltaic (PV) systems across residential, commercial, and industrial sectors. However, solar power generation is highly dependent on environmental conditions, including solar irradiance, ambient temperature, cloud cover, humidity, and wind speed. These variations create challenges in maintaining power system stability, balancing electricity demand and supply, and efficiently managing energy storage. Artificial Intelligence (AI) offers promising solutions to these challenges through advanced forecasting, intelligent decision-making, and automated energy management. This paper presents a comprehensive review of AI-based techniques for solar energy forecasting and management, focusing on machine learning (ML), deep learning, weather data integration, and smart energy systems. Methods such as Random Forest, Support Vector Regression, Artificial Neural Networks, Long Short-Term Memory networks, and hybrid forecasting models are discussed in terms of their operating principles, applications, advantages, and limitations. The paper also examines the integration of AI with smart grids, battery energy storage systems, demand-side management, and Internet of Things (IoT) technologies. Furthermore, forecasting evaluation metrics, implementation challenges, and future research directions are outlined. The review indicates that combining historical generation data with weather forecasts and real-time measurements can support more reliable solar power prediction and improve operational decision-making. The paper concludes that AI can play a significant role in developing efficient, resilient, and sustainable solar energy systems, although practical performance depends on data quality, model selection, and validation under real-world conditions.
evidence_items.title: Artificial Intelligence In Solar Energy Forecasting and Management

evidence_items.summary: Synonymous coding DNA sequence (CDS) design for plant expression constructs must balance host codon adaptation against guanine-cytosine (GC) composition, restriction-site avoidance, and sequence-integrity constraints, yet benchmark outcomes can depend strongly on the chosen codon-usage reference. Using FactorForge v3.2.0, an open-source CDS design and sequence-review workflow, we evaluated four rule-based design presets (Balanced, High-CAI, GC-target, and Assembly-friendly) on 49,257 reference-derived Nicotiana benthamiana CDS/protein records from the Sol Genomics Network (SGN) QLD183 resource (seed 320), scoring sequence integrity, a historical 55-65% GC window, and absence of BsaI/BpiI/BsmBI sites. With the legacy packaged codon reference, Assembly-friendly passed all three criteria for 63.37% of records (single fixed per-record seed 320; subject to multi-percentage-point variation across independent seed streams); with three genome-derived references its combined pass rate was 0.00% after rounding, whereas GC-target attained 22.68% in each derived condition. A separate v3.3.0 dynamic-programming (DP) execution maximizing the codon adaptation index (CAI) within the same GC window found a GC-compliant sequence for 99.83% of records (49,173/49,257; 84 NO FEASIBLE CDS; mean feasible CAI 0.9989), but 28.21% passed all criteria because Type IIS sites are outside the 1DP objective. An independent FactorForge v3.6.4 2x2 factorial evaluation (N = 49,257) crossing codon reference (legacy C1 vs. high-confidence NbeV1.1 C4) and target GC window (55-65% vs.
evidence_items.title: Constraint-Aware Coding-Sequence Design for Nicotiana benthamiana: A 49,257-Record Benchmark and Codon-Reference Sensitivity Analysis

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Deep learning has been used successfully for object detection in optical, infrared,SAR, and multispectral images of maritime environments. Nevertheless, itsdeployment in maritime security systems remains challenging. This review anal-yses major object detection architectures, sensing methods, application domains,and deployment constraints in this domain. The most frequently representeddetection architectures in the reviewed papers include You Only Look Once(YOLO) detectors (199 papers) and attention-based and transformer models(123 papers). Tracking, multimodal fusion, threat reasoning, and detector secu-rity are much less represented. There are also major deficiencies in evaluationpractices. For example, 121 out of 299 papers reporting detection metrics donot provide an intersection-over-union threshold value. Inference latency, energyconsumption, and target hardware are also insufficiently reported in many stud-ies. Besides detection accuracy, we discuss how security-task evidence affectsbenchmark selection and detector deployment in communication-aware settings.The review provides a reporting checklist and a roadmap for future research.Future work should concentrate on multimodal benchmarks, small-object detec-tion, cross-sensor generalisation, trustworthy sensor fusion, edge intelligence, andrealistic evaluation of detectors.
evidence_items.title: Deep Learning Object Detection for Maritime Security: A Critical Review of Task Evidence, Benchmark Comparability and Deployment Constraints

evidence_items.summary: Agent-based models are widely used to study complex adaptive dynamics in heterogeneous populations, largely because they capture how autonomous agents behave without central coordination. The same decentralization makes stability hard to establish analytically. We take one controlled two-state contagion model on a graph, steered by a single broadcast scalar, and study six controllers on it: a fuzzy inference system, a tabular reinforcement learner, and four ways of combining them. The analysis is a stochastic drift argument on a Perron-weighted Lyapunov function that asks of each controller only a lower bound on its effort above an activation level, not a Lyapunov function of its own. The spectral radius of the interaction operator sets a critical effort, and a controller whose floor exceeds it keeps the population regulated. Each hybrid inherits a floor from the two it combines, which separates the four: safety blending and the hierarchical override keep a floor whatever the learner does, convex fusion and switching do not. Asynchronous updates follow from the same argument; delays and interruptions do not, and are left to simulation. Its application settings are readings of one model rather than independent validations. The trained learner cuts the fuzzy controller’s cost by 61%, yet eight tuned classical and model-based baselines all cost less than any of the six. The hybrids contain the learner’s failure outside its training range, but that failure is produced by the training protocol: a wider range of initial states removes it. A controller call costs the same up to 106 agents, and three further models mark the scope: control is essential in a cascade, marginal under segregation, and counterproductive where it acts non-monotonically.
evidence_items.title: Hybrid Fuzzy–Reinforcement-Learning Control of Agent-Based Contagion Dynamics on Graphs: Drift Conditions, Topology Dependence and Benchmark Evidence

organizations: Nuclear and Radiation Safety Center of the National Nuclear Safety Administration, Ministry of Ecology and Environment (MEE), Beijing 102446, China

evidence_items.summary: Reduced-order models of the Kilowatt Reactor Using Stirling TechnologY (KRUSTY ) heat-pipe microreactor test are usually scored against curves digitized from published figures. This paper asks which of their apparent gains survive when the heat-load forcing is not measured independently. We reconstruct source-tagged power and outer-fuel-temperature series and grade the evidence at three levels: calibration (8–12 h), transfer to a later window (20–28 h), and a forward prediction (16–19.8 h) driven only by the documented reflector-platen movements. All five 20–28 h heat-load amplitudes are back-inferred from the power record of the same test, so the transfer is a transfer of thermal parameters, not an independent-input validation. Under a common load input, two thermal stores reduce the 20–28 h power root-mean-square error (RMSE) by 63.9–65.7% relative to one store. Normalized by the mean power of that window, the error falls from 15.4% to 5.6%; in absolute terms it falls from 0.278 to 0.101 kW, and the temperature RMSE from 3.60 to 1.89 °C. A third store lowers the power RMSE only to 0.096 kW, while one of its conductances reaches its upper bound, and with the fuel capacity varied the fitted total storage stays near 19.3 kJ/K, so the data constrain the total storage rather than its distribution. Among the model orders tested, two stores therefore give the best-supported balance between residual reduction and parameter stability. In an out-of-window forward evaluation that uses no post-event output and an observed initial state, the two-store model reaches 0.376 kW and 4.99 °C. The contribution is therefore a reproducible benchmark and an evidence-grading procedure, not a claim of accuracy superior to high-fidelity models.
evidence_items.title: When Does a Two-Node Thermal Model Suffice? An Evidence-Graded Reduced-Order Benchmark for the KRUSTY Heat-Pipe Microreactor Test

evidence_items.summary: Federated learning (FL) enables privacy-preserving multi-site clinical research, but orchestrating, monitoring, and interpreting federated analyses remain out of reach for the biostatisticians and clinicians who most need them. We present Starfish-FL, a multi-tier agent harness for cross-silo healthcare analytics built around the safety invariant that the LLM is advisory and cannot independently trigger consequential actions. Agents operate at three tiers. An Autonomous Experiment Agent orchestrates end-to-end experiments via CLI tools, an Embedded Router Agent handles adaptive aggregation, early stopping, and failure triage, and Controller Agent Hooks produce per-site summaries, outlier flags, and convergence signals. Three hybrid safety policies, SafeStop, SafeAggregate, and SafeTriage, gate every site exclusion, early stop, and recovery action behind deterministic preconditions, so LLM errors cannot cause unsafe state transitions, conditional on guard correctness. All agent features are opt-in and degrade gracefully to standard FL, and the platform provides 21 Python and R task implementations with built-in statistical diagnostics. Evaluated across four LLM providers with repeated-run confidence intervals, task selection reaches \({\sim}97\%\) accuracy with hosted models, the online SafeStop policy saves 50–70% of rounds with no accuracy loss, and safety-policy validation shows a 100% safe-action rate under injected failures, confirming that deterministic guards, not the LLM, preserve safety.
evidence_items.title: Starfish-FL: Harnessing Agentic Federated Analytics

organizations: Chevron USA, Inc., Houston, TX, USA
Halliburton, Houston, TX, USA
evidence_items.summary: Digital transformation has increased organizational dependence on specialized software teams, progressively distancing subject matter experts (SMEs) from direct participation in developing the tools they need most. The introduction of AI has largely reinforced this dynamic, with its value framed around task automation and workflow acceleration rather than restoring domain experts to the center of digital creation. This paper proposes a transdisciplinary framework that addresses this gap directly, positioning agentic AI as a collaborative partner throughout an SME-led co-creation process. Rather than replacing domain expertise, agentic AI enables SMEs to explore and evaluate multiple candidate solutions to domain-specific problems, supporting innovation and closer alignment between domain knowledge and delivered tools. This approach offers a step change in efficiency compared to traditional Agile product development, supporting rapid design–validation feedback loops without the overhead of multiple sprints and product increments to meet design goals. Two applied case studies in geoscience and engineering demonstrate the framework in practice. The results suggest a deliberate division of labor between SME-led co-creation for domain tools and Agile delivery reserved for solutions that warrant enterprise scale. They also raise important questions about the organizational structures ultimately required to make this shift and deliver business value.
evidence_items.title: Restoring Domain Expertise to Digital Product Development Through Agentic AI

evidence_items.summary: Researchers increasingly rely on people to produce data through online interfaces. Agentic browsers create a new challenge for these workflows because they can navigate websites and complete tasks on a user’s behalf with little technical knowledge or effort. We evaluate whether three consumer-facing agentic browsers can complete online surveys and whether recently proposed measures can detect or prevent their use. The agents received only one simple instruction, "Fill out this survey", without detailed prompting or technical optimization. We tested technical screening measures, visible and invisible CAPTCHAs, AI-specific prompt-injection checks, consistency across a longer survey, and the completion of several surveys from a single instruction. The agents completed surveys with little or no user input, maintained assigned demographic profiles, and passed all tested prompt-leaking and jailbreak-style checks. Browser metadata did not reveal automated participation, and invisible reCAPTCHA was consistently passed by some browsers. Visible reCAPTCHA created the strongest barrier, although agents could sometimes solve it or return control to the user. These findings show that widely available AI agents can take over tasks intended for human participants while producing responses that appear coherent and plausible. This raises broader questions about how researchers can verify that supposedly human-generated data were actually produced by humans.
evidence_items.title: "Fill Out this Survey": Capabilities and Detection of Agentic Browsers

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Biomedical research is constrained by the time and domain expertise required to analyze increasingly large and complex datasets. Here we present OpenScientist, an open-source agentic AI co-scientist designed to address this gap by investigating scientist-defined queries and generating verifiable, data-grounded analyses. OpenScientist was evaluated by domain experts across five biomedical case studies, completing analyses in minutes that otherwise would take months of human time and expertise. It accurately quantified Alzheimer’s blood biomarker performance, generated a plasma proteomic survival model that predicted survival in a hidden-evaluation cohort, proposed a reproducible mechanism linking tau pathology to altered lysosomal acidification, generated multiple myeloma hypotheses validated in an external cohort with attenuated signal in randomized controls, and demonstrated concordance with an independent human analysis in a blinded, prespecified proteomic comparison. These results support the use of OpenScientist to assist biomedical data analysis in concert with human experts. To support research involving sensitive clinical datasets, OpenScientist can operate in a fully air-gapped environment using open-source models for inference. OpenScientist demonstrates that open, auditable, agentic AI can support real-world clinical research by researching the literature, generating hypotheses, executing analyses, and generating insights from complex datasets.
evidence_items.title: An open agentic AI co-scientist for clinical and biomedical discovery

organizations: San Diego State University
evidence_items.summary: This paper presents BodySync AI, a multimodal calorie-tracking prototype that combines optical character recognition (OCR), object detection, pose estimation, and an agentic large language model (LLM). The system supports two tasks: extracting nutritional values from photographs of food-packaging labels, and analyzing body proportions from full-body images. Nutrition extraction uses a classical image-processing front end (perspective correction, denoising, illumination normalization, and contrast enhancement) followed by EasyOCR and rulebased parsing of calories, fat, carbohydrates, and protein. In parallel, we train a YOLOv8n nutrition-label detector on the Open Food Facts Nutrition Table Detection dataset and study the effect of training epochs, learning rate, optimizer, batch size, and input resolution in 14 controlled runs. The best configuration reaches an mAP@50 of 0.904 and an mAP@50-95 of 0.727 on the validation split. Body analysis uses MediaPipe Pose landmarks to compute normalized shoulder width, hip width, torso length, and shoulder-to-hip ratio, which feed a baseline rule-based bodytype estimate. A Groq-hosted Llama 3.1 8B agent exposes these components as tools through a natural-language interface. We describe the system as built, report the detector experiments, and outline the evaluations and learned body-composition models planned as future work.
evidence_items.title: BodySync AI: A Multimodal Agentic System for Nutrition Label Extraction and Pose-Based Body Analysis

evidence_items.summary: As agents perform tasks autonomously in local and cloud environments, auditing their execution trajectories can help service providers identify risks and improve agent harnesses and foundation models. Our analysis of production and red-team trajectories shows that some risks are repeatedly missed across auditing configurations. Overall recall obscures which risks are missed and whether higher recall comes with more false positives on legitimate behavior. Existing benchmarks offer limited insight into these failures. Generated trajectories can contain inconsistent tool calls and responses, conspicuous risky actions, or repetitive attack patterns. Grouping results by risk type also makes it difficult to tell whether auditors overlooked evidence, accepted an unsupported conclusion, or lacked information needed to make a judgment. We introduce ReA-Bench, a diagnostic benchmark for auditing responsible agent behavior. It organizes auditing challenges into six tiers: internal safety knowledge, contradictions within trajectories, evidence retrieval in long contexts, verification of sources and reasoning, indirect steering, and missing information. It includes challenging benign cases in which actions resemble risky ones but are consistent with the task and its authorization. It also provides paired trajectory versions to test whether auditors detect the same risks more reliably when the trajectory is shortened or missing information is supplied. Most samples are drawn from real production trajectories, with scenarios manually selected and adapted to preserve realistic tasks and risks that could plausibly arise during execution.
evidence_items.title: ReA-Bench: Benchmarking Responsible Agent Auditing

evidence_items.summary: Surround-view video understanding in autonomous driving is a crucial capability for Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) to achieve reliable driving reasoning. Real-world driving often requires information beyond the front-view camera. Existing MLLMs primarily focus on front-view information, while their spatio-temporal understanding and reasoning abilities remain unknown. To address this gap, we propose MVDriveBench, a high-information-density video QA benchmark for autonomous driving, characterized by synchronized surround-view inputs, spatio-temporal understanding, and reasoning-chain-oriented evaluation. We design 12 categories of QA tasks that cover the complete reasoning pipeline from low-level visual perception to high-level driving decision-making, enabling a systematic evaluation of MLLMs surround-view spatio-temporal understanding and reasoning capabilities in complex driving environments. We conduct a comprehensive evaluation of 23 open-source, closed-source, and expert MLLMs on MVDriveBench. The results show that current MLLMs still exhibit insufficient surround-view spatio-temporal reasoning ability. Meanwhile, closed-loop evaluations of specialist models in AlpaSim reveal a correlation between surround-view spatio-temporal reasoning capabilities and closed-loop driving performance, highlighting the importance of comprehensive multi-view understanding for reliable vehicle control.
evidence_items.title: Can MLLMs Reason over Surround-View Driving Videos? A Multi-View Autonomous Driving QA Benchmark

evidence_items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) have been shown to exhibit strong Python preferences when generating project-level code, but there is currently no systematic way to measure this behaviour across new models. To bridge this gap, we introduce LangChoiceBench, a project-level code-generation benchmark for measuring Python preference, recommendation-implementation consistency, and language diversity. LangChoiceBench covers 28 projects across seven software areas where Python is often a poor default. We evaluate 25 diverse LLMs and find that Python remains heavily over-selected, recommendation-implementation consistency is low, and smaller open-weight models generally show stronger Python preference and lower language diversity. We further analyse 9,826 reasoning traces and find that most Python choices are automatic or driven primarily by ease, rather than explicit consideration of project requirements. In a smaller but important set of cases, models fabricate contextual support for choosing Python - a failure mode we call phantom evidence - or produce code that contradicts the language selected in their own reasoning.
evidence_items.title: LangChoiceBench: Measuring and Explaining Programming-Language Choice in LLMs

evidence_items.summary: Establishing a clear link between model predictions and the visual evidence that supports them is critical for transparency and reliability in multimodal reasoning, yet current multimodal large language model (MLLM) evaluations do not explicitly enforce this alignment. Existing benchmarks assess either textual answer correctness or pixel-level localization in isolation, leaving the coupling of reasoning and grounding an open challenge. We introduce VISTAQA, a comprehensive benchmark for joint evaluation of free-form answer correctness and pixel-level evidence grounding in visual question answering. VISTAQA comprises 1,157 expert-curated samples spanning six task types and six visual domains, ranging from direct perception to compositional and relational reasoning. VISTAQA requires models to not only answer correctly, but to also provide precise segmentation masks that support their answers. It also includes hallucination-aware examples where no valid visual evidence exists. To support this enhanced evaluation, we introduce GROVE, a unified evaluation metric that enforces joint correctness by combining textual accuracy and grounding quality via a per-sample geometric mean, ensuring neither dimension can compensate for deficiencies in the other. Comprehensive experiments across grounding-aware models and hybrid pipelines with general-purpose MLLMs reveal that even the strongest systems achieve limited performance under GROVE, highlighting a substantial gap between answer accuracy and visual evidence alignment. Project page can be found at https://vistaqa.github.io.
evidence_items.title: VISTAQA: Benchmarking Joint Visual Question Answering and Pixel-Level Evidence

evidence_items.summary: Intracranial aneurysms (IAs), characterized by unpredictable growth and risk of rupture, are a major cause of stroke and can lead to life-threatening hemorrhages with high mortality and long-term disability. With aging populations, the incidence and overall burden of cerebrovascular diseases are expected to increase, highlighting the need for scalable approaches to analyze complex medical data and improve population-level understanding of these conditions. While digital twins and deep learning offer promising avenues for improving diagnosis, prognosis, and treatment, their effectiveness is limited by the scarcity of large-scale, high-quality medical data and corresponding labels. We present Synthetic VAsculature (SynVA), a modular toolkit for vascular mesh generation and anatomically consistent aneurysm synthesis. SynVA combines novel flow-matching-based methods for generating healthy vessel meshes with learning-based approaches for anatomy-conditioned aneurysm mesh generation; it computes aneurysms from pre-existing vascular geometries rather than generating them in isolation. In addition, we introduce the SynVA procedural model for vascular and aneurysm synthesis based solely on physiological principles and statistical priors, which enables the generation of large-scale datasets. To this end, we release a dataset of 50,000 fully labeled mesh samples for a variety of downstream vision tasks. Extensive quantitative and qualitative evaluations show that SynVA generates realistic vessel geometries and anatomically plausible aneurysms, with only minor trade-offs between expert-perceived realism and similarity to real aneurysms. Moreover, pretraining on SynVA data improves point-cloud segmentation and morphological parameter estimation on real data. Code will be released upon acceptance.
evidence_items.title: SynVA: A Modular Toolkit for Vessel Generation and Aneurysm Editing

evidence_items.summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated potential in automating scientific ideation, yet current approaches relying on iterative prompting or complex multi-agent architectures often suffer from hallucination or computational inefficiency. A critical bottleneck in applying Reinforcement Learning (RL) to this open-ended domain is reward hacking---where models exploit imperfect evaluation proxies to maximize scores without producing genuine scientific innovation. To address these limitations, we propose an RL framework explicitly tailored for high-quality scientific idea generation. We propose the first multi-agent reward function designed to serve as a judge, decoupling methodological validation from implementation details while providing strict binary rewards that are robust to reward hacking. To effectively optimize against this sparse signal, we utilize an unbiased variant of Group Relative Policy Optimization to mitigate artificial length bias. We ground our training in a curated dataset of problem-solution pairs extracted from ICLR 2024 and NeurIPS 2025 proceedings. Experiments demonstrate that our framework significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baselines across expert-evaluated metrics of novelty, feasibility, and effectiveness.
evidence_items.title: Debate as Reward: A Multi-Agent Reward System for Scientific Ideation via RL Post-Training

evidence_items.summary: Museum records express how people understand heritage objects through cultural and historical relations. Recovering these human attributions from images is a technical challenge for vision-language models (VLMs). We introduce Appear2Meaning, a cross-cultural benchmark of 750 museum objects for image-only recovery of title, culture, period, origin, and creator. Its evaluation framework distinguishes field-level from complete-record compatibility and uses human validation for semantic judgement. Across nine VLMs, mean field accuracy is 36.16--49.82%; 7.20--17.02% of records have all four contextual fields compatible, and 2.13--7.87% have all five, including title. For the two tested models, image-only input yields 12.6--32.2 percentage points higher reference compatibility for culture, period, and origin than a museum-and-title-only control.
evidence_items.title: Appear2Meaning: A Cross-Cultural Benchmark for Structured Cultural Metadata Inference from Images

evidence_items.summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed in socially sensitive domains, yet their unpredictable behaviors, ranging from misaligned intent to inconsistent personality, pose significant risks. We introduce SteerEval, a hierarchical benchmark for evaluating LLM controllability across three domains: language features, sentiment, and personality. Each domain is structured into three specification levels: L1 (what to express), L2 (how to express), and L3 (how to instantiate), connecting high-level behavioral intent to concrete textual output. Using SteerEval, we systematically evaluate contemporary steering methods, revealing that control often degrades at finer-grained levels. Our benchmark offers a principled and interpretable framework for safe and controllable LLM behavior, serving as a foundation for future research.
evidence_items.title: How Controllable Are Large Language Models? A Unified Evaluation across Behavioral Granularities

evidence_items.summary: The rapid development of deepfake video technology has not only facilitated artistic creation but also made it easier to spread misinformation, which is increasingly difficult to identify. Traditional deepfake video detection (DVD) methods face issues such as a lack of transparency in their principles and insufficient generalization capabilities to cope with evolving forgery techniques. This highlights an urgent need for detectors that can identify forged content and provide verifiable reasoning explanations. This paper proposes the explainable deepfake video detection (EDVD) task and designs the EDVD-LLaMA multimodal, a large language model (MLLM) reasoning framework, which provides traceable reasoning processes alongside accurate detection results and trustworthy explanations. Our approach first incorporates a Spatio-Temporal Subtle Information Tokenization (ST-SIT) to extract and fuse global and local cross-frame deepfake features, providing rich spatio-temporal semantic information input for MLLM reasoning. Second, we construct a Fine-grained Multimodal Chain-of-Thought (Fg-MCoT) mechanism, which introduces facial feature data as hard constraints during the reasoning process to achieve pixel-level spatio-temporal video localization, suppress hallucinated outputs, and enhance the reliability of the chain of thought. In addition, we build an Explainable Reasoning FF++ benchmark dataset (ER-FF++set), leveraging structured data to annotate videos and ensure quality control, thereby supporting dual supervision for reasoning and detection. Extensive experiments demonstrate that EDVD-LLaMA achieves outstanding performance and robustness in terms of detection accuracy, explainability, and its ability to handle cross-forgery methods and cross-dataset scenarios. Compared to previous DVD methods, it provides a more explainable and superior solution.
evidence_items.title: EDVD-LLaMA: Explainable Deepfake Video Detection via Multimodal Large Language Model Reasoning

evidence_items.summary: Gemini Embedding v2 — Determinism Benchmark for Semantic Retrieval Determinism benchmark for semantic retrieval with gemini-embedding-2 (stable, GA 2026-04-22; replaces gemini-embedding-001), using the same methodology as the speedrunpapi exact-embeddings benchmark: exact SHA-256 match of embedding vectors across runs, same-bits invariance across batch sizes, identical cosine top-k rankings, Spearman vs human scores — plus a CUDA-Q kernel as a GPU-path control.… See the full description on the dataset page: https://huggingface.co/datasets/igorholt/gemini-embedding-v2-determinism-benchmark.

evidence_items.summary: An embodied speaker's expressiveness depends not only on what is said, but also on how the voice sounds and how the body moves. However, existing joint speech-motion generation models are largely driven implicitly by transcript semantics or intermediate speech representations, offering little explicit control over motion hierarchy, body parts, or vocal style. To bridge this gap, we construct MotionSpeech, a structured benchmark for controllable joint speech-motion generation that includes transcripts, voice-style descriptions, and motion conditions at two hierarchical levels. Building on this benchmark, we propose DuoFlow, a dual-stream latent flow transformer that jointly denoises speech and motion under a shared noise level and a unified second-based temporal coordinate. Modality-specific residual connectors inject structured conditions into the corresponding streams, layer-wise bidirectional cross-modal attention coordinates their generation, and a monotonic phoneme pathway combines normalized progress anchors with CTC supervision to strengthen speech temporal modeling. DuoFlow provides a unified interface for fine-grained motion and vocal-style control and demonstrates the ability to synthesize high-quality, synchronized, and instruction-consistent speech-motion sequences.
evidence_items.title: DuoFlow: Towards Synchronized Speech and Motion Generation with Fine-Grained Control

evidence_items.summary: A social robot has to keep track of the people around it over time to plan its motion, a task handled by 3D multi-object tracking. For the LiDAR modality, trackers usually sit on top of a detector and link its detections across frames with a separate motion model or re-identification network. We instead show how a 3D LiDAR detector itself can be turned into a tracker by adding an instance-level contrastive objective on its intermediate voxel features. Each embedding is read from the voxels inside a detected box, and boxes are matched across frames by cosine similarity and the Hungarian algorithm, without a motion model. The detector backbone is fine-tuned together with this objective, which learns identity-aware features while leaving detection accuracy essen- tially intact. Because the method uses only the voxel features that Li- DAR detectors already produce, it is backbone-agnostic. On the JRDB 3D tracking leaderboard our LiDAR-only tracker ranks first on HOTA (38.58) and IDF1 (37.99), 13.04 and 9.30 points above the next pub- lished method, and second on MOTA and OSPA. Code is available at https://hermak56.github.io/CLIFT/.
evidence_items.title: CLIFT: Contrastive LiDAR Instance Features for 3D Pedestrian Tracking

evidence_items.summary: The article examines the use of artificial intelligence (AI) in everyday research work, including searching for sources, translation, summarization, term extraction, editing, and abstract preparation. The material comprises publications on computational linguistics, language models, machine translation, literature reviews, academic writing, and the disclosure of AI use. The sources are compared by type of language operation, author’s role, risks, and methods for verifying the result. It is shown that such tools are useful for processing existing research material but do not replace the selection of a research topic, evaluation of sources, construction of arguments, or formulation of conclusions. To maintain research integrity, bibliographic records should be verified against external sources, summaries should be checked against the original texts, the author’s position should be preserved, and the AI tools used should be openly disclosed.

evidence_items.summary: In many long-horizon settings, an agent's own choices create future constraints: committing finite capacity establishes future obligations and forecloses later opportunities. Sustaining performance therefore requires both keeping evolving plans feasible and comparing the value of resource allocations with the alternatives they displace. Recent benchmarks increasingly evaluate LLM agents in continuing operations, but give less attention to how agents keep their own commitments feasible while reassessing resource allocations as opportunities change. We introduce OutfitterBench, where agents manage an outdoor-equipment rental business for 200 days, purchasing from a 46-product catalog and handling roughly 1,100 reservation requests. Under a fixed capital ceiling, reservations and uncertain walk-in demand compete for reusable equipment whose availability changes over time. Experiments with seven frontier LLMs show that several agents underperform a simple rule-based baseline, while only the leading agent consistently surpasses it. Trajectory analysis shows that some agents apply known constraints inconsistently and make new decisions that conflict with existing commitments. Agents with more reliable fulfillment can still secure low returns from comparable commitments or delay resource reallocation. The leading agent better connects preparation with economic choices but also misses opportunities for more profitable asset use. These findings highlight limitations in sustaining coherent resource plans and reassessing their value over time. The benchmark code is publicly available at https://github.com/adminblackjack/OutfitterBench.
evidence_items.title: OutfitterBench: Evaluating LLM Agents on Long-Horizon Resource Allocation and Commitment Coordination

evidence_items.summary: As AI conference submissions grow rapidly, AI reviewers are being considered as an alternative. However, simply imitating human reviewing is problematic because reviewing serves multiple purposes, including evaluating papers' soundness, interestingness, and clarity, the last two of which are subjective. In this work, we focus solely on evaluating soundness, the most important and objective criterion, and define the learning objective as jointly maximizing (1) precision, based on the soundness and substantiveness of review points, and (2) recall, the coverage of high-quality reference review points. Under this problem formulation, we construct a quality-labeled review point dataset, PaperSound-23K, using 1K ICLR submissions and 23K human-written and LLM-generated review points. Using this dataset, we train an AI reviewer model, PaperCritic, through reinforcement learning with the F1 score of precision and recall as the reward. Our experiments show that PaperCritic outperforms frontier models and models trained with other AI reviewer training methods on an in-domain test set. Surprisingly, learning to review ICLR submissions also transfers to reviewing Nature-family papers and even to out-of-domain reviewing tasks (e.g., code review, legal contract review, and feedback on story writing).
evidence_items.title: PaperCritic: Training AI Reviewers to Assess the Soundness of Papers

evidence_items.summary: Web agents powered by large language and vision-language models are increasingly applied to realistic browser work that spans heterogeneous applications, multimodal content, and stateful workflows. However, existing reproducible web-agent benchmarks cover only a small number of web applications drawn from a few software categories, and restrict modality to text and vision. Live benchmarks broaden site coverage but sacrifice reproducibility, since pages and data drift between runs. Moreover, existing benchmarks do not meaningfully evaluate whether agents can understand and use audio and video content embedded within web tasks. To address these gaps, we introduce WebArena-Pro, a benchmark comprising 300 tasks across 20 self-hosted web applications in six domain categories, spanning distinct interface conventions, workflows, and data models. Across the evaluated agents, the best performance is achieved by both Codex with GPT 6.1 Sol and Claude Code with Claude Opus 5.5 at 62.3%, followed by OpenCode with Kimi 3.1 Pro at 60.7%. The strongest GenericAgent configurations, Gemini 3.1 Pro omni and Gemma4 31B, both achieve 30.3%. Among reproducible, human-curated web agent benchmarks, WebArena-Pro provides the broadest application coverage and the most comprehensive multimodal support to date. The benchmark treats audio and video as core observations alongside text and vision, with dedicated actions for extracting information from each. WebArena-Pro runs each task in isolation and supports reproducible, parallel evaluation. Tasks are authored through a dedicated annotator interface, filtered by LLM-assisted triage, and finally validated by humans before release. Project page: https://webarena-pro.github.io
evidence_items.title: WebArena-Pro: A Heterogeneous, Multimodal, Reproducible Benchmark for Web Agents

evidence_items.summary: With the rapid advancement of Large Language Models (LLMs), an increasing number of users are turning to LLM-powered agents for conversational shopping in e-commerce. However, the user needs continue to change as new product categories, procurement scenarios, and feature requests emerge. At the same time, the product's execution harness-including its tools, skills, and operating procedures-continues to evolve to support increasingly sophisticated interactions. These changes create two practical challenges: 1) Demand drift alters the distribution, intent, and complexity of user requests, causing a model trained once to fall behind; 2) Harness evolution requires the model to use newly introduced capabilities correctly without losing behavior that users already rely on. Periodic manual retraining is too delayed and labor-intensive for this setting. To address these challenges, we present G-CAST, a governed continual self-training system that converts daily production evidence under evolving demand and capability contracts into reward-routed, entropy-prioritized training data and governed reward evolution. Governed checkpoint transition under cumulative evaluation controls each model update, enabling the agent to learn newly introduced behaviors without sacrificing previously accepted capabilities. Experiments on a real production e-commerce agent show that G-CAST achieves stronger adaptation to newly introduced demand while better preserving previously accepted behavior compared with a strong autonomous post-training baseline. Ablations further show that both reward-routed, entropy-prioritized data orchestration and governed reward evolution are important to these gains. G-CAST is now deployed in Yuancai(http://cai.1688.com/), a B2B procurement agent on Alibaba's 1688 platform.
evidence_items.title: G-CAST: Governed Continual Self-Training for E-Commerce Agents under Evolving Demands

evidence_items.summary: Underwater image enhancement is challenging to evaluate due to the lack of clean reference images, so researchers rely on no-reference image quality assessment (NR-IQA) metrics. However, it remains unclear whether these metrics agree with human judgments. We evaluate 73 handcrafted underwater, learned underwater, vision-language and general-purpose metrics against human preferences on five references: four published opinion-score sets and a new paired-comparison study. For each metric, we measure how often it selects the same image as people when comparing versions of the same scene. We further test whether simple image edits and small adversarial perturbations raise metric scores above the enhancement people preferred, and whether scores decrease as repeated generative edits add noise. Our results show that no metric consistently matches human preferences. The best worst-case Cohen's kappa over the five references is only 0.23 (Q-Align), while two raters in our study agree with a median kappa of 0.41. The widely used UCIQE often favors edits that people reject. On a Nano Banana Pro replica chain that should leave the image unchanged, only 22 of 73 scores decrease at every checkpoint, while noise grows by 2.5 times. We also introduce TrustUIQA, a benchmark that combines the human references, our study choices, the edited, attacked and generated images, and the scores of every metric on every image. The code is available at https://github.com/TrustUIQA/TrustUIQA and TrustUIQA at https://huggingface.co/datasets/TrustUIQA/TrustUIQA.
evidence_items.title: Do Underwater Image Quality Metrics Agree with Human Perception? A Benchmark with Human Choices, Simple Edits and Generative Drift

evidence_items.summary: Open driving releases and usage-based insurance programs often claim to prevent privacy breaches by omitting GPS records when sharing or collecting vehicle data. However, removing GPS coordinates from driving logs does not erase the location information carried by vehicle signals. While prior route-inference attacks have demonstrated that speed, steering, and driving events can be matched to road networks to reconstruct trajectories, existing studies rely on inconsistent prior assumptions and evaluation metrics and are tested only on small, restricted datasets, making their results difficult to compare and their real-world effectiveness uncertain. We release CANTraj, a naturalistic driving dataset pairing decoded CAN events with time-aligned GNSS trajectories (3,940 drives, 454 drivers), and CANTraj-Bench for evaluating trajectory recovery (3,675 drives, 431 drivers, 1,380 hours, 85,919 km). On 776 evaluation drives from 94 unseen drivers, we compare six re-implemented attacks and benchmark baselines under explicit information-access protocols, paired comparisons, and metrics incorporating failures. Experiments show that combining steering signals with road-network constraints yields the largest gain: With a known start and heading, adding steering to speed raises the online map filter's five-minute route recovery from 56% to 87%, with a median average displacement error of 43 m versus 921 m for map-free dead reckoning. Offline beam search recovers 88% of test routes with the heading and 81% without it. Because methods fail on different windows, we also evaluate an LLM harness that selects among candidate routes on 659 five-minute windows; its best configuration recovers 79% of routes on test and 83% on few-shot, outperforming the best baseline on test and matching it on few-shot. Data and code at huggingface.co/datasets/HenryYHW/CANTraj and github.com/WangYuHang-cmd/GPS--CAN.
evidence_items.title: CANTraj: Recovering Vehicle Trajectories from CAN Signals in Naturalistic Driving

evidence_items.summary: Text-to-SQL systems translate natural language questions into SQL queries over increasingly complex databases. However, widely used benchmarks evaluate questions independently, overlooking settings where earlier queries over the same database can supply joins or calculations for a new question. We introduce HARE (History-AwaRe Text-to-SQL BEnchmark) to measure the accuracy and cost of adapting historical SQL. HARE comprises 1,600 requests derived from a fixed pool of 823 verified queries across four datasets. Annotations record which components each request preserves and which edits it requires, distinguishing whole-query adaptation from partial reuse. Our method, MEM-SQL (Memory-EMpowered Text-to-SQL), stores whole-query templates, reusable SQL blocks, and mappings from domain concepts to schema elements. MEM-SQL uses a layer only if every requirement assigned to it has a match above that layer's threshold. With On-demand Schema Linking (OSL), MEM-SQL consults the schema only when no layer qualifies or the generator judges retrieved evidence insufficient. Across six language models on HARE, mean execution accuracy rises from 37.1% for Direct Generation without history to 50.0% for MEM-SQL, with 76.6% fewer input tokens and 68.8% lower latency on average. Further analysis shows that requests reusing several verified queries remain a bottleneck, with accuracy falling from 56.7% to 29.7%, most sharply when reused components must be placed in a new query structure or combined with a shared join. Applying OSL to three other memory designs consistently reduces generation cost, while its accuracy benefit depends on the memory design. Verified history can thus make generation both more accurate and cheaper, but its value depends on the evidence retained and when the system consults the schema.
evidence_items.title: MEM-SQL: Memory-Empowered Text-to-SQL

evidence_items.summary: The release of GPT-6 Astra marks the emergence of a new paradigm in robotics: agentic robotics. Within weeks, frontier models with agentic harnesses matched or exceeded task-specific policies on many embodied benchmarks. Instead of training a dedicated policy for each family of tasks, an agentic robotic system applies a foundation model to open-world embodied tasks. It operates in a closed loop: observing the environment, interpreting user intent, reasoning about the task, invoking skills and tools, verifying outcomes, and adapting its strategy. Despite these advances, the community has yet to converge on a shared definition, a reliable evaluation framework, or a research roadmap. We argue that Embodied System 2, realized by a foundation model together with an embodied harness, forms the decision-making core of agentic robotics. Its central challenge is to translate general-purpose reasoning into effective and verifiable actions under physical constraints such as limited reaction time, mechanical limits, unpredictable environment changes, and irreversible consequences. Motivated by this perspective, we propose an evaluation framework that measures both model capabilities and closed-loop system performance. Furthermore, we identify the principles that carry over from digital to physical agents and the challenges that must be addressed to achieve reliable physical autonomy. On top of the Embodied System 2 and the evaluation framework, we envision a research roadmap toward sustained autonomy: the ability to perform work safely and reliably with progressively broader responsibility, from executing individual primitives to fulfilling standing roles.
evidence_items.title: Envisioning Agentic Robotics: A New Era of Robotic Systems

evidence_items.summary: Efficient batch execution of agent tasks is critical to LLM training and development workflows, including benchmark evaluation, synthetic-data generation, and RL rollouts. Since these tasks alternate between LLM inference and environment interaction, we present coordinated optimizations to reduce batch makespan, the time required to complete all tasks in a batch. For hybrid LLMs, a workload-based resource model guides GPU-memory allocation between key-value (KV) cache and recurrent state and provides a reference sample concurrency to exploit parallelism while limiting recomputation. Trajectory-aware routing and scheduling promote cache reuse while balancing worker load. Under constrained environment capacity, we decouple sample admission from environment execution and introduce Chain-Advancing Action Scheduling (CAAS), which prioritizes long chains using observed progress to shorten the batch tail. Controlled replay combines actual inference with recorded environment responses and durations for ablations of individual optimizations. Live evaluations with Ling-3.0-Flash and Ling-3.1-Flash on the BFCL, SWE-bench Multilingual, WideSearch, and MCP-Atlas benchmarks demonstrate makespan reductions of 10.4% to 65.0%, while evaluation scores remain aligned. Furthermore, these methods have been successfully applied to training and evaluation workflows for the Ling-3.x model series, accelerating the model-development cycle.
evidence_items.title: Reducing Batch Makespan for LLM Agent Workloads through Inference-Environment Coordination

evidence_items.summary: We present EvenVLM, the first text and multimodal (VQA) dataset for Even (Lamut), an endangered Northern Tungusic language spoken by approximately 6,800 people in Siberia. Our dataset comprises 50,521 structured Even-Russian entries extracted from dictionary and phrasebook sources via GPT-4o Mini-based parsing, from which we synthetically generate 107,543 training examples spanning translation, grammar, reading comprehension, and semantic classification. To address tokenization inefficiency on Even's agglutinative morphology, we propose a three-step tokenizer expansion algorithm that adds Even-specific graphemes (eng, oe, o-umlaut), whitelisted vocabulary, and BPE merges, reducing average tokens per word by 27% (4.99 to 3.64). Using LoRA fine-tuning of Qwen3-VL-4B, we adapt the model for text tasks (0.53% trainable parameters, rank 32) and separately for visual question answering (rank 64, frozen vision encoder). Our best configuration achieves 11.4% exact match and a 13.6 weighted score on text benchmarks, 0.1283 chrF for sentence translation, and 65% accuracy on VQA (up from 0% for the base model and text-only fine-tuning). We release our datasets, evaluation benchmarks, and training pipeline to support further research on Even and other low-resource languages.
evidence_items.title: EvenVLM: A Text and Multimodal Dataset for the Even Language with Vision-Language Fine-Tuning

evidence_items.summary: Controllable real-world video generation models can condition on a rendered graybox proxy video, which fixes layout, motion and camera. Coding agents can build such videos by reconstructing a 4D scene in Blender, yet no benchmark checks both these videos and the long, multi-shot scenes behind them. We introduce VibePrevisBench, a benchmark for 4D scene reconstruction: an agent turns a brief into an executable 4D scene and renders its proxy video. Its 242 tasks span four input kinds, including scripts, photos, continuations, and reference videos. Each delivery is scored along two evaluation dimensions. Rule-based Scene Check re-runs the code and compares the exported 4D scene with hidden ground truth facts in nine dimensions. VLM-based Screen Check asks a VLM judge whether the facts that pass can be recognized in the proxy video. We analyze the evaluation results and trajectories of 11 frontier coding agents and identify three key observations. First, multimodal understanding separates the agents, especially in understanding space and camera motion. Second, all agents seem to already master basic camera work and staging, and fail at challenging requests. Third, agents inspect their own renders but fail to correct their errors. Agents thus need better visual understanding of space and camera, explicit checks for challenging requests, and item-by-item verification of renders against the brief.

evidence_items.summary: This review develops a mathematically structured account of topological data analysis (TDA), focusing on persistent homology and its applications to machine learning and large language model (LLM) analysis. It systematically introduces the fundamental concepts of metric and topological spaces, simplicial complexes, chain complexes and homology, filtrations, persistence modules, persistence diagrams, and stability results. Particular attention is given to the mathematical properties of Vietoris–Rips and Čech complexes, the interpretation of homology groups, and methods for comparing persistence diagrams. Applications to neural networks and LLMs are examined through geometric filtrations of embedding and activation spaces, attention-derived complexes, and zigzag persistence across transformer layers. Recent studies are critically compared in terms of their topological constructions, analyzed models and datasets, evaluation protocols, empirical findings, and computational limitations. Particular attention is given to the analysis of representation dynamics, model alignment, and hallucination detection, while distinguishing experimentally validated approaches from proposed mathematical extensions. The review also examines the influence of metric selection and filtration parameters, the computational challenges associated with large point clouds and higher-dimensional homology, and the limitations of interpreting topological characteristics in linguistic and semantic terms. Potential mathematical directions, including multiparameter persistence and functorial analysis of representations, are also discussed. The main contribution of this review is a critical mathematical synthesis connecting the theoretical foundations of persistent homology with recent developments in LLM analysis.
evidence_items.title: Mathematical Foundations of Topological Data Analysis and Its Applications to Machine Learning and Large Language Model Analysis
